presentations.presentation_title: Seismic Precursory Process Transitions during a Plinian Eruption: A Case Study from the 2014 Kelud Eruption
presentations.abstract: This study investigates precursory characteristics associated with Plinian eruptions at Kelud volcano, Indonesia, and examines the implications of these findings for forecasting future large-scale explosive eruptions at other volcanoes, with emphasis on Sakurajima. The 2014 Kelud eruption was preceded by a sequence of precursory phenomena, such as increased gas emissions and ground inflation from December 2013. Immediately before the eruption, seismicity became dense, evolving into continuous tremor-like waveforms. To address this complexity, seismic energy partitioning was performed using high-frequency (HF) and low-frequency (LF) bands. Cumulative of LF seismic energy was subsequently used as input for the Failure Forecast Method (FFM).Spectral analysis of VT earthquakes revealed systematic temporal changes in source parameters. Seismic moment increased sharply on 13 February, rupture length gradually decreased from 9 February onward, and stress drop showed progressive acceleration culminating on the eruption day. Cumulative seismic energy curves exhibited contrasting behaviors: HF energy accelerated earlier (9 February), whereas LF energy showed abrupt acceleration on the eruption day, with LF energy density dominating immediately prior to eruption, indicating intensified fluid-related processes. FFM analyses applied to four successive periods yielded eruption time predictions with progressively shorter lead times, culminating in a prediction within minutes of the actual eruption onset. These results indicate that FFM performance systematically improves as the eruption approaches.A conceptual eruption process model derived from the 2014 Kelud eruption identifies transferable features of Plinian activity. The early stage is marked by rapidly increasing VT seismicity and ground deformation, interpreted as magma intrusion into the brittle crust generating high-frequency signals. This is followed by a stage dominated by accelerated LF seismicity, reflecting increased volatile content and enhanced gas exsolution. The final stage involves rapid decompression, which promotes accelerated gas release and ultimately triggers the Plinian eruption, providing a framework applicable to understanding precursory dynamics at similar volcanoes.

presentations.presentation_title: An Attempt to Estimate the Eruption Timing of Submarine Volcanoes Using the Paleomagnetic Field Intensity Record
presentations.abstract: Determining the absolute age of submarine volcanoes erupted within the last 100,000 years is generally difficult. Since paleomagnetic field intensities (paleointensities) are characteristic of a specific time period, combining paleointensity data with geomagnetic models has strong potential for dating submarine volcanic eruptions. However, a robust method for determining paleointensity from whole-rock mid-ocean ridge basalts has not yet been fully established. We conducted paleointensity and rock magnetic experiments on whole-rock basalt samples collected from a conical cone located on the spreading axis of the Central Indian Ridge. All samples were collected in 2006 by the manned submersible Shinkai 6500 during R/V Yokosuka YK05-16 expedition. The site-mean paleointensities of 33.0 ± 1.0 μT and 35.8 ± 1.7 μT suggest that the lavas erupted within a short period of less than 200 years. A suite of rock magnetic parameters was measured; Accepted samples exhibited higher Curie temperatures, lower remanent magnetization, higher ratios of saturated remanent magnetization to saturation magnetization (Mrs/Ms), and contributions from magnetically harder minerals compared to rejected samples. These results indicate that rock magnetic pre-selection is effective in improving paleointensity acceptance rate. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations show that rejected samples commonly contain skeletal titanomagnetite grains approximately 5–10 µm in size, implying cooling conditions different from those of accepted samples. Comparison of the site-mean paleointensity with the International Geomagnetic Reference Field Model (IGRF-13) (Alken et al., 2021, EPS), and the gufm1 model (Jackson et al., 2000, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London.) constrains the eruption age to be older than 1590CE. Furthermore, comparing paleointensity curves derived from the BIGMUDI4k.1 (Arneitz et al., 2019, PEPI) and ArchKalmag14k.r (Schanner et al., 2022, JGR Solid Earth) geomagnetic field models reveal overlapping solutions for two candidate eruption periods of 7575–1675 BCE and 25–1590 CE.

presentations.presentation_title: Relationship Between Ballistic Projectile Ejection Velocity and Infrasound Pulse Accompanying Vulcanian Eruptions
presentations.abstract: Ballistic projectiles from Vulcanian eruptions are among the main hazards of active volcanoes worldwide, with meter-sized ejected blocks reaching up to several km from the vent. For those larger blocks, the ejection velocity is a dominant factor in determining the maximum reach distance and the hazard area. We examine the relationship between the ejection velocity of ballistic projectiles (V max ) and the infrasound signals, both originating from explosions. Target events are eruption sequences at Sakurajima and Suwanosejima volcanoes in Japan. Our infrasound records show that the peak amplitude and pulse width of the pressure pulses accompanying explosions correspond to the V max intensity. The features represent that the overpressure P 0 at the shallow conduit gas pocket and syn-explosion volatile emission contribute to V max . To take both waveform features into account, we introduce a peak amplitude of the time-integrated infrasound pulse as I max , considering the geometrical decay of infrasound amplitude. By examining 2560 events at Sakurajima and Suwanosejima, we obtained the relation V max = 40I max 0.116 , which constrains the maximum V max range as a function of I max . Based on our considerations with theoretical ballistic launching models, we inferred another relation of V max =3.40P 0 0.255 behind the above V max -I max relation. The V max -P 0 indicates that V max increases with both P 0 and the amount of volatile emission, consistent with observed infrasound waveform characteristics. We further investigate a V max /V max ’ ratio sequence along with eruptive activity, where V max ’ is the expected maximum V max value with 40I max 0.116 . The ratio has relatively higher values at the beginning and later phases of eruptive episodes. The above sequence can represent volatile emissions being dominant in the following two scenarios: fed by the magma chamber under relatively volatile-rich conditions at the beginning of the eruptive episode, and syn-explosion volatile emission increasing due to decreasing conduit permeability during the later eruptive phase.

presentations.presentation_title: Paleomagnetic Estimation on the Timescale for the Eruptive Sequence of the 45 Ka Shikotsu Caldera‑forming Eruption
presentations.abstract: Our new paleomagnetic data provide the timescale for the eruptive sequence of the 45 ka Shikotsu caldera-forming eruption of VEI 7. The duration of the entire sequence is estimated to be centuries, which is considerably longer than previously thought. The studied volcanic sequence, located at ~10 km from the caldera rim, includes five units of pyroclastic flow deposits and an uppermost pyroclastic surge deposit. The ash matrix samples of the pyroclastic deposits, predominantly composed of juvenile material, were collected into aluminum and plastic cubes, which were precisely oriented using an originally designed tool set. These paleomagnetic directions determined from the sequence of the six units demonstrate a curve of paleomagnetic secular variation, which has a total angular distance of 14.4 ± 4.1 degree. The observed distinguishable paleomagnetic directions indicate that the earlier four units were formed by four distinct eruptions over a period of 240 ± 70 years with repose times of decades between the eruptions. The indistinguishable paleomagnetic directions indicate that the three late-stage units were erupted in a short period, decades or less. Our new paleomagnetic data, combined with the reported petrological change in pumice, suggest that the extractions of crystal-poor rhyolitic melt from the magma chamber occurred in multiple eruptions over a considerable period (> 100 years).

presentations.presentation_title: Thermal Evolution Modeling of Magma Chamber Formation Considering Eruptive Heat Loss
presentations.abstract: The rapid assembly of large-scale magma bodies prior to eruption is a key focus in volcanology (e.g., Takahashi, 2025). While magma supply drives reservoir growth, eruptions provide significant thermal feedback by rapidly removing heat. We have investigated the long-term growth of large magma chambers by developing a numerical model that integrates: (1) varying short-term and long-term magma supply rates, (2) host-rock rheological controls on eruption timing, and (3) heat loss associated with eruptive events.We extended the incremental sill intrusion model (Annen, 2009) to include eruptive heat removal. Eruption triggers are defined by the accumulation of overpressure from intrusions, balanced against the viscoelastic relaxation of the host rock and crystal mush. Thermophysical properties, including temperature-dependent melt fraction and latent heat, were calibrated for subduction zone environments.In our simulations, 100-m thick andesitic sills (volumes: 1.96 to 31.4 km 3 ) were intruded at the crustal boundary (10 km depth) over 1 million years. We adjusted the long-term supply rate Q long and the short-term rate Q short , testing Q short /Q long ratios from 1 to 5000. Eruptions occurred when the overpressure exceeded 10 MPa and the volume ratio of eruptible magma (melt fraction >0.6) to the total magma is larger than 0.1.The results are categorized into three evolutionary paths: (i) sustained eruptive activity, (ii) eventual cessation of eruptions despite continued intrusion, and (iii) no eruption occurrence. This modeling framework quantifies how the interplay between magmatic flux and eruptive cooling determines the ultimate scale and lifespans of trans-crustal magmatic systems.Using natural supply rates, the model's eruption volumes <10km 3 are 1.5 orders of magnitude smaller than observed, likely because it ignores processes like volatile exsolution or roof collapse. However, it successfully reproduces magma accumulations comparable to large caldera eruptions, suggesting the framework can effectively constrain both long-term and short-term supply rates.

presentations.presentation_title: The Bound Growth of Induced Earthquakes Could De-risk Hydraulic Fracturing
presentations.abstract: The world's energy supply depends critically on hydraulic fracturing (HF) to access otherwise uneconomical resources. Unfortunately, HF also has the potential to induce larger earthquakes – with some projects being prematurely terminated because of perceived earthquake risks. To de-risk HF, we use a suite of statistical tests to discern if some physical process has restricted the growth of earthquake magnitudes. We show that all stage stimulations at both UK PNR-1z and Helsinki St1 indicate bound fracture growth, implying a more controllable operation. Contrastingly, stimulations at Utah FORGE and UK PNR-2 sequentially transitioned into unbound fault reactivation. The problematic stages (that ultimately led to the termination of PNR-2) are clearly distinguishable. We postulate that our research can discriminate fracture stimulation from fault reactivation, contributing to the de-risking of HF operations worldwide. Our statistical tests provide a framework for model falsification, which can guide physical insights into the bounding processes.

presentations.presentation_title: Poroelastic Stress Transfer and Seismic Zoning at the Geysers Geothermal Field
presentations.abstract: Fluid extraction and injection associated with geothermal energy production perturb megapascal-scale crustal stress. Although they have been proven to result in seismic ruptures, fault-scale seismic response remains poorly constrained in the surrounding areas. The Geysers geothermal field in California has been operating since 1960 for over 66 years, extracting 2.5x10 7 m³/yr of fluid on average. Such volume loss has been shrinking the shallow crust and triggering poroelastic stress changes at and around the reservoir. These stress changes then impact the nearby faults. The Geysers is hosted within the Franciscan Subduction Complex and is structurally controlled by a dense fault network associated with the San Andreas fault system, primarily including the Maacama and Bartlett Springs fault zones, as well as numerous subsidiary strike-slip and extensional structures. Unevenly distributed seismicity around the geothermal field reveals the non-trivial stressing mechanisms amid production or injection processes. The analysis focuses on the co-production period spanning 2017–2025, constrained by Sentinel-1 observations. The velocity fields estimated through Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) indicate localized maximum subsidence >10 mm/yr within the central production area, consistently observed in both ascending and descending viewing geometries. Poroelastic finite element models (FEMs) driven by geothermal production and injection histories are used to simulate the spatiotemporal evolution of reservoir pore pressure, stress tensor, and surface deformation associated with geothermal fluid extraction. Modeled deformation patterns and stress changes are evaluated against observed deformation fields, while InSAR observations are additionally used to estimate fault creep along selected structures. The observed seismic zoning at Geysers is investigated by accounting for and projecting poroelastic stress changes onto the geometry of Maacama and North Roger Creek faults. Overall, this study will provide important insights into fault stability and seismic hazard, helping the community to assess the seismic hazard and strive for a safer community.

presentations.presentation_title: Pre-existing Structures and Stress Variations Jointly Control the Induced Seismicity in the Enhanced Geothermal System of Gonghe Basin, China
presentations.institution: Sourthern university of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Integrating microseismic observations with borehole logging constraints from China’s first EGS demonstration project in the Gonghe Basin, we investigate the multiscale seismic response to stimulation under complex fault architecture and heterogeneous stress conditions. We compiled a high-resolution catalog for the 2021 stimulation and circulation campaign (7,346 events; M L −2.0 to 2.18) and identified distinct earthquake clusters that delineate structurally controlled seismicity consistent with pre-existing faults of diverse orientations (strike/dip). We resolved 173 focal mechanisms for M L ≥ 0.5 events, indicating reverse and strike-slip faulting as the primary styles. Stress inversion yields a well-constrained NE–SW SHmax orientation consistent with the regional stress field. Using focal-mechanism-based calibration of stress magnitudes, we estimate an unusually low effective friction coefficient, μ ≈ 0.23 (95% confidence interval: 0.19–0.48), which may reflect weak mineral phases (e.g., chlorite). Overpressure estimates indicate that ~63% of events required ≥10 MPa of excess pore pressure for fault reactivation, implying that moderate pressure perturbations can promote slip within a subcritical, weak-fault system. Overall, these observations suggest that seismicity patterns at the ~1 km scale are governed by near-critical stress conditions and mechanically weak faults, allowing injection-induced pressure changes to trigger slip even on unfavorably oriented structures. In contrast, at the near-well (~1–100 m) scale, acoustic image logs show a stable mean SHmax direction but reveal strong depth-localized rotations. Depth-domain correlation analysis further indicates that near-well seismicity peaks within specific depth intervals and aligns more closely with these stress-rotation horizons than with maxima in conductive-fracture density.

presentations.presentation_title: Rupture Cascade Initiated by Wastewater Disposal: Nucleation and Domino Effect of Canada’s Largest Induced Earthquake
presentations.abstract: In late November 2022, an M L 5.6 earthquake (mainshock) occurred near Peace River, Alberta, Canada, followed by two M L 4.8+ events in mid-March 2023. Previous studies linked these sequences to local disposal activities based on regional seismic networks that were poorly instrumented near the epicenters. In early December 2022, a local seismic array was deployed surrounding the mainshock for high-resolution monitoring of seismicity. By integrating the array data with key analyses, this study presents a coherent narrative of how wastewater disposal destabilized basement structures and triggered multiple kilometer‐scale ruptures. Using the array data, we identify two seismicity clusters flanking the foreshock-mainshock sequence: a northwestern NE-SW-trending cluster and a southeastern NW-SE-trending cluster that includes the March 2023 M L 4.8+ events. These two clusters form T-shaped swarms governed by strike-slip and reverse-slip faulting, respectively. Their spatial distributions and focal mechanisms delineate a NW-SE-striking, NE-dipping basement fault truncated by a conjugate boundary to the NW. Most events are located within the basement, while a subset of swarms lies in the basal reef formation and is spatially connected to a nearby well with over 10-year injection history. This hydraulic connection is supported by numerical simulations of subsurface pore-pressure evolution: injection at this reef-targeted well likely transmitted >0.01-MPa pressure into the fault. Instead, fluids injected into shallower units were isolated from the basement by overlying shale sequences. Coulomb stress modeling further reveals pervasive earthquake interaction following mainshock nucleation. The three largest events impose stress increases exceeding 0.025 MPa on southeastern neighboring faults, indicating direct triggering of the March 2023 earthquakes. Overall, the earthquake sequences likely reflect a rupture cascade initiated by wastewater disposal and sustained by fault interaction. Nearby disposal into the reef formation nucleated the mainshock in November 2022; this mainshock further triggered two moderate events in March 2023.

presentations.presentation_title: Strategic Monitoring and Research Initiatives for Volcanic Hazards of Mt. Baekdu: the Role of the Volcano Specialized Research Center (VSRC), South Korea
presentations.abstract: Mt. Baekdu, situated on the border between North Korea and China, represents the most significant volcanic threat to the Korean Peninsula and East Asia. This risk is underscored by its historical "Millennium Eruption," which reached a Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) of 7 in 946 AD, and more recent volcanic unrest observed between 2002 and 2005. Following the global impact of the 2010 Icelandic eruption, the South Korean government initiated comprehensive R&D projects to mitigate potential volcanic hazards. Central to these efforts was the establishment of the Volcano Specialized Research Center (VSRC) by the Korea Meteorological Administration in 2018. The VSRC focuses on identifying volcanic precursors and monitoring surface deformation through long-term collaborative research with China, utilizing advanced geodetic and geochemical techniques such as Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), Electronic Distance Measurement (EDM), and hot spring gas and water analysis. Additionally, the VSRC develops volcano monitoring and hazard mapping techniques while fostering domestic interest in volcanology through the publication of government reports and public newsletters. Furthermore, as a core member of the Asian Consortium of Volcanology (ACV), the VSRC aims to enhance national monitoring capabilities and ensure a robust, collective response to future volcanic activity in East Asia. Acknowledgments; This work was funded by the Korea Meteorological Administration Research and Development Program under Grant KMI2018-02710.

presentations.presentation_title: Flank Instability of Mauna Loa Volcano, Hawai‘i, Modulated by Magma Intrusion and Eruption
presentations.abstract: Mauna Loa, largest volcano on earth, erupted in 2022 for the first time in 38 years. The volcano’s structure consists of a summit caldera, two rift zones, and a basal décollement located approximately 10 km below sea level. Previous studies have identified continuous seaward shear slip on the southeastern décollement, which drives flank instability and interacts with magma intrusion (Varugu and Amelung, 2021). In this study, we modeled ground deformation before and after the 2022 eruption using GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) data to determine how the eruption influenced this instability.We employed a model consisting of a spherical source, a dike, and a shear dislocation on the décollement. Modeling results indicate that the depths of the spherical source and dike became significantly shallower after the eruption. Notably, the slip rate of the décollement decreased drastically from approximately 34.0 cm/yr before the eruption to 3.59 cm/yr immediately after, indicating a near-cessation of the slip.To investigate the cause of this cessation, we calculated the Coulomb stress change on the décollement caused by the eruption. The analysis yielded a negative Coulomb stress change of approximately -0.067 MPa, suggesting that the eruption mechanically suppressed the décollement slip. This interpretation is further supported by a significant decrease in seismic activity around the décollement. Subsequent analysis revealed that the décollement slip resumed around 2024, with the slip rate recovering to approximately 27.4 cm/yr. This resumption correlates with positive Coulomb stress changes induced by subsequent magma intrusions. These findings demonstrate that the behavior of the décollement is controlled by the balance between the negative stress change caused by the eruption and the positive stress changes from later magma intrusions.

presentations.presentation_title: Quantifying Pyroclastic Flow Hazard Assessment Using Insights from Lava Flow Modeling: Application to Shinmoedake Volcano
presentations.institution: National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience
presentations.abstract: Lava dome collapse–type pyroclastic flows are hazardous phenomena that can occur suddenly with little or no clear precursory signals. Although numerous numerical studies have investigated their dynamics, key characteristics such as runout distance and impact area strongly depend on the prescribed source conditions, making quantitative hazard assessment challenging. In this study, we propose a method to constrain the source conditions of dome collapse–type pyroclastic flows by incorporating insights from lava flow modeling. We apply this approach to Shinmoedake volcano, where future eruptions may involve lava overflow from the crater followed by pyroclastic flows. The lava flow is simulated using a depth-averaged Bingham fluid model with rheological parameters (viscosity and yield strength) calibrated to reproduce the 2018 effusive eruption at Shinmoedake. This framework enables accurate estimation of the spatial distribution and thickness of the lava flow. The modeled thickness and elevation at the lava-flow front are then used to provide physically based constraints on the source conditions for subsequent pyroclastic flow simulations. The pyroclastic flows are simulated using the depth-averaged dense granular gravity current model, faSavageHutterFoam. The results indicate that higher lava yield strength produces thicker lava accumulations, resulting in larger collapse volumes and longer pyroclastic flow runout distances. Furthermore, increased yield strength elevates the lava-flow front (i.e., the pyroclastic flow source location), promoting more efficient runout due to slopes that exceed the basal friction angle. This methodology for constraining source conditions is also applicable to simplified approaches such as the energy cone model and may contribute to the standardization of quantitative pyroclastic flow hazard assessment.

presentations.presentation_title: Testing Monitoring Methods for Island and Submarine Volcanoes in the Southwest Pacific
presentations.abstract: Operating a dense monitoring network is difficult on remote islands or submarine volcanoes. We are developing and testing new monitoring tools to improve the situation. Here, we report four challenges. [1] We tested seafloor seismic observation using Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) on the Tonga domestic cable. The first was for a week in February 2023, and the second was from August to December 2025. We identified many volcanic-like small earthquakes.[2] We conducted satellite thermal monitoring using a real-time volcano observation system (RealVOLC) and its extension, both operated at the University of Tokyo. We conducted feasibility studies to compare the performance of eruption detection using satellite and local monitoring data.[3] A compact and mobile observation package was developed for rapid installation. We installed the package in about an hour of on-site work. Then, the information (e.g., seismic waveforms and spectra) was shown on the prescribed website every 10 minutes. We are improving its operational stability and developing other packages with lower power consumption.[4] Effective data analysis methods using a limited number of stations are essential for monitoring oceanic volcanic. We developed seismo-acoustic signal detection methods and applied them to capture the sequence of the giant eruption of the Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha’apai volcano on January 15, 2022, using data recorded in Fiji. This study is a part of the SATREPS Project for Disaster Risk Reduction of Widespread Volcanic Hazards in Southwest Pacific Countries, funded by JICA and JST.

presentations.presentation_title: Publishing Collaborative and International Volcanology
presentations.abstract: Volcanoes do not care about borders. This point is reflected in the increasingly international and collaborative nature of volcanology as a discipline, studied using bibliometric data. Research published in volcanology-specific venues (Journal of Volcanology and Geothermal Research, Bulletin of Volcanology, Journal of Applied Volcanology, Volcanica) demonstrate a progressive rise in the percentage of international collaboration over the timeframe investigated (1999–2022), from around 30% in 1999 to averages of around 60% over 2020­–2022. This is notably higher than generalist journals such as Nature and Science. In recent years, the open access journal Volcanica has implemented a number of language-related initiatives aimed at improving accessibility of research. These include the possibility to include additional abstracts in languages other than English, and a fully bilingual special issue. Second-language abstracts have proven popular with authors, allowing research to be showcased in French, German, Icelandic, Persian, and Turkish, among other languages. Moreover, the bilingual special issue, which included the simultaneous publication of translated works, affords a unique look at article access by readers solely as a function of language. For the majority of items in the special issue (which included Reports articles, a preface, and an editorial), the Spanish-language version was downloaded more often than the English-language counterpart. In general, we note that Spanish-language versions of these articles are persistently accessed more frequently than the English-language equivalents, suggesting that research is making its way to the community for whom it is most useful while still being accessible by international collaborators. Is this a viable option for other article types, other languages, and other volcanic regions? The possibility of simultaneous publication of research in multiple languages may be a step towards better valorising the contribution of volcanologists around the world as well as facilitating both the local and global objectives and application of volcanological research.

presentations.presentation_title: Triggering of Two M5 Earthquakes in the Weiyuan Shale Gas Field, China
presentations.institution: Shenzhen Research Institute, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
presentations.abstract: Understanding how hydraulic fracturing triggers earthquakes—particularly rare but destructive events—is critical for mitigating induced-earthquake hazards. Here, we document a clear transition from fault quiescence to mechanical chaos preceding two M L ≥ 5 earthquakes (ML 5.6 in September and M L 5.4 in December 2019) in the Weiyuan shale gas field, China, where hydraulic fracturing targeted the Silurian Longmaxi Formation (Shale strata I).From 2015 to early 2018, extensive hydraulic fracturing was conducted at multiple well pads surrounding the target fault zone. During this phase, the fault zone remained largely quiescent, despite the migration of low-magnitude (M L < 3) seismicity toward the fault. This apparently “lazy” fault behavior fundamentally changed following direct injection into the fault zone at the H39 platform. Fluids migrated downward from shale strata I into the Cambrian Jiulaodong Formation shale (shale strata II, ~460 m thick), ultimately triggering the M L 5.6 earthquake in September 2019 after a prolonged 11-month preparatory phase, with the rupture occurring beneath the thick shale strata II.Seismicity induced by injection at the H39 platform also migrated toward the hypocenter of the December M L 5.4 earthquake but stalled approximately 1 km from the eventual rupture nucleation point. The M L 5.4 event was triggered during hydraulic fracturing at the H50 platform, migrating seismicity to the mainshock hypocenter suggest elevated pore pressure triggered the two events. In contrast to the earlier earthquake, the rupture of the ML 5.4 event occurred above shale strata II, suggesting that this thick shale layer acted as a barrier that inhibited rupture propagation in both events.

presentations.presentation_title: Normal-faulting Earthquakes Under a Compressional Stress Regime, Insights from the Weiyuan Shale Gas Field, China
presentations.abstract: It is well known that stress fields are important for earthquake generation and may govern the faulting types. However, here we report abundant small-magnitude normal faulting earthquakes in the Weiyuan shale gas field, China, a region with dominant compressional stress field and thrust-faulting earthquakes. Benefiting from our deployed dense arrays, we are able to construct high-resolution earthquake catalog. Most earthquakes are concentrated in depths slightly below the shale formation and are driven by pore pressure diffusion. We also apply SKHASH to determine focal mechanisms of small earthquakes using P polarities picking from PhasetNet+. The results show a number of normal-faulting events, which are validated by detailed comparison with nearby reverse-faulting events. These normal-faulting events are spatially clustered near hydraulic fracturing platforms, but show no clear spatial separation with the dominant reverse-faulting events, suggesting that they likely arise from highly localized stress heterogeneities. The coexistence of opposite faulting types in such a setting underscores the complexity of stress perturbations associated with shale gas development and highlights the need for heightened attention to seismic hazard assessment in these regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Probing Fluid-faulting Processes within Complex Fault Systems During Fluid-induced Earthquake Sequences
presentations.abstract: Crustal fluids play a critical role in earthquake triggering and fault slip, producing diverse spatiotemporal patterns of seismicity across tectonic settings. Fluid-induced seismicity offers a natural laboratory to investigate fluid–fault interactions under comparatively well-constrained conditions. In this lecture, I synthesize observations from wastewater-injection–induced seismicity in Oklahoma and geothermal stimulation at Utah FORGE to address two key questions: (1) what controls fault activation during fluid injection, and (2) how stress evolves in space and time in fluid-rich environments. For both regions, dense focal mechanism catalogs are derived using machine-learning-based polarity picks. In Oklahoma, optimally oriented, near-vertical planar faults exhibit burst-like seismicity with persistent activity on a main fault, whereas geometrically complex fault networks generate swarm-like behavior. At Utah FORGE, the largest and most sustained seismic cluster corresponds to a near-vertical fracture favorably oriented in the ambient stress field, requiring minimal pore-pressure increase for reactivation. Subsurface stress conditions are inferred using multiple proxy measures, including b-value, stress drop, inverted SHmax amplitude, and pore pressure. At Utah FORGE, mapped stress indicators show a gradual transition away from the stimulation point and spatial patterns consistent with independently estimated b-values. In both regions, larger earthquakes preferentially occur in high-stress areas, while early activation seismicity concentrates in lower-stress zones. These observations suggest that fluid pressure governs fault activation, whereas the pre-existing stress distribution largely controls the occurrence of larger events.

presentations.presentation_title: Seismic Attenuation as Direct Evidence Tracking Fluid Movement
presentations.institution: Shenzhen Research Institute, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
presentations.abstract: The interplay between fluids and faults is an important topic in both induced and natural earthquakes, yet the roles of fluid migration and pore-pressure diffusion in triggering seismicity remain poorly constrained. Tracking subsurface fluid movement is therefore critical. In this work, we show earthquake waveform attenuation provides direct evidence for monitoring fluid migration. In the Weiyuan shale gas field, previous reports indicate that hydraulic fracturing at the H37 platform led to fluid intrusion into a nearby platform during the stimulation period. Consistent with this, we observe a streak of small-magnitude seismicity occurring beneath the target reservoir that migrates ~1 km from the H37 well toward the neighboring well. These events exhibit strong attenuation, characterized by the absence of high-frequency energy. This case demonstrates that attenuation-based waveform analysis can provide direct observations of fault-hosted fluid migration.

presentations.presentation_title: Uranium Behavior Under Variable Geochemical Conditions During Water–rock Interactions: Batch Experiments from the Okcheon Metamorphic Belt, Korea
presentations.institution: Department of Environment and Energy, Jeonbuk National University
presentations.abstract: Uranium behavior in water–rock systems is governed by complex interactions involving redox reactions, secondary mineral formation, and aqueous complexation. In this study, batch experiments were conducted to evaluate the effects of pH, carbonate buffering, uranium spiking, and temperature on uranium behavior using a uranium-bearing coaly slate–artificial groundwater system from the Boeun-gun area of the Okcheon Metamorphic Belt, Korea. The coaly slate contains approximately 99.6 ppm of uranium, mainly hosted in uraninite and ekanite. Artificial groundwater simulating the groundwater chemistry of the study area was reacted with the coaly slate under five experimental conditions: three non-buffered experiments at 15 °C (Batch 1, acidic pH 5; Batch 2, alkaline pH 9; and Batch 3, uranium-spiked groundwater at 2 mg L⁻¹) and two carbonate-buffered experiments at 15 °C (Batch 4) and 30 °C (Batch 5). In the non-buffered systems (Batches 1–3), rapid acidification occurred immediately after reaction initiation due to pyrite oxidation, resulting in acidic, high-Eh conditions that promoted the formation of secondary Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxides and Fe-bearing secondary phases. Uranium concentrations increased rapidly during the early stages in Batches 1 and 2 before approaching near-equilibrium levels, whereas uranium concentrations in Batch 3 decreased progressively with time, indicating effective uranium removal through adsorption or surface complexation onto iron (oxyhydr)oxides. In contrast, carbonate-buffered systems (Batches 4 and 5) maintained near-neutral pH throughout the experiments and exhibited a gradual increase in dissolved uranium concentrations over time. Uranium speciation was dominated by aqueous carbonate complexes, with Ca₂UO₂(CO₃)₃ prevailing in Batch 4 and UO₂(CO₃)₂²⁻ dominating in Batch 5, reflecting the combined influence of carbonate chemistry and temperature. Overall, the results demonstrate that uranium behavior is controlled by distinct geochemical mechanisms under acidic and carbonate-buffered conditions.

presentations.presentation_title: Status Report of North American-pacific Geopotential Datum of 2022
presentations.abstract: The North American–Pacific Geopotential Datum of 2022 (NAPGD2022) is being developed to replace the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 (NAVD 88) and to provide a modern, accurate height reference for Pacific North America, American Samoa, and Guam/CNMI. The datum is defined by the gravimetric geoid model GEOID2022, which represents the surface of zero orthometric height. GEOID2022 is jointly developed by the United States, Canada, and Mexico using terrestrial gravity data, GRAV-D airborne observations, recent satellite gravity models, and satellite altimetry. The model achieves formal accuracies of approximately 1–2 cm in flat areas and 2–3 cm in mountainous areas and includes a dynamic component to maintain accuracy over time. Official companion models of gravity, deflection of the vertical, and topography enable computation and reduction of geopotential at the topographic surface. This presentation summarizes the current status of NAPGD2022, with emphasis on the computation, validation, and availability of GEOID2022.

presentations.presentation_title: Formation and Preservation of Paleoproterozoic Boron-rich Evaporites
presentations.institution: Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences
presentations.abstract: Most large evaporitic borate deposits formed in the Cenozoic; ancient large deposits are rare. The Liao-Ji orogenic belt of the North China Craton hosts several Paleoproterozoic metamorphosed major evaporitic borate deposits. These stratiform borate deposits formed in carbonate rocks interlayered with ca. 2.15 Ga volcanic rocks. Phase modelling, Zr-in-titanite temperatures, LA-ICP-MS dating constrain peak P–T conditions of regional granulite facies metamorphism of the Wengquangou deposit to 750–800°C, 0.8 GPa at 1.87 to 1.84 Ga. This high-grade metamorphism is critical as it transformed soluble evaporitic borate minerals into little soluble suanite and ludwigite and thereby prevented later dissolution of the evaporitic deposit. Heavy δ 11 B (+7.5 to +9.8 ‰) of borate minerals (suanite, ludwigite and szaibelyite) and δ 34 S V-CDT of pyrrhotite (+8.7 to +16.1 ‰) values demonstrate marine contributions to the budget of these isotope systems. The boron-bearing marbles are enriched in Mg, Fe, K, U, and Pb that likely originated from the weathering and hydrothermal leaching of local bimodal volcanic rocks. Our data show that ancient evaporitic borate deposits formed by similar processes as modern ones, involving the leaching and mobilization of boron from volcanic and sedimentary rocks, transport of boron into a continent-marginal basin, and concentration of boron by evaporation. The rare preservation of ancient borate deposits does not indicate that they rarely form, but rather that they are generally not preserved as regions hosting major evaporitic borate deposits seldom undergo subsequent high-grade metamorphism.

presentations.presentation_title: Mantle Plume Control on Basin Development: New Tectono-magmatic Scenario for the Formation of the Eastern Mediterranean Basin
presentations.abstract: The formation of the Eastern Mediterranean basin is widely explained by passive rifting and strike-slip tectonics, while magmatism was not considered a factor in this process. However, a new integrated analysis of deep seismic reflection data (≥7 km), gravity, and magnetic surveys presents a different picture. Instead of relying solely on passive extension, the data indicate active, plume-related extension characterized by at least ten discrete magmatic-driven forced swells (~40 km wide domal structures) with reliefs of hundreds of meters that developed across the eastern Mediterranean during the Late Jurassic–Early Cretaceous transition, coinciding with the decay phase of the Levant mantle plume. These swells are found in both marine and land areas, showing regionally consistent evidence of magmatic activities within a pre-existing basin floor. They all follow a similar evolutionary pattern: forced folding of existing strata, semi-concentric swell growth, crest uplift, formation of carbonate platforms and atolls, progressive onlap along the flanks, subsequent cooling, and final burial. This interpretation greatly enhances the understanding of magmatism’s role in shaping basin geometry, local uplifts and subsidence history, depositional architecture, and the initial tectonic conditions of the Eastern Mediterranean during a critical phase of geodynamic evolution. It indicates that decaying plume activity, rather than passive extension, was the main driver of crustal architecture and thermal structure during Cretaceous basin development. Once magmatic and thermal support diminished in the late Cretaceous, a short-lived Senonian compression phase hindered regional thermal subsidence. Once ended, the basin rapidly subsided to its current depths, while the swells persisted as seamounts until most were buried under younger sediments. These findings are a significant shift in understanding the formation of the eastern Mediterranean and have important implications for the basin’s thermal history.

presentations.presentation_title: Late Archean Mantle Evolution Inferred From Highly Siderophile Element Geochemistry Of Komatiites And Basalts In Yilgarn Craton Western Australia
presentations.abstract: Highly siderophile elements (HSEs) are key tracers of Earth’s early differentiation due to their strong affinity for iron and efficient sequestration into the core during core formation. Although elevated HSE abundances in the modern mantle are commonly attributed to late accretion, the timing, efficiency, and degree of mixing of late-accreted material within the Archean mantle remain debated. Komatiites and related basalts provide insight into these processes due to their derivation from high degrees of mantle melting.Komatiites from the Yilgarn Craton of Western Australia define multiple parental melt signatures, exhibiting at least three HSE compositions around ~2.7 Ga, distinguished by variable absolute HSE abundances. These observations raise debate over whether the signatures reflect mantle source heterogeneity or variable magmatic processes such as fractional crystallisation and sulphide saturation. This study evaluates these alternatives using major and trace element geochemistry, HSE abundances, and Re–Os isotopes from komatiites and associated basalts from surface outcrop and drill core.The datasets reveal systematic HSE and Os isotopic variations consistent with magmatic evolution. Despite significant sulphide interaction and sediment assimilation linked to the formation of massive sulphide ores. This interpretation is supported by the fact that the majority of the data exhibit (1) near-chondritic relative proportions, for Os-Ir and Pt-Pd, interpreted to be inherited from the mantle source, and (2) the absence of resolvable radiogenic Os excursions from chondritic initial compositions. MgO–Cr–Ru systematics indicate that the apparent diversity of parental melt compositions reflects variable olivine and chromite fractionation from a single mantle-derived melt rather than multiple discrete mantle sources. Estimated HSE concentrations of the Yilgarn komatiite mantle source correspond to ~58–81% of present-day mantle values, consistent with incomplete late Archean mantle homogenisation.

presentations.presentation_title: Constraints on the origin of ultrahigh pressure peridotites from Western Gneiss Region, Norway, based on highly siderophile element geochemistry
presentations.abstract: The elemental abundances of the primitive mantle provide fundamental constraints on Earth’s building materials and differentiation processes. Among these, highly siderophile elements (HSE; Os, Ir, Ru, Pt, Pd, and Re) exhibit broadly chondritic relative abundances, which cannot be reproduced by metal–silicate partitioning, even at high pressure, leading to the late accretion hypothesis. Time-resolved estimates of mantle HSE abundances therefore have the potential to reveal the temporal evolution of mantle HSE inventories and to constrain the presence and timing of late accretion events. However, widely used estimates of primitive mantle composition are based primarily on peridotites from lithosphere formed after the Proterozoic. Here we investigate peridotites from the Western Gneiss Region (WGR), Norway. Previous studies have reported Archean model ages and ultrahigh pressure origins for some WGR peridotites, but the depth and timing of these processes across the region remain poorly constrained. As such, we present new whole-rock major, trace, and HSE concentration data, along with Re-Os isotopic compositions for peridotites collected from widely distributed bodies throughout the WGR. The WGR peridotites define a clear melt-depletion trend among relatively immobile elements (e.g., Al, Yb, Lu, and Sc), indicative of low-pressure melting within the spinel stability field. In addition, systematic variation in 187 Os/ 188 Os and HSE ratios (e.g., Pd/Os) are consistent with the melting, with the most refractory sample exhibiting a highly unradiogenic 187 Os/ 188 Os ratio of 0.10528 ± 0.00004. The corresponding Re-depletion model age of ~3.1 Ga suggests that extensive melt extraction occurred in a shallow Archean mantle environment. In contrast, the least depleted sample provides a first-order estimate of pre-melting mantle HSE composition, comparable to that of the primitive mantle, suggesting that primitive-mantle-like HSE compositions existed in the Archean mantle and offering time-resolved context for primitive mantle HSE estimates.

presentations.presentation_title: Integrating Accessory Mineral Geochemistry with Machine Learning in Detrital Mineral Studies
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Detrital accessory minerals such as zircon and monazite are widely used in studies of paleogeography, orogeny, and resource exploration. Although U–Pb ages obtained from individual grains provide the most important constraints, information on formation environments, e.g., source rock types, remains a major weakness in detrital mineral studies and requires a geochemical fingerprinting approach.In this study, we introduce a machine learning–based classification model for source rock types using trace element compositions of accessory minerals. Trace element compositions are multivariate and exhibit nonlinear characteristics, which cannot always be adequately captured by conventional empirical classifications or univariate indicators. Our approach aims to improve discrimination accuracy by statistically learning such complex patterns and to objectively evaluate model performance for unseen data. Appropriate treatment of compositional data, imbalanced datasets, and missing values is essential for improving the robustness of classification models.As an application example, we apply this framework to detrital monazite from major river sands in North and South American continents. We carried out trace element and Nd isotope analyses as well as U–Pb dating. Trace element compositions indicate that the age distribution of monazite reflects both igneous and metamorphic sources. In addition, the Nd isotopic records reveal isotopic evolution linked to the supercontinent cycle. By comparing monazite with zircon, we demonstrate that monazite serves as a more sensitive archive of crustal reworking through geological time.

presentations.presentation_title: Branching Between Normal and Abnormal Grain Growth in a Pinned Olivine–Spinel System: Implications from Takashima Dunite Xenoliths
presentations.abstract: All time-dependent records in rocks reflect thermodynamic non-equilibrium states. Grain-size evolution is one of the most important carriers of such time information because it reflects the relaxation of microstructure toward equilibrium. Grain size generally increases with annealing time, and experimental grain-growth rates can therefore be used to estimate residence times by fitting a power-law relation. In natural rocks, however, this experimental assumption is sometimes questionable because rocks commonly contain impurities. Grain growth in the presence of impurities is particularly complex. For example, theoretical studies suggest that impurity-bearing systems may evolve toward a characteristic grain size while a subset of grains becomes abnormally large; in such cases, the evolution does not follow a simple power-law relationship. This study aims to elucidate grain-growth mechanisms in a simple matrix–secondary-phase system and to identify the conditions that control the transition between normal grain growth (NGG) and abnormal grain growth (AGG). We use Takashima dunite xenoliths from Saga Prefecture, Japan, as a case study. These xenoliths constitute a relatively simple two-phase system of olivine and chromian spinel. Spinel is uniformly distributed and commonly occupies olivine triple junctions, producing a classic pinned microstructure, whereas some xenoliths contain olivine megacrysts larger than 1 cm. We interpret these megacrysts as products of localized pinning loss followed by rapid, selective growth. Their occurrence appears stochastic and may become more frequent with longer annealing durations. To evaluate this interpretation and to explore whether NGG and AGG can constrain timescales, we propose a new equation describing olivine grain growth and solve it to determine the branching conditions for NGG versus AGG. We integrate microstructural observations, machine-learning-based quantitative characterization of grain boundaries, and physically based grain-growth simulations to test the plausibility of NGG and AGG and to assess their potential for extracting time information from natural rocks.

presentations.presentation_title: Temporal Variability in Melt Supply and Spreading at the Marie Celeste Transform Fault, Central Indian Ridge
presentations.abstract: The Marie Celeste Transform Fault (MCTF) is a major oceanic transform offsetting the slow-spreading Central Indian Ridge by more than 200 km. Its southern steep fault wall preserves an uninterrupted record of oceanic crust formation spanning over 11 million years. In fall 2024, we conducted an integrated geological and geophysical survey along the MCTF using R/V Hakuho-maru, aiming to investigate temporal variations in mid-ocean ridge processes and mantle heterogeneity.Prominent transverse ridges developed on both north and south walls of the MCTF between 13 and 5 Ma. During this period, abyssal hill trends rotated slightly, reflecting plate motion changes that likely drove ridge formation. Our survey primarily covered the transform valley and southern ridge segment. We identified several oceanic core complexes formed between 2.5 and 3 Ma, along with two large off-axis seamounts erupted near the ridge axis, indicating significant variations in melt supply on a million-year timescale. Magnetic lineations were clearly detected, allowing geochron identification back to chron C5ACn (~14 Ma). Zircon U–Pb dating of gabbroic samples correlates well with magnetic anomaly ages. Average spreading rates over the past 10 Myr are estimated at 19 mm/yr on the eastern flank and 22 mm/yr on the western flank, consistent with global plate models, though detailed analysis reveals fluctuations between 3 and 8 Ma. Crustal thickness, derived from satellite gravity and new bathymetry, shows variations on 2–3 Myr scales.Systematic rock sampling was conducted at 10–30 km intervals along the southern fault wall. At each station, dredging at 2–5 sites at different depths recovered a complete crustal section, including gabbro from deeper sites and dolerite and basalt from shallower levels together with their variably altered equivalents.. Preliminary analysis indicates lithological differences with depth compared to previous MAR transverse ridge studies.

presentations.presentation_title: The Role of Altered Oceanic Crust in Continental Growth: Insights from Hg-O-Hf Isotopes and Seismic Analyses in East Cathaysia
presentations.abstract: Situated along the southeastern margin of the South China Craton, East Cathaysia has undergone a complex tectonic history and is uniquely characterized by the widespread Mesozoic intrusive and volcanic rocks. Significantly, many of these igneous rocks exhibit unusually low δ 18 O values, the origin of which remains highly controversial. Such depleted oxygen signatures are variously attributed to the partial melting of either hydrothermally altered oceanic crust (AOC) or juvenile continental crust. Resolving this debate is crucial for identifying fossil oceanic remnants and understanding their contribution to the region’s crustal architecture.To characterize the crustal structure and composition, we deployed a seismic array consisting of 100 short-period stations and collected 60 granite samples for geochemical analyses. We applied ambient noise tomography and receiver function analysis to construct an S-wave velocity (Vs) model of the upper and middle crust, together with the crustal thickness (H) and Vp/Vs ratio (κ) at each station. While both West and East Cathaysia exhibit comparable crustal thicknesses (28–33 km), East Cathaysia shows higher Vp/Vs ratios (>1.75), suggesting a more mafic deep-crustal composition. Geochemical constraints from coupled O-Hf isotopes necessitate a low-δ 18 O component in the magma source, which cannot be explained by simple mixing between mantle-derived magmas and typical continental crust. Crucially, the positive Hg isotopic compositions provide a distinct marine trend, identifying the low-δ 18 O source as the partial melting of AOC rather than juvenile continental materials.Integrating seismic and geochemical evidence, we propose a geodynamic model in which the collision of the West Cathaysia continental plate and the East Cathaysia oceanic plate resulted in the emplacement of a fossil oceanic crust in the middle to lower crust below the present East Cathaysia. This process highlights the critical role of remnant oceanic pieces in driving the vertical and lateral growth of continents.

presentations.presentation_title: Lava Lobe Flow Direction Analysis of the Northern Oman Ophiolite: Implications for Paleospreading-axis Geometry
presentations.institution: National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: In the northern Oman ophiolite, lava sequences erupted and emplaced both on- and off-axis are preserved with less stratigraphic or structural deformation. In this region, temporal and spatial variations in magmatism along the paleo-ridge axis have been discussed based on the geological structures of gabbroic rocks and sheeted dike swarms (e.g., Miyashita et al., 2003). In the Wadi Fizh area, located at the end of a paleo-ridge segment, facies analysis of V1 lava flows revealed that the lower flows formed on-axis, whereas the upper flows were emplaced off-axis (Kusano et al., 2012).In this presentation, we use flow directions of lava lobes as indicators of topographic changes near the paleo–spreading axis and examine whether these directions vary systematically along the ridge axis. In the Wadi Fizh area, V1 lava lobes show plunges ranging from 0° to 40°, with trends between 30° and 190°. In the Bani Ghayth area, plunges range from 50–60° and 10–40°, with trends of 30–50°, ~120°, and 190–210°. In the Salahi area, plunges vary from 0° to 60°, with trends of 120–200° and 310–340°.The southeastward flow directions observed in all three areas indicate that the paleo-oceanic ridge axis was located west of the northern Oman ophiolite. The poor directionality of flow trends in the Fizh area corresponds to the frequent occurrence of pillow lavas, whereas the more uniform flow trends in the Ghayth and Salahi areas correspond to fewer pillow lavas. The strong directionality of lava‑lobe trends in the Bani Ghayth and Salahi areas likely reflects local topographic controls, such as lava‑flow fronts or fault scarps.

presentations.presentation_title: Mantle Heterogeneities Induce Time- and Space-varying Magmatism at the Migrating Ultraslow Southwest Indian Ridge
presentations.institution: Université Paris Cité / National Centre for Scientific Research
presentations.abstract: The link between mantle heterogeneity as depicted by geochemical and seismic studies and the magmatism emplaced on the divergent plates remains elusive. Here, we derive variations of magmatism from marine magnetic data and trace mantle heterogeneities beneath the eastern Southwest Indian Ridge over 27 Ma. Three states of magmatism, robust, intermediate, and starved, are identified from the amplitude of magnetic anomalies. Comparing the distribution of magmatism on orthogonal and oblique ridge sections supports an asthenospheric source not moving with the plates and ridge as the predominant source of magmatic variations, suggesting that these variations are linked to different amounts of fertile and refractory mantle in the asthenosphere sampled by the ultraslow spreading center. This study offers an approach to reveal deep mantle heterogeneities from shallow crustal observations.

presentations.presentation_title: Broadband Ground‐motion Parameters Estimation Using Physics‐based Simulated Low‐frequency Waveforms and Deep Learning
presentations.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Accurate prediction of broadband ground motion parameters is important for earthquake disaster prevention and mitigation. Due to the lack of high wave number components in the source rupture process and velocity models, physics‐based ground motion simulation methods can only reliably produce low‐frequency ground motions (<1 Hz). In this study, we developed a deep learning network, LFW2BBP, which maps physics‐based simulated low‐frequency ground motion waveforms to broadband ground motion parameters. The LFW2BBP extracts features of low‐frequency ground motion in time domain waveform, time‐frequency domain spectrum, and spectral acceleration and integrates these features to establish a relationship with high‐ frequency ground motion parameters. Sensitivity tests were conducted to verify the stability and robustness of the LFW2BBP. Finally, we combined physics‐based simulation and LFW2BBP to predict broadband ground motion parameters for the 2016 Mw 7.0 Kumamoto earthquake. The predicted results show good agreement with the observations.

presentations.presentation_title: The Development of Long-window Regional Phase Picking Model
presentations.institution: Earthquake Research Institute,The University of Tokyo.
presentations.abstract: In regions where local seismicity is sparse and active-source surveys are limited, obtaining reliable constraints on crustal structure and ground stability remains challenging. In such settings, subsurface characterization must rely largely on regional and teleseismic earthquakes recorded by available seismic networks. These seismograms are often long and noisy, and robust structural studies require consistent and accurate picking of the first-arriving P- and S-phase onsets from low–signal-to-noise records. Reliable P/S picks are also a prerequisite for exploiting later phases—such as crustal reverberations, Moho reflections, and depth phases—that can provide key constraints on lower-crustal and Moho seismic velocity structure. Consequently, a phase picker that can operate on long time windows is needed to robustly identify onsets in these extended regional and teleseismic recordings. We present SegFarPhase, a deep-learning regional phase picker designed to incorporate long time-window. SegFarPhase follows a U-Net encoder–decoder architecture and employs the hierarchical Transformer-based SegPhase (Katoh et al., 2025) as a bottleneck module, enabling self-attention over widely separated time samples. The model takes 4-minute three-component velocity waveforms as input and outputs probabilities for P, S, and noise classes, normalized to sum to one at each sample. SegFarPhase was trained and evaluated on the Curated Regional Earthquake Waveforms (CREW; Suarze and Beroza, 2024) benchmark (epicentral distance >100 km). On CREW, the model achieved strong detection performance and small arrival-time residuals, with most P and S picks concentrated within a few seconds of the reference labels at high posterior probability. Attention-map analysis further indicated that different heads emphasize complementary waveform attributes, including onsets as well as noise and coda, suggesting effective exploitation of contextual cues. In this presentation, we report the performance evaluation of SegFarPhase and demonstrate its application to regional earthquake data recorded in Singapore.

presentations.presentation_title: Augmenting Well-log Data Using Supervised Machine Learning Models
presentations.abstract: Well logs construct a primary observational basis for subsurface prospecting and reservoir evaluation. These data provide continuous, depth-indexed measurements that encode lithologic variability, structural features, and petrophysical conditions underground. In practice, well-log records frequently contain missing intervals caused by tool malfunction, acquisition constraints, borehole conditions, or operational interruptions. Such discontinuities can bias stratigraphic interpretation, obscure the formation boundaries, and undermine downstream analyses—including reservoir/aquifer delineation and quantitative resource assessment—where consistency across depth is critical. This study addresses the problem of missing-interval reconstruction by developing a supervised machine-learning framework for augmenting absent log segments and restoring the depth-continuous profiles. Unlike conventional gap-filling approaches (e.g., linear interpolation or moving-window averaging) that impose simplistic assumptions on log behavior, supervised models can learn nonlinear, multivariate relationships among co-recorded logs and thereby generate reconstructions that are more consistent with geological patterns. We evaluate a suite of supervised algorithms, including linear regression, random forests, gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost and LightGBM), and ensemble configurations (e.g., AdaBoost variants), with the goal of identifying a robust and generalizable model for producing geologically plausible imputed segments and improving the completeness and reliability of stratigraphic analysis.

presentations.presentation_title: Detection of Seismic Events in Historical Seismic Waveform Records Based on Deep Learning
presentations.abstract: Recent remarkable advances in artificial intelligence technology have raised expectations for discovering new seismic events from historical seismic waveform records. We introduce our recent activities related to this: (1) detection of low-frequency tremors based on ResNet in seismograms drawn on papers using pens (Kaneko, Nagao et al., 2023), and (2) detection and classification of volcanic events in smoked paper records based on DETR.

presentations.presentation_title: Integrated GPU Computing Platform for Efficient Fenics Geodynamic Simulation
presentations.abstract: Numerical geodynamic modeling advances understanding of mantle dynamics, enabling the resolution of slab–plume interactions, the growth of large low-shear-velocity provinces, and other lower-mantle processes. However, because such models demand high resolution and impose a computational burden, boosting solver performance with GPUs is essential. Geodynamic codes achieve high performance on multi-core CPUs, yet full exploitation of modern GPUs remains limited. Among the iterative schemes used in mantle dynamics, velocity pressure splitting methods such as Uzawa iteration require almost exclusively sparse matrix–vector products and vector updates, operations that map efficiently to GPUs. We integrate GPU acceleration directly into the finite-element framework FEniCS, routing all linear-algebra operations through PETSc’s CUDA back-end. A GPU-enabled Uzawa solver is first validated on canonical Stokes benchmarks, matching CPU accuracy while delivering 3–10× speed-ups on a single RTX A6000 Ada card versus 32 CPU cores. The same computational approach is then applied to tectonic-scale scenarios, including a 2-D subduction zone and a continental rift model with strongly temperature- and stress-dependent viscosity. GPU execution cuts total wall time by a factor of three for meshes containing 3 million unknowns, all without changing the high-level Python scripts. Multi-GPU runs using two devices further extend this benefit by distributing both computation and VRAM usage via MPI-based domain decomposition, enabling larger problem sizes and sustaining additional speedups at higher resolution where communication overhead is amortized. Composed purely of open-source components (FEniCS, PETSc, CUDA, and Python), our setup can be redirected to other geodynamic tasks, including multi-phase flow, coupled thermo-chemical convection, and planetary-mantle modeling, by simply adjusting material-property and parameters without rewriting any kernels. This study demonstrates that an open-source GPU workflow is now powerful enough to remove the performance bottleneck that has long restricted continental-scale geodynamic simulations to large CPU clusters.

presentations.presentation_title: Preliminary Results on the Detection and Analysis of Repeating Earthquakes in the Korean Peninsula
presentations.abstract: Rapid advances in AI detection and GPU-accelerated computing are reshaping earthquake monitoring by enabling high-resolution analyses. In and around the Korean Peninsula, Han et al. (2024) constructed a comprehensive catalog for the period 2012–2021 using an AI picker, revealing numerous compact earthquake clusters. Recently, Jung and Sheen (2025) identified a repeating earthquake (RE) family in the Gyeryongsan area, suggesting that some clusters in the Korean Peninsula may be associated with recurrent rupture. In the idealized sense, REs represent events that rupture exactly the same fault area with the same slip, generating essentially identical waveforms. In practice, RE candidates are identified by high inter-event waveform cross-correlation, strong overlap in rupture areas, and small magnitude differences (Uchida and Bürgmann, 2019). Motivated by these criteria, we perform a systematic search for REs across clustered sequences in Korea.Using the Han et al. (2024) catalog, we clustered earthquakes via DBSCAN (≥10 events, 0.01° radius). We selected clusters with robust station coverage while excluding the 2016 Gyeongju and 2017 Pohang sequences, offshore seismicity, and known quarry-blast regions. This process yielded 93 candidate clusters. We applied a refined GPU-accelerated template matching (Beauce et al., 2017), using earthquakes from the candidate clusters as templates, to continuous data from 2008 to 2025 to detect additional events. Including the newly detected events, we performed cluster-wise relative relocations and identified RE candidates using three criteria: cross-correlation ≥0.9, hypocentral separation less than 80 percent of the larger-event rupture radius, and magnitude difference ≤0.3 (Jung and Sheen, 2025).This study compiled a database of clustered-earthquake families, including candidate REs, and produced an enhanced catalog for the Korean Peninsula. The resulting dataset is expected to provide a useful foundation for future RE-focused studies, such as assessing recurrence behavior and tracking temporal changes in clustered seismicity.

presentations.presentation_title: The Utility of Cryptotephra-stratigraphy Methods in East Asia: Unraveling Hidden Eruption History, Tephra Footprint and Eruption Dynamics
presentations.institution: Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Recent advances in cryptotephra extraction and analytical techniques have driven significant progress in global tephrochronological studies, providing critical tools for breakthroughs in volcanology, palaeoclimatology, and archaeology. East Asia, a volcanically active region hosting numerous Quaternary volcanoes, constitutes a critical domain for tephrochronological applications. While previous research on East Asian volcanism is extensive and well-documented, studies have predominantly focused on macroscopically visible tephra horizons. Pioneering work by cryptotephra researchers, including our team, has now extended these microstratigraphic methods to lacustrine and marine sedimentary archives across East Asia, generating new insights. This presentation highlights advances in East Asian cryptotephra research, including: (1) identification of previously unrecognized eruptions (e.g., the ~30 ka Changbaishan eruption); (2) expanded spatial footprints of key marker tephras (e.g., transcontinental dispersal of Russian tephra to Japan); (3) high-precision dating of eruptive events (Ko-g, Ma-f~j, U-1) and sedimentary sequences (East/Japan Sea marine record); and (4) new constraints on timescales and mechanisms of caldera evolution (Aira caldera). We thus advocate systematic application of cryptotephra methods across the boarder Asian realm, which may catalyze transformative advances in Asian tephrochronology.
presentations.session_title: Multidisciplinary Perspectives On Asia-Pacific Volcanism: Eruption Histories, Magmatic Plumbing Systems And Volcanic Processes

presentations.presentation_title: Petrological Monitoring on Volcanic Ash in Japan: Advancements and Perspectives
presentations.institution: National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience
presentations.abstract: Petrological characteristics of volcanic products record the eruption mechanism such as magma storage, ascent, and fragmentation processes. Thus, continuous petrological monitoring of volcanic products is essential for reconstructing and prediction of transition of eruptive activity. Especially, volcanic ash is suitable for the monitoring because it is widely dispersed and can be collected at considerable distances from the erupting vents, allowing continuous monitoring throughout an eruptive sequence. Volcanic ash has long been analyzed by individual institutions for diverse scientific objectives in community of volcanology in Japan. These efforts have significantly advanced our understanding about the eruption mechanisms, and enabled the identification of transition of ongoing eruptive activity based on petrological characteristics of volcanic ash particles. Particularly, recent advances in on-site monitoring have made rapid assessments of the evolution of ongoing eruptions increasingly feasible. To achieve more effective eruption monitoring, the development of comprehensive and integrated analyses system of the petrological characteristics is required. In April 2024, the Headquarters of Volcano Research Promotion was established within the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) of Japanese government. Under its policy framework, a Volcanic Products Analysis Center (tentative) dedicated to the petrological monitoring is being established at the National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience (NIED). This center aims the comprehensive and integrated analyses of volcanic products including volcanic ash particles, thereby advancing the scientific basis of prediction of eruptive transition. The combination of the on-site monitoring and comprehensive petrological analyses in the center is expected to derive timely and practical understanding of volcanic activity for disaster mitigation.

presentations.presentation_title: A Ranking System for Clinopyroxene-based Geothermobarometers: Application of Machine Learning to Increase the Accuracy of Magmatic Pressure-temperature Estimate
presentations.abstract: Clinopyroxene (cpx) is commonly found in a variety of igneous rocks and thus has been widely used to calculate magmatic pressure–temperatures and reconstruct volcanic plumbing systems. Recent studies exploiting machine learning produced a number of cpx-based thermobarometer models using distinct calibration datasets and algorithms, posing challenges in identifying models applicable to given magmatic systems. Model performance was commonly assessed based on in-distribution data (i.e., data drawn from the same underlying distributions as the calibration dataset), yielding uncertainties underestimated relative to out-of-distribution (OOD) samples. Here, we propose a machine-learning-based framework to rank clinopyroxene-based thermobarometers and identify unsuitable ones for natural samples of interest. The framework consists of two main parts: (1) applying an OOD detection scheme to exclude unsuitable models based on the bulk-rock/melt composition and pressure–temperature of the natural and experimental datasets, and data-driven feature-space OOD diagnostics, and (2) applying deviation functions obtained for individual thermometers to predict P–T deviations for natural samples and identify models giving the lowest deviation. The framework was tested using a dataset compiled from published experiments showing no overlap with the calibration datasets of all thermobarometers considered in this study. The P-Ts calculated for the test dataset using our favorable models show lower root-mean-square errors than any single model, indicating a better performance by ~0.4–0.6 kbar and ~10–14 °C. We find that this framework is effective for natural systems where different models yield greatly different P and/or T estimates. Examples such as the dacitic magma of Toba caldera (Sumatra) and basaltic-andesitic magma of Merapi volcano (Indonesia) were investigated and will be reported in this presentation. This work was supported by the Hong Kong Research Grants Council (ECS 27302423 and GRF 17308825, awarded to W-R. Li) and is part of the PhD thesis of X-Y. Liu.

presentations.presentation_title: Holocene Activity at Mount Daisen Volcano: Insights from Petrography and Geochemistry of Deposits from Kirin-sawa Eruption
presentations.abstract: Petrographic and geochemical characteristics of rocks contained in pyroclastic flows provide valuable information about magma storage conditions and magmatic processes preceding eruptions. This study describes a recently discovered pyroclastic flow at Mount Daisen, named the Kirin Sawa block-and-ash flow (BAF), from a petrographic and geochemical perspective to provide insights into magma evolution during the last stage of the eruptive history at Mount Daisen. Mount Daisen is the largest Quaternary volcano in the Southwest Japan Arc. The youngest previously known eruptive products are dated at 20.8 ka; however, recent paleomagnetic analyses and radiocarbon dating confirm a series of Holocene eruptions, suggesting that the youngest eruptive history is more complex than previously thought. One of these products is the Kirin Sawa BAF, which is tentatively interpreted as being related to a dome-forming eruption. A representative set of samples was collected from this deposit, and petrographic analyses, mineral chemistry analyses of plagioclase, amphibole, and pyroxene by EPMA, and whole-rock geochemistry by XRF were performed. Results show that compositionally, all samples are dacites with an adakitic signature. Plagioclase phenocrysts dominate, followed by amphibole, orthopyroxene, biotite, oxides, and quartz in a glassy matrix mainly composed of plagioclase microlites. Plagioclase crystals exhibit three predominant textures: patchy zoning, sieve texture, and normal zoning; additionally, plagioclase rims exhibit high Fe contents compared to the cores. Amphiboles are Mg-rich (tschermakite–Mg hornblende) and exhibit breakdown rims, intergrowths, and strong zoning. Pyroxenes are classified as enstatite (En65–En80) and occur as microcrystals. The texturally distinct plagioclase populations and high Fe rims indicate the occurrence of a magmatic chamber destabilization before eruption. A three-stage model for magmatic processes and eruptive style is proposed, involving mafic magma injection followed by rapid magma ascent and surface lava-dome formation.
