presentations.presentation_title: Linking Zircon Geochronology and Crystal Records to Pre-eruptive Magmatic Conditions at Mt. Shamao, Tatun Volcano Group (TVG), Taiwan
presentations.abstract: Multiple lines of evidence demonstrate that the Tatun Volcano Group (TVG), northern Taiwan, hosts an active magmatic system, highlighting the need to robustly constrain its eruption history. Given its proximity to the Taipei metropolitan area, defining eruption timing and pre-eruptive magmatic conditions is critical for volcanic hazard assessment. Mt. Shamao is a prime target for this work because it represents one of the youngest eruptive centers in the TVG, yet its eruption age remains debated and the conditions preceding eruption are poorly constrained. Zircon double dating indicates that Mt. Shamao erupted during the late Pleistocene (~16 ka). Zircon crystallization ages further record protracted growth over ~200 kyr, with episodic magma fluxes reflected by multiple discrete crystallization peaks at ca. 23, 60, and 117 ka. Mt. Shamao lavas are porphyritic hornblende andesites dominated by plagioclase (35–37%), amphibole (12–15%), and minor pyroxene (~5%). Plagioclase phenocrysts commonly display disequilibrium textures, including sieve structures, resorption surfaces, complex zoning, large anorthite spikes (>10 mol%), and melt-inclusion–rich zones, and occur as single crystals, synneusis clusters, and glomerocrysts. Amphiboles define two populations: 1) large magnesiohornblendes with thin opacitic reaction rims, and 2) zoned crystals containing pargasitic rims or internal domains within dominantly magnesiohornblende compositions. Pyroxenes are mainly orthopyroxene with clinopyroxene rims. These features indicate multiple episodes of mafic recharge accompanied by reheating and partial re-equilibration of crystals with the surrounding magma. Mineral thermobarometric estimates span a wide pressure range, indicating crystal scavenging from a vertically extensive, transcrustal reservoir spanning approximately 20–8 km depth and affected by episodic mafic input. Shallow crystallization depths (~4 km) recorded by large magnesiohornblende crystals, which are not resolved by present geophysical models, suggest the presence of either ephemeral or volumetrically limited, water-rich upper-crustal reservoir that also contributed to the dome-forming eruptions.

presentations.presentation_title: Temporal Variation in Seismic Velocity within the Accretionary Prism of the Nankai Subduction Zone: Implication for Fluids, Stress Field and Plate Coupling
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Temporal variations in seismic velocity due to various factors, such as large earthquakes, volcanic activities, and seasonal variations, have been investigated using ambient noise correlations. Although these studies mainly focus on land variations, submarine cases have also been investigated (Ikeda and Tsuji, 2018; Tonegawa et al. 2022). In the Nankai subduction zone, a permanent cabled network of ocean bottom seismometers has been deployed since 2010 (Dense Oceanfloor Network system for Earthquakes and Tsunamis: DONET). Using ambient noise records of the DONET stations, Tonegawa et al. (2022) revealed that the seismic velocity gradually increases over 10 years at the accretionary prism toe, and interpreted that such increases are caused by fluid drainages due to the horizontal compression of the sediments. Because the previous study investigated the temporal variation in seismic velocity until the beginning of 2021, I extended the analyzed period until December 2025 in this study. Results show that the velocity increases observed at the prism toe have stopped between 2022 and 2024, and again they have started in 2025. In other regions, seismic velocities in the Kumano Basin and near Muroto south of Shikoku increased, while those in accretionary prism toe off Shikoku and Kii Peninsula do not vary significantly. If I compared this pattern to the plate coupling distribution (e.g., Takemura et al. 2022), the distributions of the velocity increase and large shear stress changes are partly coincided each other. Also, referring to the distributions of large shear stress changes, I estimated the areal changes (compression or extension) at the seafloor using Okada model (Okada, 1985). The results show the compressional field at the seafloor above the strong coupling, indicating that the plate coupling distribution potentially influence the temporal variation in seismic velocity of the accretionary prism through both the fluid amount affected by the stress field.

presentations.presentation_title: Tidal Strain Dependence of Seismic Attenuation
presentations.abstract: Small stress changes induced by Earth tides are known to trigger micro-earthquakes and slow-slip events (e.g., Cochran et al., 2004; Thomas et al., 2009). While tidal responses in seismic velocity and attenuation (Q -1 ) have been reported in shallow sedimentary layers (e.g., Yamamura et al., 2003; Takano & Nishida, 2023), detecting such subtle variations at greater depths remains challenging due to increased rock stiffness. This study aims to quantify the tidal strain (ε) dependence of Q -1 in the crust and uppermost mantle.We analyzed aftershocks (M2–5) of the 2008 Iwate-Miyagi Nairiku earthquake occurring between 15 June 2008 and 10 March 2011. Hypocenters obtained from the Japan Meteorological Agency unified catalog were relocated using the double-difference method. ε was calculated on a grid with a horizontal interval of 0.2° and a depth interval of 10 km using the TidalStrain.2 (https://www.mri-jma.go.jp/Dep/sei/fhirose/research/TidalStrain.html). We estimated the ray-path average of the linear strain parallel to the wave propagation direction for each event-station pair by linearly interpolating and converting the six components of strain tensor at each grid point. To extract Q -1 , we employed the Twofold Spectral Ratio (TSR) method. This approach can estimate uniformed Q -1 in the analysis region by taking the ratio of spectral ratios from two events recorded at two different stations. We categorized the TSR into bins based on the magnitude of ε and performed stacking within each bin. Q -1 was then estimated by fitting the theoretical equation to the stacked TSR of direct P wave. Our result suggests a positive correlation between ε and Q -1 . This observation is consistent with rock experiments, where increased strain leads to higher intrinsic attenuation. We further discuss the depth dependence of this tidal sensitivity, providing new constraints on the rheological properties in the crust to uppermost mantle.

presentations.presentation_title: Time-lapse In-situ Vp/vs Analysis of Hydraulic-fracturing-induced Earthquakes
presentations.abstract: Pore pressure change has been long recognized to play a critical role in triggering earthquakes related to fluid injection in subsurface energy development. However, tracking pore pressure evolution during/after industrial operation has proven challenging. In this study, we present an improved non-tomographic time-lapse Vp/Vs ratio monitoring strategy using dense nodal array data in two shale gas development regions of active hydraulic fracturing (HF). In the Changning region of Sichuan Basin, China, we observe in-situ Vp/Vs ratios increase from ~1.73 to 1.80, approximately 5-10 days prior to the occurrence of magnitude M3-4 earthquakes on pre-existing faults that intersect with hydraulic fractures. Using an experimental effective-stress framework, we also estimate a corresponding pore-pressure increase of around 10-20 MPa, which may drive fluid diffusion to prime a larger fault area in anticipation of M3+ earthquakes. We will further apply this technique to the Montney Formation in Northeast British Columbia, Canada, where the Northern Montney has experienced frequent M3-4 HF-induced earthquakes in the past five years. When enabled with real-time data telemetry, the in-situ Vp/Vs approach may provide a new monitoring strategy that complements event-magnitude-based traffic light protocols to improve seismic hazard assessment and mitigation during active hydraulic fracturing operations.

presentations.presentation_title: Pore Pressure Diffusion and Fluid-induced Seismicity in the Baihetan Reservoir, Southwest China
presentations.institution: University of Science and Technology of China
presentations.abstract: Large-scale hydropower reservoirs can induce seismicity by perturbing crustal stress and pore pressure conditions during impoundment. In this study, we investigate the coupled hydromechanical processes associated with the Baihetan Reservoir in southwest China, located near the northern Xiaojiang and Zemuhe fault systems. Using seismic ambient noise interferometry, we monitored the temporal variations in seismic velocity associated with a ~50 m rise in water level. Our observations reveal pronounced depth- and region-dependent velocity changes. At shallow depths (~200 m), widespread velocity reductions are attributed to pore pressure diffusion, while localized velocity increases at greater depths (~600 m) are linked to elastic loading. Notably, we identified a fluid-active region, where persistent velocity reductions occur, suggesting deeper fluid penetration in this area. To validate these observations, we constructed a nonlinear poroelastic model based on Biot’s theory of poroelasticity, which successfully reproduces the observed shallow velocity changes. Modeling results suggest that the fluid-active region is characterized by relatively high permeability. High-resolution seismic tomography models obtained using the tomoDDMC technique further reveal low S-wave velocity and high Vp/Vs anomalies extending to ~4 km depth, providing evidence for deep fluid migration within this region. Induced seismicity is preferentially clustered along structural transition zones between high and low velocity and Vp/Vs anomalies. Furthermore, source parameter analysis further reveals that earthquakes within the fluid-active region exhibit significantly lower stress drops, implying reduced fault strength due to fluid infiltration. This integrated analysis highlights that pore pressure diffusion governs seismic triggering in permeable zones in the Baihetan Reservoir and offers a comprehensive framework for understanding stress-fluid interactions in tectonically active reservoir settings.

presentations.presentation_title: Revisiting the Origin and Significance of the Paleoproterozoic Complex in the Himalaya: New Insights from Apatite Geochemistry
presentations.abstract: This study examines the tectono-thermal evolution of the Paleoproterozoic complex in the Arun area, eastern Nepal, highlighting the role of apatite geochemistry, along with zircon U–Pb dating and whole-rock analyses. New zircon dating from orthogneisses in the Main Central Thrust (MCT) zone and High Himalayan Crystalline Sequence (HHCS) yield crystallization ages of ca. 1.79–1.78 Ga and 1.85–1.81 Ga, respectively. Combined with published data, coeval Paleoproterozoic magmatism in the HHCS and Lesser Himalayan Sequences support a once-unified continental crust. Detrital zircon data from HHCS metasediments indicate deposition during the Paleoproterozoic, contemporaneous with magmatism. Whole-rock-apatite compositions exclude an I-type origin, while high Y and low Ce-As contents in apatite supports a crustal-derived S-type affinity. Negative Eu anomalies in apatite from MCT orthogneisses imply plagioclase-rich protoliths; in contrast, apatite from HHCS orthogneisses lacks Eu anomalies and shows low Mn-Y contents, suggesting garnet-bearing, plagioclase-poor protoliths. The Paleoproterozoic magmatism was likely driven by rift- or plume-related processes, ultimately leading to the development of a passive margin. Multiple pulses at ca. 1.87, 1.82, and 1.79 Ga, with mafic underplating, triggered crustal melting. Protolith differences in the MCT hanging wall reflect lateral variations in HHCS lithostratigraphy, more pronounced than previously recognized.

presentations.presentation_title: Decoupled Hydrogen-Halogen Diffusion in Apatite Records Rapid Magma Ascent
presentations.institution: Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, The University of Hong Kong
presentations.abstract: Magma ascent rate governs the critical transition between explosive and effusive volcanism, yet quantifying this rate remains challenging. Apatite volatile zonation (F-Cl-OH) offers a promising speedometer, though its application to complex eruption cycles requires rigorous kinetic validation. Here, we explore the utility of this chronometer by investigating the 2006 Rabaul eruption, sequentially comprising sub-Plinian, effusive, and Vulcanian phases. High-resolution nanoscale secondary ion mass spectrometry (NanoSIMS) mapping and multi-component (F-Cl-OH) diffusion modelling (Li et al., 2020) reveal a notable feature in the explosion products: OH abundance deviates from apatite stoichiometry-based prediction and its zoning distances consistently exceed those predicted by F-Cl-OH diffusion models. This may indicate a decoupling between hydrogen (fast) and halogen (slow) diffusion, driven by abrupt changes in water fugacity associated with bubble nucleation and growth during decompression. This process is supposedly more prominent during explosive phases. Incorporating the hydrogen diffusion, we calculate ascent durations to be merely minutes to hours for explosive phases, corresponding to average ascent rates exceeding 1 m/s. These agree with the instantaneous velocities derived from bubble number density (~60 m/s), which captures a "snapshot" of rapid decompression at fragmentation (Bernard & Costa, 2024) and needs to be higher than the average rate from degassing to eruption recorded by apatite, provided a non-linear acceleration. In comparison, apatite in lavas records smaller H gradients, supporting longer durations (~weeks to months) of magma stalling and degassing, consistent with previous studies (Bernard et al., 2022). These findings not only validate volatile-in-apatite chronometry but also refine the method by accounting for rapid H diffusion during bubble nucleation, offering a tool to trace magmatic processes at an hourly temporal resolution. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (42303046) and Hong Kong Research Grants Council (GRF 17306324).

presentations.presentation_title: Refining Tephrostratigraphic Correlation Methods Using Zircon Trace Elements, Hf Isotopes, and Hosted Melt Inclusion Geochemistry: a Taupō Volcanic Zone Case Study
presentations.abstract: Tephrostratigraphy is an important tool in geoscience that can be applied for paleoenvironment reconstructions, modelling tectonic and petrogenetic processes, and even dating and correlating important archaeological or paleontological events. However, its application becomes challenging in older deposits where volcanic glass has been completely altered by weathering. For this reason, alternative approaches are needed to fingerprint weathered tephra layers that no longer preserve their original geochemical fingerprint in their volcanic glass shards and most primary minerals. This study focuses on zircons, as this mineral is highly resistant to alteration, pressure and temperature, and can preserve primordial information for long periods of geological time. Therefore, their hosted melt inclusions can remain protected from post-depositional alteration, maintaining the geochemical signature of the magma at the time of entrapment. Zircon trace-elements geochemistry and εHf isotopic signatures are further evaluated as complementary correlation tools and indicators of magma source characteristics.The Taupō Volcanic Zone (TVZ), Aotearoa/New Zealand, provides an ideal case of study to test these methods due to their widely documented tephrostratigraphic record. Well-studied rhyolitic tephras from Taupō and Okataina calderas are used as reference deposits where volcanic glass shards remain preserved. Major and trace element geochemistry of glass shards is directly compared with melt inclusions to assess their geochemical resemblance and their suitability for tephra fingerprinting. This approach further enables the evaluation of zircon crystal morphologies associated with melt inclusion entrapment, identifying populations that most likely crystallised during the final stages of the magma prior the eruption.This research highlights the potential use of zircons, not only for geochronology, but as geochemical tools to extract primordial information from old altered volcanic deposits. Moreover, these methodologies can be transferred for correlating volcanic deposits and reconstructing magmatic processes across older volcano-sedimentary basins worldwide.

presentations.presentation_title: New Experimental Data for Apatite-melt Volatile Partitioning in Intermediate-felsic Magmas
presentations.institution: The University of Hong Kong, The Australian National University
presentations.abstract: For apatite to be a useful monitor of volatiles in magmas we must first determine the partitioning of volatiles between apatite and melts. Here, we investigated CO 2 , hydroxyl, fluoride, chloride and sulfur partitioning between apatite and synthetic rhyolite/andesite melts at 3 to 10 kbar and 800 to 900 °C, using piston-cylinder apparatus. Volatile concentrations in the experimental charges were measured by secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) and electron probe microanalysis. Our results show that melt composition influences the crystallization behavior of apatite, with rhyolite melts containing smaller crystals than those in andesite, regardless of run duration. The presence of fluorine in the system favors partitioning of chlorine into the melt phase. The partition coefficients will be reported in the presentation. These results provide insights into apatite crystallization behavior and contribute to accurate modeling of apatite-melt volatile partitioning in igneous systems. This work was supported by Hong Kong Research Grants Council (ECS 27302423).

presentations.presentation_title: Zircon Petrochronology of the World’s Youngest Topaz Rhyolites and Implications for Pegmatite Genesis
presentations.abstract: Topaz rhyolites represent erupted equivalents of evolved silicic melts and offer a rare opportunity to investigate pronounced magma differentiation without complexities imposed by plutonic textural maturation typical of pegmatites. Topaz rhyolites are marked by exceptional enrichment of incompatible elements, which parallels that of pegmatites, yet their volcanic expression preserves clearer snapshots of the magmatic processes that generate economically important critical mineral assemblages in pegmatites. Here, we present case studies from two of the world’s youngest topaz rhyolites: the Quaternary Blackfoot (Idaho) and Mineral Mountains (Utah) volcanic fields, both situated within the Great Basin extensional province. Zircon from these rhyolites displays high abundances of non‑stoichiometric components (Y+REE, Hf, Th, U), sometimes leading to exsolution of phases enriched in these elements. Other accessory minerals where Y and Th are stoichiometric components include clinofergusonite and thorite, respectively. Near‑ and sub‑solidus Ti‑in‑zircon temperatures, coupled with low Eu/Eu*, indicate nearly complete solidification of crystal mushes in the shallow crust. Zircon Hf–O isotopes demonstrate that mantle‑derived parental magmas assimilated minor amounts of Archean basement prior to zircon saturation; subsequent melt evolution proceeded with negligible crustal contamination. Thermal histories modelled from zircon crystallization ages and temperatures indicate magma pulses that remained above the solidus only for <100 kyr, consistent with intermittent recharge and solidification cycles. Progressive temporal evolution toward more highly fractionated melt compositions in both fields supports episodic rejuvenation of small upper‑crustal reservoirs by mantle‑derived recharge. The formation of pegmatite‑like melts erupted as topaz rhyolites is intimately linked to mantle magmatism interacting with Archean crust during Basin and Range extension. Zircon and other accessory minerals in topaz rhyolites thus provide a unique framework for quantifying melt differentiation processes and the concentration of critical elements in subvolcanic magma reservoirs that are likely precursors for pegmatites.

presentations.presentation_title: Cathodoluminescence and chemical composition of apatite from the Cordon Syenite Complex, Isabela, Philippines: Implications for porphyry Cu-Au exploration
presentations.abstract: The Cordon Syenite Complex in Isabela, Philippines represents a multi-phase alkalic intrusive complex that hosts several porphyry Cu-Au and epithermal Au deposits. In this study, we focus on the Quemaldero porphyry Cu-Au prospect, which is characterized by porphyritic intrusive rocks varying from monzonite to syenite. The porphyritic monzonite and porphyritic syenite contain apatite as an accessory phase within a groundmass composed of K-feldspar, plagioclase, clinopyroxene and biotite. Optical cathodoluminescence highlights different crystal zones of brown and greenish yellow. Major and trace element composition of apatite in the porphyritic syenite is distinct from those of the porphyritic monzonite. Sulfur content of apatite from the porphyritic syenite reaches up to ~0.6 wt%, while only up to ~0.2 wt% from the porphyritic monzonite. Apatite from both rocks show enrichment of light REE compared to heavy REE, with a more negative Eu anomaly in the apatite of the porphyritic monzonite. Apatite is also present in rocks that contain Cu mineralization accompanied by pervasive albitization of the groundmass. Cathodoluminescence spectra of both apatite from the weakly-altered and mineralized rocks have highest peaks at ~380 nm. Outer crystal zones of apatite from the mineralized rocks have higher intensity in the red region (~700 nm). The apatite from the mineralized rocks geochemically resembles the apatite from the porphyritic syenite in terms of halogens, S and REE contents. Higher S content of apatite in the porphyritic syenite is consistent with favorable conditions for porphyry Cu mineralization. In this study, we demonstrate that mineral chemistry of apatite is a potentially effective tool for delineating which intrusive phases are more related to mineralization.

presentations.presentation_title: Joint Vp–vs Inversion Based on Guided P–surface Cross-term Signals
presentations.institution: University of Science and Technology of China (USTC)
presentations.abstract: Recent advances have demonstrated the potential of guided P waves for subsurface imaging. However, high-quality guided P-wave observations typically rely on dense active-source surveys, which are costly and environmentally intrusive. In passive seismic data, guided P waves are generally weak and difficult to identify in ambient noise, motivating the development of alternative approaches for extracting guided-wave information.Here, we identify a previously underexplored cross-term signal from the cross-correlation of continuous industrial vibrations generated by geothermal power plants, which we term the guided P–surface phase. This phase arises from the interaction between surface waves at a virtual source station and guided P waves recorded at receiver stations. Compared with conventional guided P-wave phases in correlograms, the guided P–surface phase preserves clear dispersive characteristics, exhibits stronger energy, and is better separated in arrival time from other correlation phases, resulting in sharper and more coherent multimode dispersion patterns. Leveraging these advantages, we perform a joint inversion of surface waves and guided P–surface waves to retrieve subsurface P-wave velocity (Vp) profiles. The resulting Vp structure is consistent with S-wave velocity (Vs) models derived from surface waves alone and correlates well with known regional geological features. Our results demonstrate the significant potential of guided P–surface cross-term phases for passive seismic tomography and provide a new avenue for subsurface velocity imaging and monitoring.

presentations.presentation_title: A Decade of Spectral Source-Parameter Estimates for Earthquakes in the Korean Peninsula from 2012 to 2025
presentations.abstract: Seismic source parameters such as seismic moment, corner frequency, and stress drop are widely used to characterize rupture processes and regional seismotectonic properties (Kaneko and Shearer, 2014). They provide fundamental constraints on earthquake source scaling and help interpret spatial variations in earthquake behavior across tectonic provinces. For the Korean Peninsula, Rhee and Sheen (2016) estimated these parameters for 651 earthquakes during 2001–2014 and highlighted spatial variations in stress drop. Recent densification of the seismic network in the Korean Peninsula increases station coverage, which can improve the robustness of spectral source parameter estimates. It remains important to examine whether these patterns persist when the dataset is extended using consistent processing. In this study, we update the catalog through 2025 to provide an updated reference for the Korean Peninsula and to reassess whether previously reported regional patterns persist. We processed 1,433 earthquakes during 2012–2025 (M L ≥ 2.0) using SourceSpec (Satriano, 2022) to construct a catalog of source parameters. Three-component seismograms were analyzed, and deep-learning–based picks (Hong et al., 2023) were used to define S-wave signal and pre-event noise windows. SourceSpec computed displacement spectra, corrected for geometrical spreading and regional attenuation (Kim, 2007) and then inverted the spectra using a Brune source model (Brune, 1970) to estimate M 0 and f c with uncertainties. The updated catalog provides a consistent reference dataset for future source parameter studies and for interpreting regional seismotectonic characteristics in the Korean Peninsula.The resulting catalog enables systematic assessment of M W –f c scaling behavior and mapping of stress drop variations across major tectonic provinces in the Korean Peninsula. We discuss how spatial patterns in stress drop may reflect regional differences in crustal strength and stress state, and we will compare our updated estimates with Rhee and Sheen (2016) to provide context for regional patterns.

presentations.presentation_title: Multi-image Fusion of Dispersion Energy Images for Enhanced Surface Wave Inversion
presentations.abstract: Surface wave inversion is a widely used approach for estimating subsurface shear-wave (S-wave) velocity structures, and its accuracy and stability largely depend on the completeness and reliability of the extracted dispersion information. In practical applications, dispersion energy images derived from a single acquisition configuration often suffer from limited frequency coverage or ambiguous modal features due to constraints imposed by observation geometry and data quality. These limitations can adversely affect the robustness of dispersion curve inversion and, consequently, the reliability of S-wave velocity models. To address this issue, this study proposes a multi-image fusion strategy to enhance surface wave inversion by integrating dispersion energy images obtained from multiple seismic acquisition configurations. By exploiting complementary frequency content and modal characteristics across different energy images, the proposed approach improves the continuity and clarity of dispersion features prior to inversion. The fusion framework is developed based on kernel principal component analysis, with the Nyström approximation employed to reduce computational cost and memory demand, thereby improving computational efficiency and practical applicability. The effectiveness of the proposed fusion-assisted inversion strategy is demonstrated using both synthetic and field data examples. The results show that dispersion curves extracted from the fused energy images exhibit broader frequency coverage and clearer modal patterns compared to those obtained from individual datasets. Consequently, the subsequent surface wave inversion yields more accurate and stable S-wave velocity profiles. These findings indicate that multi-image fusion of dispersion energy representations can significantly enhance the reliability of surface wave inversion, particularly in complex geological settings involving multiple acquisition geometries.

presentations.presentation_title: Imaging the Mantle Transition Zone Discontinuities Using SKS-to-P Receiver Functions
presentations.abstract: Combined analyses of P-to-S (Ps) and S-to-P (Sp) receiver functions (RFs) can tightly constrain velocity gradients across subsurface discontinuities. While Ps RFs are widely used to image structures from the crust to the mantle transition zone (MTZ), applications of Sp phases are largely limited to resolving lithospheric boundaries due to their near-critical incidence angles at deeper interfaces. Specifically, Sp conversions from the 410- and 660-km discontinuities are detectable only within epicentral distance ranges of ~80‒104° and ~95‒106°, respectively. Beyond 85°, interference from core-refracted phases near the S-wave arrival further limits Sp RF imaging of the MTZ. Here, we evaluate the effectiveness of core-refracted SKS-to-P (SKSp) RFs for MTZ imaging using teleseismic observations collected across the contiguous United States. Waveform modeling indicates that the deep, near-vertical SKS phase yields observable MTZ conversions (SKS410p and SKS660p) over ~85‒120°. However, our data reveal pervasive coherent energy that interferes with both phases within this range. For example, these target signals, especially SKS410p, overlap with MTZ conversions from other S phases at distances <100°, including direct S, ScS, and SKKS. Moreover, SKSp MTZ conversions are contaminated by intricate, source-dependent arrivals, ranging from free-surface P-wave multiples for deep-focus earthquakes to multiple conversions at both receiver- and source-side MTZ boundaries for shallow events. In this study, we introduce a data-screening strategy that narrows the respective distance ranges to 96‒107° for SKS410p and 90‒105° for SKS660p, and excludes data affected by additional coherent energy. The retained SKSp RFs produce MTZ topographic images that are generally consistent with those derived from Ps RFs, with correlation coefficients of ~0.5 for both discontinuities. The 660 image is substantially more reliable than the 410 image, as SKS660p experiences less interference from coherent noise than SKS410p.

presentations.presentation_title: Exploration of Natural Hydrogen Resources in the Kurosegawa Tectonic Zone Using the Magnetotelluric Method
presentations.institution: Dept of Earth Resources Engineering, Kyushu University
presentations.abstract: Natural hydrogen is gaining significant attention as an untapped subsurface resource essential for realizing a carbon-neutral society. Focusing on serpentinite bodies within the Kurosegawa Tectonic Zone in Kyushu, this study conducted a broadband magnetotelluric (MT) survey in Gokase Town, Miyazaki Prefecture. The study area is characterized by highly alkaline hot springs (pH 9.3) and drill cores containing intensely sheared serpentinite mixed with fresh peridotite, suggesting active hydrogen generation driven by ongoing serpentinization. The MT survey revealed low-resistivity structures corresponding to the serpentinite body, fluid pathways, and fracture systems. In this presentation, we discuss a hydrogen migration model based on the estimated subsurface resistivity structures.

presentations.presentation_title: Taiwan’s Natural Hydrogen Potential from a Geophysical Perspective
presentations.abstract: The global demand of hydrogen in 2024 has reached nearly 100 Mt and is increasing. Instead of engineering production of hydrogen, the existence of natural hydrogen attracts more and more attention. The natural hydrogen could be generated from different ways. Among all, the radiolysis, the deep-seated and the serpentinization are most common. In Taiwan, the subduction of the Eurasian Plate beneath the Philippine Sea Plate along the Manila Trench could cause the serpentinization in southern Taiwan. Serpentinization is a form of low-temperature (0 to ~600 °C) metamorphism of ferromagnesian minerals in mafic or ultramafic rocks. However, during a serpentinization, hydration of the mantle wedge above the subducting plate could occur. The density of partial mantle wedge will therefore decrease and a heat of 40kJ per mole of water will be released. As a result, we may observe a corresponding low bouguer (gravity) anomaly and a high heat-flow at surface. Because the mantle wedge consists of high iron-rich rocks such as peridotite, the serpentinization process will cause the iron minerals to be oxidized. Thus, a high magnetization area could also be observed together with the generation of the hydrogen. Taking into account all the existing geophysical data in Taiwan, we show that the area to the south of the Xinwulu River in northern Taitung County, Taiwan, could meet the geophysical conditions for the existence of natural hydrogen at depth. To assess the potential of the natural hydrogen in Taiwan, further geologic, geochemical and geophysical studies are necessary.

presentations.presentation_title: Mineralogical and Geochemical Factors Affecting Hydrogen Generation during Low Temperature Serpentinization
presentations.abstract: Geologic hydrogen has been recently proposed to be an energy source with relatively low cost and low carbon footprint compared with other hydrogens (e.g., green and blue hydrogens). Among various potential mechanisms to generate hydrogen in subsurface environments, serpentinization of ultramafic rocks in ophiolite belts is most feasible in the areas with active tectonic settings such as Japan (Ballentine et al., 2025). While serpentinization reaction has been known to occur at high temperature environments (e.g., 200 – 300ºC), such as mantle wedge during subduction, it may also occur near surface environments (e.g., <100ºC), which shows the highest hydrogen fluxes to the surface (Aquino et al., 2025). However, there is a gap in the rate of hydrogen production on low temperature serpentinization between the field measurements and experimental/theoretical estimates. Therefore, we investigated mineralogical and geochemical factors affecting the hydrogen generation in series of batch experiments by comparing (1) various types of ultramafic rocks as the starting materials (Ohtomo et al., 2025). Results of the batch experiments show that fresh harzburgite samples yielded the highest amounts of hydrogen, whereas serpentinized samples tend to generate lower amounts of hydrogen. This suggests that hydrogen was primarily generated by dissolution of olivine and pyroxene. Chemical compositions of the recovered solution indicate that samples with fresh peridotites results in lower pH (8.1 – 9.0 at 25ºC) as well as higher dissolved Si and Ca concentrations. Mg-bearing silicates likely buffered the solution at the pH. Therefore, we propose that dissolution of pyroxene promotes precipitation of the Mg-bearing silicates and hydrogen generation. Another series of batch experiments, in which chemical reagents were added to a fresh harzburgite, demonstrate that hydrogen generation was enhanced in Si-rich solutions, which may provide a new insight into preferable conditions to generate more hydrogen in near surface environments.

presentations.presentation_title: Assessing the Potential of Natural Hydrogen Resources in Eastern Taiwan Using Soil and Vent Gas Geochemical Surveys
presentations.abstract: As Taiwan advances toward its 2050 net-zero emissions target, hydrogen energy has been designated as one of the nation’s twelve Key Strategic Technologies. Natural hydrogen has attracted growing global attention due to its low production cost, zero carbon emissions, and continuous natural replenishment, yet its occurrence and geological controls in tectonically active regions remain poorly constrained. This study investigates the potential presence and characteristics of natural hydrogen in eastern Taiwan, focusing on the Qingshui geothermal field in Yilan and the Luoshan mud volcano field in Hualien. An integrated approach combining in situ soil gas measurements with laboratory-based gas compositional analyses was employed. A total of 108 field measurement sites were surveyed, and 35 gas samples were analyzed using gas chromatography. The results reveal two distinct degassing systems. The Qingshui geothermal field represents a fault-controlled hydrothermal system with hydrogen concentrations up to 996 ppm, but gas compositions are dominated by carbon dioxide (>95%), indicating strong decarbonation and hydrogen dilution. In contrast, the Luoshan mud volcano field exhibits a methane-dominated sediment-hosted system, where hydrogen concentrations fall within recognized anomaly thresholds. Overall, this study provides the first field-based evidence for indigenous natural hydrogen resources in eastern Taiwan.

presentations.presentation_title: Nedo Geologic Hydrogen Program
presentations.institution: New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization
presentations.abstract: NEDO (New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization) has launched the Frontier Development Program to promote R&D and commercialization in the frontier fields that the country should tackle, with the aim of creating new industries by 2040. NEDO has selected "Utilization of Unused Subsurface Resources" as one of the frontier fields, and the geologic hydrogen was selected as one of the research topics in the field. Low-cost and clean hydrogen is considered to be essential to achieve carbon neutrality, and both academia and industry are showing strong interests in geologic hydrogen in Japan. A call for proposals on geologic hydrogen was made, and 5 awardees have been selected and announced on May 23 rd , 2025. In this presentation, the Frontier Development Program and the NEDO Geologic Hydrogen Program will be introduced. The future direction of geologic hydrogen in Japan will be also discussed.

presentations.presentation_title: Effect of Seamount Subduction on Seismic Couping: Constraint from Morphology and Heat Flow in Hyuga-nada, Western Nankai Trough
presentations.institution: Earthquake Research Institute, The University of Tokyo
presentations.abstract: Subducting seamounts modify stress and strength conditions along megathrusts, influencing earthquake generation and weakening interplate coupling. In Hyuga-nada, where no M8-class earthquakes have been recorded, the Kyushu–Palau Ridge (KPR) is subducting and slow earthquakes cluster around the subducted KPR (sKPR). To investigate structural and thermal controls, we combined BSR-derived and surface heat flow measurements with seismic reflection data. The sKPR underlies the Toi Seamount, with its edges defined by magnetic anomalies and seafloor slopes. Frequent low-frequency tremors coincide with steep basement gradients, suggesting that sKPR “edges” regulate tremor activity.Seafloor morphology and deformation patterns reflect KPR subduction: compressional structures dominate the N–NW, including NE–SW ridges and exhumed thrusts, whereas the SE side shows extensive collapse and landslide deposits. BSR-derived heat flow around sKPR is low (~40 mW/m²), consistent with the cold, old WPB crust. Even lower values (~25 mW/m²) occur above thrusts on the northern side, likely due to sediment thickening and reduced thermal gradients caused by seamount-induced compression and sediment blockage by Toi Seamount.In contrast, anomalously high surface heat flows (>300 mW/m²) near thrusts in front of Toi Seamount suggest focused fluid discharge. Supporting evidence includes proximity to thrust scarps, a low-velocity zone near tremor clusters, and pore-water chemical anomalies. Poroelastic modeling indicates that seamount loading can drive fluid circulation if permeability is high. However, data remain limited and alternative explanations cannot be ruled out; direct confirmation of fluid expulsion awaits future studies.

presentations.presentation_title: Onshore-offshore Geodetic and Seismic Constraints on Fault Interactions Between Eastern Taiwan and the Southern Ryukyu Subduction Zone
presentations.abstract: The southern Ryukyu subduction zone, adjacent to northeastern Taiwan, is a complex transitional region where oblique plate convergence, back-arc rifting, and upper-plate deformation intersect. Using integrated onshore and seafloor geodetic data and seismicity, we investigate fault slip behaviors near the southern termination of the Ryukyu subduction zone. We identify a slow-slip event (SSE) that occurred in May 2022 and lasted for about one year off the northeastern coast of Taiwan. GNSS stations from Yilan to Nanao recorded southeastward displacements of approximately 5–15 mm during the SSE. We inferred the SSE source using a uniform-slip elastic dislocation model. The preferred model requires ~12 cm of slip on a 60-km-long and 120-km-wide fault segment on the plate interface, equivalent to a Mw 7 event. These motions show a strong temporal correlation with plate-interface seismicity beneath the Nanao forearc basin. Furthermore, adjacent seafloor geodetic measurements from 2022 and 2023 deviate from the secular trend and require an additional southward motion component to be explained. This interval also coincides with elevated seismicity rates and earthquake swarms near Hualien prior to the 3 April 2024 Mw 7.3 earthquake, suggesting that these SSEs might have contributed to the stress loading preceding the 2024 earthquake. Integrating offshore and onshore geodetic monitoring is essential to understanding the complex fault interactions between eastern Taiwan and the southern Ryukyu subduction zone.

presentations.presentation_title: Measurement of Seafloor Crustal Movement in the Ryukyu Trench
presentations.abstract: The Ryukyu Trench is the plate boundary where the Philippine Sea Plate subducts beneath the Eurasian Plate. Near Okinawa Island, a source region is thought to have generated a tsunami earthquake in 1791 during the Ryukyu Kingdom period (Nakamura et al., 2013), and a previous study in 2018 estimated the extent of the coupling zone using seafloor geodetic observations (Tadokoro et al., 2018). The East China Sea is characterized by complex tectonics, including back-arc spreading (Sibuet et al., 1987), but the distribution of islands limits the availability of continuous onshore GNSS stations, making it difficult to constrain crustal deformation using land-based observations alone. To address this limitation, we reanalyze seafloor geodetic data along the Ryukyu Trench by incorporating additional observations since 2018, as well as data from two newly established seafloor sites. The data were acquired using the GNSS-Acoustic technique, which combines GNSS positioning at the sea surface with acoustic ranging to seafloor transponders (Spiess et al., 1998). Data processing and analysis were performed using the open-source software GARPOS (Watanabe et al., 2020). We analyzed the data at three sites: RKB (2011-2024; 12 times), RKC (2016-2023; 4 times), and RKD (2016-2022; 3 times). The derived site velocities are 3.8 mm/yr to the southwestward at RKB, 18.0 mm/yr to the west at RKC, and 30.1 mm/yr to the southwest at RKD, relative to Okinawa Island. The site velocities at RKC and RKD have large uncertainties; however, further improvement is expected by using additional observational data and refining parameters in analysis, such as the initial conditions used in the inversion. The resulting spatial variations in horizontal velocity provide new constraints on the distribution of inter-plate coupling and the deformation processes associated with subduction and back-arc tectonics along the Ryukyu Trench.

presentations.presentation_title: Seamount Subduction and Crustal Deformation Along Subduction Margins: Are Marine Terraces Grooves of the Earthquake Record?
presentations.institution: National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Holocene marine terraces record past relative sea-level changes and have been widely interpreted as important geomorphic evidence of crustal deformation associated with megathrust earthquakes.However, many marine terraces have been discussed primarily in terms of their correlation with coseismic uplift, without being evaluated using kinematically or mechanically consistent deformation models. As a result, a fundamental criticism remains unresolved: coseismic uplift should be canceled by interseismic subsidence.We evaluate the persistence of surface deformation through repeated earthquakes using a suite of existing and newly constructed subduction models. We systematically examine (i) the effects of the presence or absence of plate-interface roughness, (ii) the sensitivity of the results to different boundary conditions, and (iii) apply our models to the Boso Peninsula, where plate-interface geometry is well constrained by seismic surveys.Our analyses lead to four main conclusions: (1) Bumps on the plate interface can act as primary control on surface deformation. (2) The amount of residual surface deformation is determined primarily by plate-interface geometry, regardless of the coupling zone configuration. (3) Marine terraces can be preserved only where coastlines are located within both the coseismic uplift zone and the long-term uplift zone. (4) In models incorporating rough plate-interface geometry, stress boundary conditions are more appropriate than displacement boundary conditions.The formation of marine terraces along subduction margins is controlled more strongly by the plate interface geometry than by earthquake magnitude. This implication is consistent with the observation that many prominent Holocene marine terraces are located above regions where subduction of seamounts has been inferred.Meanwhile, resolving kilometer-scale plate-interface geometry requires intensive seismic surveys, and such data are available only in limited regions. We therefore argue that robust inference of past megathrust earthquakes from marine terraces requires detailed geomorphic and geological investigation with improved geophysical constraints on subsurface plate structure.

presentations.presentation_title: Structural Segmentation of Magmatic Intrusions and Fluid Distribution in a Back-arc Rift: Seismic Studies in the Southern Okinawa Trough
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: The Okinawa Trough is an active continental rift system transitioning from continental extension to incipient seafloor spreading. Understanding how deformation and magmatism are spatially segmented in such back-arc settings is essential for linking upper-plate tectonics to subduction-zone processes. In the southern Okinawa Trough, pronounced variations in faulting, magmatism, seismicity, and hydrothermal activity indicate strong structural segmentation.Here we present new multichannel seismic reflection data that constrain the pseudo-three-dimensional geometry of igneous intrusions and associated fluid and gas distributions beneath the Yaeyama Rift, one of the active rift segments in the region. Our dataset comprises seven profiles across the rift axis and one along-axis profile acquired during two R/V Hakuho-maru cruises (KH-23-11 and KH-21-3). The seismic images reveal marked along-rift variations in intrusion morphology and rift architecture.Beneath the Yaeyama Knoll, where high-temperature hydrothermal venting has been documented, a kilometer-scale intrusive body characterized by low seismic reflection amplitudes—likely representing a complex network of dikes—reaches the seafloor. In contrast, an adjacent rift segment hosts a buried intrusion capped by thick sediments and ring-fault–bounded graben structures, suggesting localized caldera collapse. Additional narrow intrusions occur along rift margins and off-axis regions associated with dense arrays of normal faults.These intrusion and fault characteristics vary systematically along the rift axis. The width of the axial intrusive body decreases westward, accompanied by reduced fault displacement, whereas the central and eastern segments exhibit larger fault offsets and greater subsidence. These along-rift variations suggest differences in rift maturity, with the western segment representing a younger stage characterized by active dike intrusion. This interpretation is consistent with the observed distribution of seismicity, including recurrent seismic swarms concentrated in the western segment, interpreted as being induced by ongoing or migrating dike intrusions.

presentations.presentation_title: Characterizing Complex Air Traffic Kinematics Through Seismic and Acoustic Observations
presentations.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Aircraft generate distinctive Doppler signatures in seismic and acoustic recordings, yet most analyses assume constant-velocity flight. In reality, aircraft frequently accelerate, decelerate, and turn, producing more complex signals that demand refined interpretation. We integrate analytical modeling, finite-difference simulations, and Bayesian inversion to recover full flight kinematics from seismic and acoustic data. The approach accurately reconstructs acceleration, deceleration, and turning trajectories, validated using both field observations and archival datasets, including the September 11, 2001 aircraft impact on the World Trade Center. Results resolve previously inaccessible parameters such as acceleration profiles and turning radii, highlighting the potential of seismoacoustic monitoring for aviation safety, airspace management, and forensic event reconstruction.

presentations.presentation_title: Water-depth-controlled Spectral Fringes in Coastal Seismic Signals from Marine Surveys
presentations.institution: University of Science and Technology of China (USTC)
presentations.abstract: We report a series of seismic signals recorded by seismic stations in northern Norway that propagate over large distances and exhibit relatively high-frequency content (5–20 Hz). These signals display strong, time-varying spectral power across multiple frequencies, which we refer to as spectral fringes.We detect these signals and analyze their temporal distribution, then apply beamforming and ray-tracing techniques to locate their sources. The inferred times and locations coincide with official records of local geophysical surveys, suggesting that the signals are generated by seismic survey vessels.To test this hypothesis and investigate the generation mechanism, we construct a layered medium model consisting of a finite water layer over a solid half-space, representing the operational environment of the vessel. Using apparent slowness estimates from beamforming and the model’s boundary conditions, we derive a relationship between the system’s modal frequencies and water-layer thickness. Based on water depth variations along the vessel’s trajectory, we compute the expected frequency evolution and generate theoretical spectral fringes, which show good agreement with the observations.This study elucidates the generation mechanism of a distinctive coastal seismic signal and highlights its potential for improving the interpretation of non-tectonic seismic events and for imaging subsurface structure.

presentations.presentation_title: Low-angle Subduction of the Indian Plate and Earthquake Stress Field Below the Eastern Himalayas
presentations.institution: Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: The Eastern Himalayas region represents active intercontinental convergence and tectonic strike-slip extrusion. It frequently produces large earthquakes that devastate population centres for millions of people. However, there is no accepted explanation for how the widespread strike-slip motion and plate convergence deformation cause the frequent earthquakes. Here, we use new data from our recently deployed broadband seismic array in the Eastern Himalayas region to determine the regional stress field and detailed structural information about the converging plates. The stress field obtained from the earthquake focal mechanisms shows dominant north–south horizontal compression. Across the Eastern Himalayas region from south to north, the identified Indian crust exhibits low-angle subduction of the crust–mantle boundary Moho and flat-ramp geometry of the plate interface termed as the Main Himalayan Thrust. We suggest that the generation of megathrust earthquakes and the uplift of the broad mountains beneath the Eastern Himalayas region can be explained by the dominant north–south compression and a gentle underthrusting of the Indian plate.Reference: Bai, L., Li H., Chen, Z., Zhan, H., Li, G., Mori, J. Ding, L., 2025. Low-angle subduction of the Indian plate and megathrust geometry below the eastern Himalaya, National Science Review, 2025. Nwaf460. https://doi.org/10.1093/nsr/nwaf460.

presentations.presentation_title: Feasibility of S-net Ocean-Bottom Seismograph Waveform Data for FAMT analysis
presentations.abstract: Estimating earthquake source parameters in subduction zones is challenging because strong structural heterogeneity affects seismic waveforms and station coverage is typically one-sided, with most stations located on land. To address these issues, we have developed the First-motion Augmented Moment Tensor (FAMT) analysis (Okamoto et al. EPS 2017, 2018), which simultaneously inverts short-period (4–40 s) first-motion P-waveforms and long-period (10–40 s) full waveforms using synthetic waveforms calculated from a unified land–ocean 3-D structural model. In this study, we investigate the applicability of ocean-bottom seismograph (OBS) waveform data to FAMT analysis, using acceleration records from the Seafloor Observation Network for Earthquakes and Tsunamis along the Japan Trench (S-net). The quality of OBS data is assessed by estimating roll and pitch angles from the head and tail portions of waveforms and confirming their consistency. The records are then rotated into horizontal and vertical components and integrated to obtain velocity waveforms. Components exhibiting abnormal offsets or amplitudes significantly inconsistent with synthetics are excluded based on visual inspection and residuals from preliminary FAMT analysis, as they may indicate abnormal sensor motion or unmodeled fine-scale structure. Synthetic waveforms are calculated using the Heterogeneity, Oceanic-layer, Topography Finite-Difference Method (HOT-FDM; Nakamura et al. BSSA 2012). We apply FAMT analysis to Mw 5–6 events in the source region of the 2011 M9 Tohoku-oki earthquake, using both land-based (F-net, KiK-net) and OBS (S-net) data. The synthetic short-period P-waveforms calculated using the optimal source parameters from the FAMT analysis generally match well with the S-net observations. Long-period full waveforms also reproduce characteristics of the observed waveforms. These results demonstrate the feasibility of S-net OBS waveform data and the HOT-FDM for FAMT analysis. We are grateful to NIED for providing the waveform data. This research is supported by JSPS KAKENHI (20K04101), and JHPCN projects (jh200059-NHA ― jh250084).

presentations.presentation_title: A Seismological Analysis and Forensic Study of the April 22, 2011, Explosion in the Taipei Metropolitan Area
presentations.abstract: On April 22, 2011, a serious fireworks and explosive powder accident occurred in the Taipei metropolitan area, triggering a major fire and a series of subsequent explosions that resulted in multiple casualties and significant structural damage. This study provides a detailed description of the seismological observations of the incident and presents a comprehensive case analysis. Seismo-acoustic signals generated by the explosions were recorded by nearby strong-motion stations and by several broadband seismic stations located as far as 20 km from the source. Infrasound data from this event were used to reconstruct the timing sequence of the subsequent explosions. By jointly analyzing co-located ground motion and acoustic signals, we estimated the proportion of energy released into the atmosphere by the surface air blast, showing that the energy propagated as acoustic waves was significantly greater than that converted into seismic waves. Through systematic analysis of explosion-induced ground motion data and ground truth verification, this study confirms that seismic observations alone can independently determine the explosion location and origin time, providing critical supporting evidence for forensic investigations. These findings highlight the critical role of a dense seismic network in the monitoring, localization, and characterization of explosion events.

presentations.presentation_title: Quantitative assessment of earthquake predictability and predicting powers of forecasting models
presentations.abstract: It is not easy to make deterministic predictions of earthquakes. However, earthquakes are not completely unpredictable. There exists a substantial gap between complete randomness and complete predictability. From an information-theoretic perspective, this article illustrates how the predictability of the earthquake process can be quantified, and shows that earthquake forecasting can be regarded as the process of constructing models that capture predictable structure in observed seismicity relative to complete randomness. This viewpoint distinguishes between model consistency, achievable performance bounds, and genuine gains in information content. It shows that earthquake forecasting remains an active and scientifically challenging field in which both progress and fundamental limitations must be carefully assessed. An entropy-based perspective provides a unifying framework for quantifying predictability, comparing different forecasting models, and clarifying how far observed seismicity departs from purely random behavior. Within this framework, it is essential to distinguish between incremental improvements achieved through model calibration and genuine gains in information content, as well as to recognize the intrinsic upper bounds on forecasting performance imposed by the stochastic nature of the system. In this context, magnitude forecasting emerges as a particularly important direction for future research. Particularly, moving beyond the Gutenberg–Richter law and the assumption of magnitude independence opens avenues for incorporating additional physical constraints and statistical structure. Continued advances along these lines not only deepen our understanding of earthquake processes but also offer the prospect of fundamentally improving the predictive power of seismicity models.

presentations.presentation_title: Dynamic Rupture Simulations on the Central Range and Longitudinal Valley Faults for the 2022 Taiwan Chihshang Earthquake
presentations.abstract: On September 17 and 18, 2022, the M L 6.6 Guanshan and M L 6.8 Chihshang earthquakes struck the Longitudinal Valley in eastern Taiwan. The Chihshang mainshock caused significant surface rupture and widespread damage, representing a major seismic event. The region has traditionally been associated with the east-dipping Longitudinal Valley Fault (LVF). However, recent studies indicate that the sequence primarily ruptured a west-dipping fault plane, highlighting the active role of the Central Range Fault (CRF) and the complex interactions between these oppositely dipping fault systems. In this study, we employed the Spectral Element Method (SEM) for dynamic rupture simulations. Fault geometries were adopted from the Taiwan Earthquake Model (TEM) database, and the initial stress distribution was prescribed following a commonly adopted recipe for strong-motion simulations. Potential rupture areas and slip directions were constrained by jointly interpreting observed and simulated surface deformation and seismic waveform data, providing a consistent explanation of the observations. The simulation results reveal a multi-stage rupture process. The rupture initiated in the middle segment of the CRF, generating the first high Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) area. The rupture then propagated northward along the CRF, producing significant slip near the Yuli segment and a second high-PGA zone. In contrast, the LVF experienced an initial localized rupture near the hypocenter, followed by a second minor rupture in the north, passively triggered by the large-scale slip on the CRF. These results indicate that the rupture dynamics of the sequence were predominantly controlled by the CRF, whereas LVF activity mainly reflects a passive response to stress transfer. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the geometry of the CRF may play a significant role in controlling rupture propagation and modulating the triggering behavior of the LVF. These findings provide a dynamic perspective on the complex rupture process of the Chihshang earthquake sequence.

presentations.presentation_title: Inversion Tectonics within an Aulacogen: Insights from the Kutch Rift Basin, Western India
presentations.institution: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Bhopal
presentations.abstract: The Kutch aulacogen in western India is a Mesozoic rift undergoing post-collision inversion. We investigate the debated kinematics of the Katrol Hill Fault (KHF), one of the active faults in this highly seismic intraplate region. Previous workers have proposed that, geologically, it has behaved as a strike-slip, normal, and a thrust fault through time. To address this conundrum, we present our work on the KHF. Our field observations indicate that the KHF is not a planar structure; rather, it is a well-developed, Jurassic-over-Cretaceous, elastico-frictional thrust fault zone with a well-defined fault core and a wall-rock damage zone. The KHFZ architecture consists of a ~310 m-wide gouge-dominated fault core flanked by extensive rock-dominated hanging-wall and footwall rock-damage zones. The core comprises pulverized gouge, and the damage zone consists of deformed, fractured Bhuj sandstone rocks. An asymmetric, antiform-synform pair was associated with KHF. The KHF zone was observed to crosscut the common north-dipping limb, exposing a ~150 m-wide fault in the footwall synform. Our microstructural observations reveal intragranular and intergranular fractures in quartz and feldspar grains, confirming near-surface deformation conditions and negligible exhumation of the fault zone. Quantitative grain size analysis concurs with our field observations, where coarser grains (mean grain-size 15.57x10 3 µm 2 ) were observed in the hanging wall damage zone, and maximum grain-size reduction was observed close to the fault core (mean grain-size 0.73x10 3 µm 2 ). These outcomes confirm that the KHF is an emergent thrust fault, characterized by a well-developed core and damage zones, as well as an associated antiform-synform pair, indicating fault-propagation folding under near-surface deformation probably by flexural slip. Consequently, the inversion from an earlier extensional to the later compressional tectonics occurs along thrust faults rather than reactivated high-angle normal faults. This work provides rare insights into inversion tectonics in India's neotectonically and seismically active aulacogen.

presentations.presentation_title: Unlocking Fine-scale Crustal Deformation in Japan with Ultra-Dense GNSS Coverage
presentations.abstract: Monitoring Earth’s surface deformation is fundamental to geoscience. Japan’s nationwide GNSS array, the GNSS Earth Observation Network System (GEONET) operated by the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan, has enabled major advances in earthquake and volcanic studies. However, GEONET’s station spacing can limit our ability to resolve deformation signals with short spatial wavelengths. In the last decade, Japanese mobile network operators have built dense GNSS reference-site networks to improve positioning services. Ohta and Ohzono (EPS, 2022) showed that, with appropriate quality control, SoftBank’s private-sector GNSS data can support crustal deformation monitoring. With more than 3,300 sites, about 2.5 times as many as GEONET, the SoftBank network provides exceptionally dense sampling across the Japanese islands. To accelerate scientific use of these observations, Tohoku University’s Graduate School of Science, together with SoftBank Corp. and ALES Corporation, launched an academic–industry consortium. Results obtained through this framework demonstrate the value of ultra-dense GNSS coverage for diverse deformation processes: aseismic deformation in the Noto Peninsula (Nishimura et al., Sci. Rep., 2023), coseismic slip from the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake (Yamada et al., EPS, 2025), and afterslip off western Sado Island (Ohtate et al., EPS, 2025). The same dense coverage enables detailed mapping of interseismic strain accumulation across Japan (Ohtate et al., in revision), and an accuracy assessment shows that daily-coordinate quality is equivalent between GEONET and SoftBank (Ohta and Ohtate, EPS, 2026). In this presentation, we summarize these outcomes and discuss how ultra-dense public–private GNSS networks can expand both the scope and spatial resolution of crustal deformation research in Japan and improves monitoring of transient and steady signals. Acknowledgments: The SoftBank's GNSS observation data used in this study was provided by SoftBank Corp. and ALES Corp. through the framework of the "Consortium to utilize the SoftBank original reference sites for Earth and Space Science".

presentations.presentation_title: Development of Representative Indicators for Evaluating the Operational Performance of On-Site Earthquake Early Warning System
presentations.institution: National Center for Research on Earthquake Engineering, NIAR
presentations.abstract: Taiwan is located on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the Eurasian and Philippine Sea plates meet. Because earthquakes happen often and can be very large, they pose a serious threat to buildings and school safety. To help, the National Center for Research on Earthquake Engineering (NCREE) set up an Earthquake Early Warning (EEW) system. With 98 stations in schools across Taiwan, this system sends out alerts before a major earthquake hits, giving people valuable time to evacuate. However, after running the system for several years, there are two main challenges. First, the cost of maintaining so many stations is increasing, so we need a better way to manage resources. Second, since many schools are in crowded areas, noise from traffic and people often interferes with the sensors. This noise makes it hard to detect the first earthquake waves (P-waves) and can cause false alarms. This study looks at the data from these 98 stations over the last five years. We evaluated their performance by looking at how well they detect earthquakes, how fast they respond, and their false alarm rates. The goal is to find the best stations and identify those that are too noisy. Based on these results, we can improve the technology or move some stations to better locations. This will help the system work better during a big earthquake while keeping maintenance costs low.

presentations.presentation_title: Evaluation of Shakemap Accuracy by Using Structural Vibration Monitoring Systems for Improving Post-earthquake Decision Making
presentations.institution: National Center for Research on Earthquake Engineering, NIAR
presentations.abstract: ShakeMap representing the spatial distribution of the predicted ground motion intensity induced by an earthquake is an essential tool for post-earthquake damage and loss assessment of a target site or a target structure. It is developed based on the strong motion monitoring system as well as the ground motion prediction technique, and it is majorly applied for determining the post-earthquake emergency responses for infrastructures in Taiwan. However, its accuracy and the uncertainty range were not comprehensively discussed. In this study, the structural vibration response dataset collected from the strong motion instruments installed in several real buildings at the ground level were compiled to evaluate the accuracy of the ShakeMap. The possible factors influencing the ShakMap accuracy are discussed including the methodology of producing the ShakeMap and the distance between the target site and its closest station. The empirical equation representing the ShakeMap prediction uncertainty is developed for capturing the possible spatial distributed ground motion intensity range, and the difference of the ground motion intensity of the free-field and the structural ground level floor is also quantified. The analysis result of this study is beneficial for determining the most appropriate post-earthquake emergency response to improve the recovery work and to reduce the further impact and loss caused by the disaster earthquake.

presentations.presentation_title: Performance of the Uttarakhand State Earthquake Early Warning System during the 22 May 2025, Western Nepal Earthquake
presentations.abstract: The development of the Uttarakhand State Earthquake Early Warning System (UEEWS), based on a regional approach, was initiated in 2014 and officially launched to the public on 4 August 2021. A central server is established in Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee (IITR) to fetch the data from 170 sensors installed in the seismogenic region of Uttarakhand, a Himalayan state of India. On 22 May 2025, a light earthquake of magnitude (M w ) 4.3 at a depth of 10 Km was occurred in the western part of Nepal, as reported by the nodal agency ‘National Center for Seismology’ responsible for monitoring seismic activity in the region. The nearest seismic sensor of UEEWS’s instruments array was just at the epicentral distance of 27 Km. Three reports were generated by the server. The first report was generated based on five stations data, and system estimated low pass filtered peak displacement-based magnitude (M Pd ) 3.67 and depth 20 Km. Second report was generated based on six stations data, estimating M Pd 4.52 and depth 40 Km. Subsequently, system discarded few older P-onset and identified new P-onset picks, hence, a third report was generated based on six stations data, estimating M Pd 3.98 and depth 10 Km. Users who had installed the mobile app “BhuDEV” received warnings. After the earthquake, performance of the system was checked. For this, data recorded by the 100 sensors were processed and P- and S- onset in the recorded accelerograms were manually examined. Using the origin and reporting time of the earthquake, lead (warning) time was estimated. It was found that users who installed the mobile app received warnings ranging from seconds to tens of seconds. This article explains the working of the UEEWS, data processing methods, models used to estimate earthquake parameters, algorithms and the mode of warning dissemination in detail.

presentations.presentation_title: Pervasive Fluid Migration Pathways in Japan Subduction Zone Revealed by Tidal Sensitivity
presentations.institution: Chinese Academy of Sciences/ Earthquake research institute The University of Tokyo
presentations.abstract: The fluid migration has long been considered critical to understanding the seismicity in subduction zones. Until recently, the forearc seismic belt (FSB) had been identified by observations of ocean bottom seismometer (OBS), representing a continuous pathway of fluid migration. However, it remains poorly understood whether tidal forces that modulate Japan earthquake triggering contribute to the dynamic of this pathway. Here, we report depth-stratified regimes sensitively modulated by M2 tide via statistical analyses of earthquake periodicities using the Japanese Meteorological Agency (JMA) catalog. The most significant M2-sensitive regime confines to the Pacific Plate's subduction trajectory, whose location is consistent with that of FSB identified by OBS. The other M2-sensitive regimes are mainly located at easter coast of Honshu and Hokkaido, while being almost absent along the western Japan coast. These findings indicate that fluid migration pathways are likely pervasive throughout the Japan subduction zone. Our results reveal that the tidal forces contribute the periodical dynamic of fluid process in subduction zone, provide new insights into the evident external-source influence on fluid migration.

presentations.presentation_title: Precursory Strain Signatures of Blind Thrust Development: Insights from High-resolution Analogue Sandbox Modeling and Piv Analysis
presentations.abstract: Blind thrust faults, exemplified by the devastating 2018 Lombok earthquake sequence, pose a significant seismic hazard due to their lack of surface expression prior to rupture, often obscuring the preparatory stages of major events. This study utilizes high-resolution Analog Sandbox Modeling (ASM) integrated with Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) to capture the hidden strain accumulation preceding catastrophic failure in fold-thrust belts. The results identify a systematic three-stage evolutionary process, highlighting a critical pre-failure phase characterized by distributed shear and strain-softening. A key finding is the emergence of subtle horizontal displacement within the footwall at the leading edge of the thrust front, which serves as a precursory signal of sub-surface stress transfer toward the deformation front. This horizontal anomaly represents the quasi-static transition where tectonic loading begins to nucleate concealed structures, such as those within the Flores Back-Thrust zone, before they manifest as runaway dynamic instabilities. While challenging to detect, these findings suggest that systematic monitoring of surface geodesy in the footwall region offers a realistic and promising pathway for identifying the activation of blind thrusts. This provides a vital mechanical basis for shifting disaster mitigation strategies from reactive response toward proactive forecasting in tectonically active regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Machine Learning Reveals Divergent Controls on Oceanic Lithospheric Strength Between Primary and Secondary Plume Provinces
presentations.institution: Key Laboratory of Submarine Geosciences, Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources
presentations.abstract: Understanding the elastic behavior of the oceanic lithosphere is crucial for interpreting plate dynamics and rheology, revealing the physical mechanisms underlying seafloor evolution. The effective elastic thickness (Te) of oceanic lithosphere is conventionally attributed to thermal structure, with Te increasing as the plate cools. However, significant departures from this thermal prediction occur in tectonically complex regions, and the relative contributions of thermal, morphological, and tectonic factors remain poorly quantified. Here we apply Random Forest regression with SHAP-based interpretation to investigate Te-controlling mechanisms across two contrasting Pacific regions: the Hawaiian-Emperor Chain (Area 1), associated with a primary deep-rooted plume, and the Pitcairn-Macdonald region (Area 2), associated with proposed secondary plumes and the South Pacific Superswell. In Area 1, lineament membership emerges as the dominant predictor, overriding crustal age and producing a clear binary separation between plume-affected and unaffected lithosphere. In Area 2, crustal age dominates feature importance, and Te variability follows standard plate cooling predictions with a characteristic transition at ~50 Ma. Cross-area model transfer tests yield near-zero to negative R² values, confirming that Te-controlling mechanisms are not universal but fundamentally tied to tectonic context. We interpret the dominance of lineament membership in Area 1 as reflecting lithospheric modification associated with sustained plume activity, potentially through magmatic underplating. These findings suggest that primary plumes do not simply weaken overlying lithosphere through thermal rejuvenation but may produce lasting mechanical reinforcement, with implications for understanding plate strength evolution in hotspot-influenced regions worldwide.

presentations.presentation_title: Formation Mechanism and Global Relevance of Two-peaked Double-frequency Microseisms Beneath Arctic Sea Ice
presentations.institution: Southern Marine Science and Engineering Guangdong Laboratory (Guangzhou)
presentations.abstract: Double-frequency (DF) microseisms, generated by nonlinear interactions of ocean waves, represent the most energetic band of the seismic ambient noise field. Their energy distribution across periods is governed by wave conditions at the source and is further modulated by water depth and sediment thickness, yet the combined effects of these factors remain insufficiently understood. Here we analyze under-ice ocean-bottom seismometer (OBS) records from the eastern Gakkel Ridge and identify two distinct DF microseismic spectral peaks at approximately 1 s and 3 s periods. Polarization and correlation analyses indicate that both peaks originate from the St. Anna Trough to the south, which is relatively close to the study area and characterized by strong wave activity. The mean wave period of about 6 s in the source region explains the 3 s DF microseismic peak but does not directly account for the 1 s peak. According to Rayleigh-wave dispersion modeling, at sites in the study region where sediment thickness is less than about 800 m, the fundamental or first-overtone modes show a group-velocity minimum near 1 s, causing energy focusing known as the Airy phase. Thus, the observed two-peaked pattern likely results from the joint effects of source-region waves and thin sediments beneath the receivers. A global analysis of nearly 600 OBSs further shows that two-peaked patterns predominantly occur where sediments are thin, indicating that sedimentary modulation of DF microseisms is globally widespread.
