presentations.presentation_title: 2.5 D Crustal Structure Inversion of the Gakkel Ridge at 85°E, Arctic Ocean
presentations.institution: Key Laboratory of Submarine Geosciences, Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources
presentations.abstract: The Gakkel Ridge in the Arctic Ocean is the world’s slowest-spreading mid-ocean ridge. However, year-round dense sea ice has long hindered high-resolution imaging of its crustal structure. During the 12th Chinese National Arctic Research Expedition, a large-scale active-source Ocean Bottom Seismometer (OBS) survey was successfully conducted along the ridge between 75°E and 102°E. Despite overcoming technical hurdles in under-ice shooting and OBS recovery, the non-collinearity between shot points and stations—induced by ice drift—constrained the reliability of traditional structural inversion. To address this, we employed a seismic tomography method based on 3D ray tracing to constrain the P-wave velocity structure at 85°E. This approach effectively accounts for errors arising from non-collinear geometries. By integrating velocity anomalies and gradient patterns, we investigated the cause of the thickened oceanic Crustal Layer 2 beneath the spreading axis. Our results suggest that extensive deep fracturing beneath the axis likely drives the observed low velocities in Layers 2 and 3, as well as the deepening of the Layer 2/3 boundary. These findings provide critical structural evidence for the evolution of ultraslow-spreading ridges. Furthermore, the application of a 2.5 D inversion scheme to resolve non-collinearity in ice-covered regions is of great significance for enhancing the precision and reliability of crustal imaging under complex polar observation conditions.

presentations.presentation_title: The Upper Mantle Structure Beneath the Pamir, Tianshan and Adjacent Regions
presentations.abstract: In the northwestern India-Asia collision zone, intensive tectonic deformation (e.g., orogenic uplift and crustal exhumation) is observed, but its relationships with deep mantle dynamics remain controversial. Here, we construct a 3D P-wave velocity model of the upper mantle beneath the Pamir, Tianshan, and adjacent regions using teleseismic tomography with seismic data from 353 stations and 4743 teleseismic events. Our tomographic model reveals a striking subvertical boundary between the low-velocity central Tianshan and the high-velocity Tarim lithosphere beneath the southern Tianshan fault system, indicating that the Tarim lithosphere has been sub-horizontally compressing the central Tianshan lithosphere. Furthermore, a high-velocity anomaly is observed in the upper mantle beneath the central Tianshan, which is interpreted as the delaminated Tianshan lithosphere due to the compression of Tarim. At the Pamir-Hindu Kush region, a slab-like high-velocity anomaly extends into the mantle transition zone (MTZ) beneath the Hindu Kush. This, along with our imaged flat high-velocity anomaly beneath the Pamir, suggests that the Indian lithosphere is steeply subducting beneath the Hindu Kush and sub-horizontally underthrusting beneath the Pamir. Additionally, the underthrusting Indian lithosphere forces the Tajik lithosphere to delaminate beneath the western Pamir (~72°E), which is imaged as a southeastward-dipping high-velocity anomaly. A large-scale high-velocity anomaly is imaged near the base of the MTZ beneath the Pamir and Karakoram, which likely represents the detached Indian lithosphere due to the breakoff of the Indian slab ~20 Ma.

presentations.presentation_title: Fine Crustal Structure of the Binchuan Area, Emeishan Large Igneous Province: Insights from a Short-period Dense Seismic Array
presentations.institution: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
presentations.abstract: The Binchuan area in Yunnan Province is situated within the inner zone of the Emeishan Large Igneous Province (ELIP), a large igneous province generated by the Permian mantle plume activity that significantly modified the lithosphere. Understanding the crustal structure beneath this region is crucial for deciphering the geodynamic effects of the interaction between mantle plume and lithosphere. However, the detailed geometry and lateral continuity of the magmatic underplating remain debated due to the limited resolution of sparse regional seismic stations. To resolve this ambiguity, we utilised a short-period dense seismic array in Binchuan to investigate the fine crustal structure. We used P-wave receiver function to image the subsurface structure beneath Binchuan area. To eliminate artifacts caused by shallow sedimentary reverberations, we simulated the wavefield and applied an autocorrelation method to effectively suppress the influence of sedimentary layers. Our imaging results resolve three robust, laterally continuous positive interfaces: two strong intra-crustal boundaries at ~13 km and ~33 km, and a clear Moho at ~45 km, defining a 10–15 km-thick high-velocity lower crust. We interpret these strong intra-crustal reflectors as interfaces of magmatic underplating, representing the legacy of the ELIP intra-crustal magmatic system. Situated at the critical junction between the Inner Zone of ELIP and the Red River Fault, these findings characterize the distinct crustal structure of the ELIP marginal zone. Thus, this study provides essential high-resolution constraints on the spatial extent and structural variability of the ELIP.

presentations.presentation_title: Crustal Attenuation in China from Ml Amplitude and Lg-wave Data and New Model of Tibetan Plateau Extrusion
presentations.abstract: We have selected 396 533 ML amplitude readings from the Annual Bulletin of Chinese Earthquakes (ABCE) and 12 827 Lg-wave amplitude from waveform processing. Total 409 230 ray paths from 39 347 earthquakes recorded by 1034 stations have been used to image the lateral variations of the quality factor Q0 (Q at 1Hz) beneath the crust of China. Estimated Q0 values vary from 65 to 465 with an average of 265. Q0 values are well consistent with tectonic structures. Very strong seismic attenuation is found beneath Bayan Har and Chuandian blocks, that suggests these weak zones create the lateral slip boundaries of southern Tibet which move to east and then turn to south, and the weak zones play an important role for the uplift and spreading of Tibetan Plateau.

presentations.presentation_title: Crustal Rheology in the Se Tibetan Plateau Revealed by Lg-wave Attenuation Tomography
presentations.abstract: In response to the continuous Indian-Eurasian plate convergence, the mechanically weak crust of the Chuan-Dian block in the SE Tibetan Plateau moves southeastwards, representing one of the significant expanding margins of the Tibetan Plateau. However, the Emeishan Large Igneous Province (ELIP), characterized by localized magma-strengthened crust, is located in the passage of such crustal movement. Whether the strength contrast between the Chuan-Dian block and ELIP is large enough to impede the crustal flow remains controversial. Here, based on the Lg data from high-density ChinArray in the SE Tibetan Plateau, we invert for a high-resolution broadband crustal attenuation model. In general, the SE Tibetan Plateau exhibits widespread strong Lg attenuation over the frequency range of 0.2–2.0 Hz, which is concentrated near major strike-slip faults at frequencies above 2.5 Hz. This is consistent with a lower-crustal flow model underlying the relative movement of upper-crustal blocks. The Chuan-Dian block is characterized by a remarkably low Q_Lg, whereas the ELIP core area exhibits an abrupt ~30% increase in Q_Lg between 2.5 and 10.0 Hz, reflecting the magma-modified crust that gained mechanical strength during cooling. The lateral Q_Lg variation corresponds to a ~1 order of magnitude increase in strength, which may indicate an obstructive effect from the ELIP core. However, the broadband Q_Lg images suggest a depth-varying crustal strength, possibly due to the thermal impact of asthenosphere upwelling associated with eastward subduction of the Indian Plate. Combining with S-wave velocity and Pg-wave attenuation, our Lg attenuation suggests that the ELIP core can only block the crustal flow at shallower depths. This research was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (U2139206).

presentations.presentation_title: A Possible Northward Subduction in the Southwestern Yangtze Block During the Rodinia Assembly: New Constraints from Three-dimensional Magnetotelluric Imaging
presentations.abstract: The Yangtze block is a crucial component of the Rodinia and Columbia supercontinents, providing insights into their evolutionary history. The newly identified Caiziyuan-Tongan accretionary complex (CAC), situated on the southwestern margin of the Yangtze block, serves as an ideal window for understanding its Precambrian evolution. The exposure of the CAC suggests the presence of an ancient ocean basin that divides the Yangtze block into northern and southern micro-blocks. During the convergence of the Rodinia supercontinent, this ocean basin underwent subduction and eventual closure; however, its associated subduction polarity remains ambiguous. To address this issue, this study employed magnetotelluric in the Caiziyuan-Tongan area. Through threedimensional inversion, three distinct features were delineated: an upper crustal conductor in the southern CAC, a middle-upper crustal resistor trending stepwise north in the northern CAC, and a middle-lower crustal conductor encompassing the entire area. In conjunction with previously published geological and seismological observations, it is proposed that the first two features may be remnants associated with the northward subduction of the south Yangtze micro-block, while the third feature may indicate the existence of crustal flow related to the collision of the Indo-Asian plate. This finding enhances our understanding of the Precambrian evolution within the Yangtze block and contributes to the reconstruction of paleogeographic frameworks associated with the Rodinia supercontinent.

presentations.presentation_title: Hidden Markov Models: an Attempt to Integrate Sparce, Scarce, and Sporadic Qualitative and Quantitative Monitoring Data
presentations.abstract: Inherently complex natural systems include many multidimensional components inseparably woven together. Forecasts of these systems are required to inform decisions from emergency management to climate response. Forecasting methods rely on interpreting current knowledge and data and extrapolating the result into the future with causal and temporal assumptions. For volcanic eruption forecasts, where the natural system operates over thousands to millions of years, the temporal-recency bias of instrumental data forces assumptions of time homogeneity (stationarity) and closed-form solutions. These are significant limitations given that forecasts are intrinsically time-dependent, and system dynamics are key to future events.Here, we take a holistic approach to volcano monitoring and forecasting and consider the wider context within which a volcano sits, and the local knowledge of indigenous people who have lived alongside their volcanoes for thousands of years. We use the exemplar of Ruapehu and the Central Volcanic Plateau in Aotearoa-NZ, to demonstrate the use of a relatively flexible statistical method – Hidden Markov Models. And present the trials, tribulations, and minor successes that we have encountered while trying to simultaneously redefine what are considered valuable data (beyond instrumental readings) and knowledge (beyond scientific reports).

presentations.presentation_title: Machine-learning Analysis of Multi-parametric Monitoring Data for Eruption Precursor Detection
presentations.abstract: Volcano monitoring and eruption forecasting are inherently multiparametric, including geophysical, geochemical and environmental data. Currently, these disparate data streams need to be interpreted simultaneously by volcano experts. This approach is qualitative and subject to bias, and experts often miss subtle changes in the data which may indicate an impending eruption. The advent of machine-learning analysis has great potential to assist volcano monitoring efforts but has so far had limited success. Our aim is to develop new machine-learning techniques which can analyse multiple streams of volcano monitoring data concurrently. We will apply a technique known as diffusion modelling, which is able to detect anomalies in multivariate time-series data. We will train new models on the large volume of volcano monitoring data in New Zealand and use them to detect trends and signals which have been thus-far undetectable by human analysts. The models we produce will be applied in real-time to detect eruption precursors and calculate eruption probabilities. This will address a major vulnerability in New Zealand’s economy and society and will reduce the risk volcanoes pose to life, infrastructure and economic activity.

presentations.presentation_title: Development of Low-cost Gnss Network for Dense Ground Deformation Monitoring at Usu Volcano
presentations.institution: Institute of Seismology and Volcanology, Faculty of Science, Hokkaido University
presentations.abstract: GNSS observations provide ground deformation data with high temporal resolution crucial for understanding volcanic phenomena. However, conventional GNSS receivers cost several hundred thousand to over one million yen per unit, making dense network deployment economically challenging. Additionally, volcanic environments often lack stable power and communication infrastructure. This study develops an affordable, low-power GNSS system utilizing new-generation receiver units now available on the market. We report the preliminary evaluation results obtained from a test run around the Usu volcano where a new eruption is anticipated.We employed the U-blox F9P multi-GNSS chip (approximately tens of thousands of yen) with a JCA228B antenna. A Linux machine (Century MA-E300) running RTKLIB (Takasu, 2013) controls the receiver and provides cellular communication. Data streams to a ntrip server in real-time and is archived on an external SSD. Power consumption during transmission is ~5W, enabling solar-battery operation. The complete system costs approximately 100,000 yen—roughly one-tenth of conventional systems.A 26-station network (16 new + 10 existing sites) was established at Usu volcano. Continuous observations began in 2023. Static relative positioning showed daily scatter of ~3 mm (horizontal and vertical). Seven-day median absolute deviation over six months was 1.6 mm (horizontal) and 4.3 mm (vertical). This precision is sufficient for both eruption monitoring and preparatory process detection. During the 2000 eruption, GPS measurements captured ground deformation rates of 1.5 m/day (horizontal) during the initial 3-day period (Takahashi et al., 2002). Our system's precision enables detection of much slower preparatory deformation that may precede such rapid co-eruptive changes, enhancing early warning capabilities.

presentations.presentation_title: Stratigraphic and grain-textural constraints on rapid eruption-style transitions during recent eruptions of Mount Bromo (East Java, Indonesia)
presentations.abstract: Mount Bromo (East Java, Indonesia) has experienced at least seven eruptive episodes in the past 25 years, including major activity in 2010 and 2015. Based on observational reports and eyewitness accounts, both eruptions were characterized by repeated transitions between ash venting, passive degassing, and peak Strombolian explosions. However, the deposit-scale signatures of such short-term style transitions remain poorly constrained.Here we report results from a proximal-deposit field campaign conducted in December 2025, focusing on stratigraphic evidence for within-episode variability during recent eruptions. We logged and sampled key sections around the crater and identified two prominent Strombolian layers rich in pumice/scoria and ballistic ejecta, interbedded with ashfall and flow-related deposits that record changing eruptive dynamics.To quantify differences among deposit types and infer fragmentation and transport processes, we combine detailed stratigraphic logging with grain-size analysis, componentry, and measurements of grain morphology and surface textures (morphometry and textural classification). Preliminary results show systematic contrasts in grain morphometry and surface textures between Strombolian layers and interbedded ash-rich units, consistent with shifts in fragmentation efficiency and depositional mechanisms.These new field-based constraints provide insights into the processes driving rapid eruption-style transitions at Mount Bromo and help refine interpretations of multi-phase Strombolian eruptive sequences.

presentations.presentation_title: Modelling of CO₂ and H₂S Gas Dispersion in the Dieng Volcanic Complex, Central Java, Indonesia
presentations.abstract: The Dieng Volcanic Complex, Central Java, is a major tourist destination and a geothermal development area; however, it is also an active volcanic system with significant hazards related to phreatic eruptions and the release of toxic volcanic gases, particularly CO₂ and H₂S. Event tree analysis of eruptive activity since 1375 indicates that approximately 97% of eruptions at the Dieng Volcanic Complex are sourced from hydrothermal processes. The most active centers are Sileri, Timbang, and Sikidang craters, accounting for more than 37%, 20%, and 14% of recorded eruption events, respectively. Eruptive activity is dominated by phreatic eruptions, gas emissions, and mud discharges. Sinila Crater represents another high-risk area, with a history of phreatic eruptions that resulted in 149 fatalities in 1979.As part of volcanic hazard mitigation efforts, CO₂ and H₂S concentrations were measured at four active craters: Timbang, Sinila, Sileri, and Sikidang. Gas measurements were conducted through direct field observations using a gas sampling pump and detector tubes, as well as by gas sampling using Giggenbach tubes. Subsequently, dispersion modeling of CO₂ and H₂S gases was performed using ALOHA version 5.4.4 (Areal Locations of Hazardous Atmospheres) software developed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).The results indicate that CO₂ is the dominant volcanic gas in the Dieng Volcanic Complex, with concentrations reaching up to 40% (400,000 ppm). In contrast, H₂S concentrations range from below the detection limit to more than 120 ppm. Elevated SO₂ concentrations and N₂/Ar ratios suggest that gases emitted from the Timbang, Sinila, Sileri, and Sikidang craters have both magmatic and meteoric origins. Gas dispersion modeling shows that H₂S can be dispersed up to 265 m, whereas CO₂ dispersion distances reach up to 29 m.

presentations.presentation_title: Cyclical Eruptive Behavior at Merapi Volcano Revealed by MT-InSAR Deformation and Geochemical Time-series Analysis
presentations.abstract: Integrated analyses of geochemical and Multi-Temporal InSAR (MT-InSAR) deformation parameters reveal a cyclical pattern of Merapi Volcano over the period 1992–2018. The cycles are commonly observed through signs of persistent or episodic surface deformation and variations in silica content (SiO₂), which act as a key geochemical proxy that regulates magma viscosity, extrusion rate, and eruptive style. Periods marked by higher SiO₂ contents (54–56 wt.%) correspond to more viscous magma and reduced extrusion rates (<10⁵ m³/day). During these interval, MT-InSAR records a transition from gradual to rapid inflation, preceding relatively stable effusive activity dominated by block-and-ash flows, with low explosivity (Volcanic Explosivity Index, VEI 0–2). In contrast, lower SiO₂ values (~51–52 wt.%) coincide with markedly higher extrusion rates (>10⁶ m³/day) and sustained inflation signals, indicating mafic magma injection, increased internal pressurization, and a transition toward open-system degassing conditions that favour explosive eruptions and pyroclastic density currents (VEI 3–4). The eruptive record of Merapi Volcano exhibits a recurrent cycle with a periodicity of approximately 12–14 years, indicating systematic alternation between effusive and explosive regimes controlled by magma recharge processes and the degassing efficiency. Observations after 2018 indicate a transition toward a semi-closed magmatic system, characterized by degassed andesitic magma, low-amplitude surface inflation (~7.7 mm/yr) detected by MT-InSAR, and recurrent dome collapses without significant explosive activity. These results demonstrate that coupling high-resolution deformation monitoring with geochemical proxies, particularly SiO₂ evolution, provides a robust framework for identifying eruptive cyclicity and assessing eruption potential. Continuous integration monitoring of these parameters strengthens eruption prediction and hazard mitigation strategies in densely populated volcanic regions.
presentations.session_title: Monitoring Volcanoes Across Asia and Oceania

presentations.presentation_title: Integrating Petrologic Parameters for Volcanic Monitoring: Evidence from Two Contrasting Indonesian Volcanoes.
presentations.abstract: Petrologic monitoring provides critical insights into volcanic processes by quantifying magma dynamics and eruption mechanisms. This study compares two distinct volcanic systems—the Sunda Volcanic Complex (Pleistocene) and Galunggung Volcano (1982–1983 eruption)—to highlight the role of petrologic parameters in monitoring and hazard assessment. At Sunda, facies and volcanostratigraphic analysis reveal three eruptive periods: Pra-Sunda, Sunda and post-Sunda, each comprising opening, caldera climax phases and new volcano. Pyroclastic deposits were emplaced through fluid-escape, traction-dominated, and direct fallout flow-boundary zones. Stratigraphic units (B2, C2, C8, D1–D4, E2) show distinct decompression signatures, with decompression values observed in Unit B2 (Pra-Sunda Klimaks) and Unit E2 (Sunda Klimaks), indicating rapid magma ascent during caldera-forming eruptions. Different with post-Sunda, composite stratigraphy and sample-based decompression profiling across zones A1–C3 further confirm pressure instability and eruptive transitions. At Galunggung, tephra analyses of late eruptive phases (2b and 3) included grain morphology, bubble number density (BND), microlite number density (MND), decompression rate, and ascent rate. Phase 2b, characterized as freatomagmatic, showed increasing eruptive energy due to meteoric water interaction, while phase 3, identified as strombolian, exhibited slightly reduced energy. Conclusion, the comparative analysis underscores the effectiveness of petrologic monitoring—through facies, textural, and quantitative parameters such as BND, MND, decompression rate, and ascent rate—in distinguishing eruptive styles across different volcanic systems. These methods provide detailed, process-based information essential for improving volcanic monitoring frameworks and enhancing hazard mitigation strategies.
presentations.session_title: Monitoring Volcanoes Across Asia and Oceania

presentations.presentation_title: Impacts of Tectonic-paleogeographic Variations on Cenozoic Sedimentary Distribution in the Dangerous Grounds, South China Sea
presentations.abstract: The Dangerous Grounds, located in the southern margin of the South China Sea, has experienced three distinct tectonic evolution stages during the Cenozoic: continental rifting, breakup from the South China Block and southward drift, and collision with Borneo, accompanied by a north-to-south shift in its paleogeographic environment. This study utilized a robust dataset comprising 67 seismic reflection profiles, integrated with drilling and dredging data, to reconstruct the sedimentary filling history of the Dangerous Grounds. By correlating sediment budget outcomes with the spatial distribution characteristics of the sediment thickness, we have gained valuable insights into the region’s sedimentary evolution. Our findings reveal a progressive increase in sediment budgets across the three tectonic stages, despite relatively stable sediment budgets during the southward drift stage associated with seafloor spreading. Spatial sediment distribution shows a continued decrease in the east and expansion in the south and west. By integrating the temporal and spatial distribution of depocenters with drilling results and sediment provenance through geochemical analyses, we provide a comprehensive regional perspective on the factors controlling sediment budget trends, including regional tectonic events, monsoon, sea level change, and the river systems associated with paleogeographic environment variations. The sedimentary inputs to the Dangerous Grounds have shifted over time, with Paleocene-Eocene sediments primarily originating from the north. From the Oligocene to the Early Miocene, northern sediment supply progressively declined, while inputs from the southwest, transported through river systems originating in the Indochina and Malay Peninsulas, gradually increased. Since the Mid-Miocene, the collision with Borneo has led to enhanced sediment supply from the south, with sediments predominantly accumulating along slope edges, channel outlets, and within the Nansha Trough.

presentations.presentation_title: Oceanic–Continental Plate Evolution and Topographic Control of Cryogenian Snowball Earth States
presentations.abstract: The life cycle of oceanic plates, encompassing ridge formation, seafloor aging, basin deepening, and eventual destruction, fundamentally controls the geometric and thermal boundary conditions of Earth’s climate system. Earth experienced global glaciations during the Proterozoic, most prominently the Cryogenian Sturtian (720–660 Ma) and Marinoan (650–635 Ma) glaciations. Despite extensive modelling efforts, the contrast in duration between these events remains unexplained within a unified physical framework. Previous studies have emphasized radiative forcing and atmospheric CO₂ thresholds, often relying on idealized palaeogeographic boundary conditions, leaving the role of solid-Earth evolution under-quantified. Here we test the hypothesis that realistic Cryogenian palaeogeography and topography influence Snowball Earth steady states and thresholds. We reconstruct palaeogeographic and palaeotopographic boundary conditions at 720 Ma, 660 Ma, 650 Ma, and 635 Ma by combining full-plate tectonic reconstructions with a 3-D mantle convection model. Continental elevations are derived from mantle-driven dynamic topography and corrected for water loading and sea-level constraints, while ocean bathymetry and geothermal heat flux are prescribed using model seafloor ages and ridge geometries. These boundary conditions are implemented in a hierarchy of climate models, centered on a fully coupled atmosphere–ocean general circulation model, to explore Snowball initiation and steady states under flat and reconstructed topography. The reconstructions demonstrate differences between the Sturtian and Marinoan intervals in continental configuration, surface topography, and the spatial distribution of ridge-controlled geothermal heat flux. Preliminary results show that continental arrangements and geothermal heat-flux patterns differ between the two intervals. These reconstructed differences in palaeogeography and thermal boundary conditions suggest that the associated climate systems may differ in their large-scale structure, including meridional heat transport, sea-ice thickness distribution, and basal thermal conditions beneath marine ice. This study highlights topography as a key component of the coupled solid Earth–carbon–climate–ice system governing Earth’s extreme climatic states.

presentations.presentation_title: Zinc Isotope Evidence for Subducted Carbonate Recycling Under the Gakkel Ridge, Arctic Ocean
presentations.institution: Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources
presentations.abstract: Carbon in the asthenosphere is unevenly distributed, reflecting interactions between the depleted mantle and materials added by plumes or subducting slabs. Nevertheless, mid-ocean ridge basalts (MORB) from the Arctic Gakkel Ridge, far from any existent hotspots and subduction zones, are unusually carbon-rich. Here we show that the MORB along the Gakkel Ridge display systematically elevated Zn isotopes (δ 66 Zn=0.27‰–0.41‰) relative to typical global MORB (0.26±0.03‰). Their heavy δ 66 Zn ratios correlate with indicators for mantle source carbon enrichment. We attribute this signature to result from recycled surficial carbonates stored in deep mantle under the Arctic Ocean. These carbonate components were likely delivered by ancient oceanic subduction and subsequently entrained into the mantle upwelling feeding the Gakkel Ridge. Our results demonstrate that vestiges of past subduction can dominate carbon budgets beneath plume‑unaffected ridges, and act as a principal driver of large‑scale carbon heterogeneity in the upper mantle.

presentations.presentation_title: Seismic Receiver Function Imaging of the Lithospheric Structure Beneath Bidong Island, Eastern Malay Peninsula: Implications for Subduction Zone Evolution
presentations.institution: Key Laboratory of Submarine Geosciences, Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources
presentations.abstract: Seismic tomography has indicated that the eastern Malay Peninsula may lie near the leading edge of the Sumatran subduction slab, implying that its deep lithospheric structure is important for constraining regional subduction dynamics. In late 2023, a broadband seismic station was deployed on Bidong Island, off the eastern coast of the Malay Peninsula, through a collaboration between the Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources, China, and Universiti Malaysia Terengganu. This study analyzes teleseismic data recorded between December 2023 and June 2024. A total of 108 high-quality teleseismic events were selected based on epicentral distances of 25°–90°, moment magnitudes ≥ 5.0, and signal-to-noise ratios > 2.0. Receiver function analysis was applied to image the lithospheric structure beneath Bidong Island. The results reveal a layered crust structure characterized by seismic discontinuities at depths of approximately 3 km, 27 km, 40 km, and 80 km. These interfaces are interpreted as the sediment–basement boundary, the base of the upper crust, the Moho discontinuity, and the lithosphere–asthenosphere boundary (LAB), respectively. The inferred structure is consistent with a typical continental lithosphere and shows no clear evidence of significant modification by the Sumatran subduction system. However, given the limited temporal coverage and station aperture, further data acquisition and integrated analyses are required to robustly evaluate the influence of subduction-related processes beneath the eastern Malay Peninsula.

presentations.presentation_title: Double-layered Microseismicity in the Java Subduction Zone Revealed by Ocean Bottom Seismometer Observations
presentations.institution: Key Laboratory of Submarine Geosciences, Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources
presentations.abstract: Double Seismic Zones (DSZs), with a 20–40 km vertical separation between seismic planes, are common in the circum-Pacific subduction zones at depths ≥70 km, reflecting a colder slab with a gentle dip. To date, there have been no definitive reports of a DSZ in the Java subduction zone of the Indian Ocean. In order to better understand the precise structure of the Java subduction zone, the Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources, China, in collaboration with the National Research and Innovation Agency of Indonesia and the Universitas Gadjah Mada, conducted the "China-Indonesia Java Subduction Zone Integrated Geophysical Survey Expedition" in August 2025.A wide-angle OBS profile was conducted perpendicular to the Java trench.A total of 17 OBSs were deployed and recovered. Although the OBSs worked on the seafloor for a relatively short duration (approximately 2 days), the high tectonic activity of the subduction zone allowed for the recording of numerous natural microearthquakes.Based on OBS data acquired during this cruise, this study used the PhaseNet and NLLoc methods to identify and relocate microearthquakes. Following a selection criterion of RMS residual <0.5 s, precise hypocenters for 131 microearthquakes were localized at depths <60 km within a 50 km radius of the OBS profile. Preliminary analysis reveals that: (1) the spatial distribution of microearthquakes clearly reveals the geometry of the subducting slab, showing a dip angle of approximately 20 degrees; and (2) the seismicity within the slab exhibits distinct double-layered characteristics, with a small separation distance of approximately 10-15 km between the two layers. This distribution of double-layered microseismicity at relatively shallow depths with small separations, may indicate a colder, more brittle subducting slab. Due to the limited dataset, Future work will refine these results by integrating land-based data and a 2D active-source velocity model.

presentations.presentation_title: Constraining the Post-obduction History of New Caledonia: Insights from Weathering-related Geological Tools and a Case Example from the Nc Fluvio-lacustrine Formation
presentations.institution: Institut des Sciences Exactes et Appliquées, Université de la Nouvelle-Calédonie, Nouvelle-Calédonie
presentations.abstract: New-Caledonia (NC) is a Pacific archipelago where 1/3 of the surface is covered by ultramafic rocks due to an obduction that occurred 34 Ma. The timing of this event is well constrained due to the combined use of petrographic, thermochronological and geochronological methods. However, the Neogene and Quaternary evolution of this archipelago is still poorly known. This is mainly due to the scarcity of the geological formations derived from this period. The main continental geological witnesses of the last 30 Ma are tropical weathering covers (laterites) and continental sedimentary formations derived from their erosion. The most preserved weathering covers are developed at the expense of the distinct erosional surfaces of the NC peridotite nappe, but are characterized by a poor mineralogy dominated by iron oxyhydroxides and low radioelement contents. Such characteristics are making their dating, and thus both the reconstruction of the Tertiary erosion stages and weathering pulses, particularly challenging. Here, we will first address this challenge by exploring the geochronological methods, and their targets, that could be applied to unlock this scientific constraint. We will also present a study dealing with one of the main NC geochronological challenges: the precise dating of the Fluviolacustrine formation of South NC. The age of these intra-mountain lateritic sediments is still debated, ranging from the Miocene to the Quarternary. To better constrain its period of functioning we applied the (U-Th)/He dating of iron oxyhydroxides methodology on duricrust clasts from the basal conglomerate of this formation, as well as, on samples from its top duricrust that developed in parallel of its secondary weathering. The ages can be separate into three mains families, 10 Ma and 3.5 to 5 Ma for the basal clasts, and the Quaternary for both samples’ families. These ages will be discussed in term of paleoenvironmental and climatic conditions.

presentations.presentation_title: Assessing the Future of Mangroves on the Carbonate Islands of the Pacific Ocean: a Case Study of Sediment Eogenesis from the Ouvéa Mangrove (new Caledonia)
presentations.institution: Institut des Sciences Exactes et Appliquées, Université de la Nouvelle-Calédonie, Nouvelle-Calédonie
presentations.abstract: Mangroves are coastal ecosystems typical of intertropical areas providing numerous benefices for the functioning of the Critical Zone. They can influence coastlines geomorphology, act as a major carbon sinks and can also be considered as buffer zones for organic and inorganic particles between continents and oceans. The scientific community defends today the idea that these ecosystems would likely follow the path of the rising sea level induced by the ongoing climate change, or at least adapt through lateral accommodation. This is mainly due to the fact that their substrate is supplied both by organic, derived mainly from litterfalls, and terrigenous sedimentary inputs. However, the question of the future of such ecosystems where terrigenous sedimentation is low is still poorly explored. In this presentation, we will ask the question of the stability of a carbonated mangrove substrate in such context by studying the eogenetic processes affecting the sediments of the Ouvéa Mangrove (New-Caledonia). To do so, sediment cores of 30 cm were sampled at the base of the main mangrove species, in areas characterized by different trees-development stages. The cores were analyzed using a complementary set of mineralogical and petrographic tools, as well as geochemical analyses. Our results demonstrate that the physicochemical conditions of the cores are poorly favourable for the carbonate neoformation. However, young trees’ substrate still displays traces of aragonite and Mg-calcite crystals neoformation at depth. The mature trees also display secondary minerals neoformation (sulphates and sulphides). However, all the investigated substratum are displaying dissolution features, particularly under the mature trees. The neoformed minerals do not appear to compensate for the substrate volume loss, leading to the progressive subsidence of the mangrove. These results are confirmed by the geochemical analyses and mass balance tests associated. The long-term stability of mangroves from isolated carbonated islands of the Pacific remains uncertain.

presentations.presentation_title: Synsedimentary Deformation in a Ferruginous Detrital Formation: Example of the Southern Grande Terre Fluvio-lacustrine Formation, New Caledonia
presentations.abstract: The Fluvio-Lacustrine Formation (FFL) in southern Grande Terre, New Caledonia is an intramontane sedimentary formation composed of reworked lateritic material (mainly iron oxyhydroxides), accumulated to a thickness of up to 70 meters. These lateritic products originate from the peridotite nappe, which has been obducted since the Paleogene and exposed to humid tropical surface conditions. The morphology of the Grand Sud has allowed this accumulation to persist for at least 5 Ma, incorporating material from the entire weathering profile (from bedrock to duricrust) within a predominantly fluvial context with occasional lacustrine occurrences. The analysis of the architectural organisation of the FFL deposits has revealed four distinctive levels containing a variety of structures, most of which belong to the family of soft-sediment deformation structures (SSDS) affecting unconsolidated to poorly consolidated sediments. Among these, load structures, flame structures, convolute bedding and recumbent folds have been identified and are thought to be contemporaneous with the formation of the FFL. In addition, a final structural type has been identified, located in proximity to the remarkable levels, not yet evidently related to syn-depositional deformation. This type is characterized by straight, vertical ferruginous indurations, that cut across the sediments and may possibly indicate potential fracturing associated with fluid circulation pathways within the FFL. Although the age of the FFL is not precisely known, this synsedimentary deformation could be correlated with lithospheric bulging due to the initiation of the Vanuatu subduction zone. Other evidence suggests that the deformation affecting some of the remarkable levels is more likely of endogenous origin, involving gravitational sliding and instabilities, or rapid and/or uneven sediment loading. Consequently, the analysis of the structures (SSDS and fracturing) within each level enabled the determination of their geometric relationships and potential interactions.

presentations.presentation_title: Multi-source Offshore Event Identification from Submarine Fiber-optic Cables Using Distributed Acoustic Sensing
presentations.abstract: We present an integrated workflow for automated multi-source signal detection and classification, and demonstrate its performance using submarine Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) observations from the northeastern offshore region of Taiwan. The proposed framework combines classical seismological detection, unsupervised clustering, and deep learning–based image recognition. Candidate signals are first detected from DAS time-series using a recursive short-term average/long-term average (STA/LTA) approach, effectively suppressing background noise and constraining the analysis domain. To address low signal-to-noise conditions common in submarine environments, additional signal processing adjustments are applied. Coherent energy propagations with spatial continuity are then identified in the time–channel domain and clustered using Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN). Cluster characteristics—including spatial extent, temporal persistence, and energy distribution—provide an interpretable basis for preliminary source discrimination. To further improve classification stability and reduce manual inspection, clustered events are converted into waterfall plot images and classified using deep learning image recognition techniques, with Fourier spectral analysis serving as supplementary diagnostic information. The methodology is tested on continuous DAS records from a submarine cable deployed in a tectonically active region influenced by Ryukyu subduction system, active volcanism, strong ocean currents, and intensive vessel traffic. Detected vessel signals are validated against Automatic Identification System (AIS) records, while seismic detections are compared with regional earthquake catalogs to assess detection capability and minimum observable magnitudes. Results demonstrate that the integrated workflow can robustly detect and classify earthquakes, volcanic activity, and vessel signals in complex offshore environments. This study highlights DAS as a powerful complementary tool for offshore geophysical and maritime monitoring and provides an extensible framework for large-scale, automated multi-source DAS signal analysis.

presentations.presentation_title: Tide Modulated Ocean to Earth Energy Conversion Quantified with Coastal Fiber Sensing
presentations.institution: Institute of Oceanography, National Taiwan University
presentations.abstract: Quantifying how incident ocean waves transfer energy into seismic surface waves along the nearshore is essential for understanding coastal hazards and Earth–ocean coupling, yet time-resolved in-situ estimates have been scarce. Here we use a beach-deployed distributed acoustic sensing array co-located with an ocean-bottom node to directly measure the conversion efficiency from wave impacts to Rayleigh-type ground motion at 4–12 Hz. Frequency–wavenumber analysis, beamforming, and local back-projection consistently locate sources along a fixed, wave-breaking coastal segment, while particle-motion ellipticity confirms the Rayleigh character. Calibrating DAS strain to ground velocity and combining nearshore wave energetics yields an energy-conversion efficiency on the order of 10⁻⁶. The efficiency is strongly modulated by tide, with high-tide conditions enhancing coupling even though the source region remains stationary. Our results establish a quantitative benchmark for dynamic ocean-to-Earth energy transfer at the land–sea interface and provide a generalizable framework for coastal monitoring using existing fiber infrastructure.

presentations.presentation_title: Volcanic Eruption Tremors, Harmonic Tremor and Explosion Earthquakes in May 2025 at Sakurajima Volcano: Analyses of Das Records
presentations.abstract: During May 12 to 15 eruptive activities of Sakurajima volcano, Japan, series of relatively large explosive eruptions at Sakurajima, in addition to eruption tremors and explosion earthquakes, harmonic tremors with multiple dominant spectral peaks were frequently observed. Continuous DAS monitoring using two optical fiber cables detected these signals: one along the Nojiri River on the eastern side of the crater (approximately 4.4 km long), and another along the road encircling Sakurajima (approximately 38 km long). Data are recorded at a sampling rate of 250 Hz, with a spatial interval of 5 m and a gauge length of 10 m. The optical fiber cable along the Nojiri River extends radially from the crater but bends along the road near its midpoint. We applied complex principal component analysis (Nishimura et al., 2025) to the seismic records to determine the apparent propagation direction and velocity of the seismic waves based on arrival time differences between adjacent points. In addition, records from the cable along the circumferential road were analyzed to investigate the radiation characteristics of the seismic waves. The results indicate that at frequency bands of 1-6 Hz, the seismic waves were propagated from the crater direction. The apparent propagation velocities were approximately 0.8 km/s in the 1–3 Hz band and about 1.2 km/s in the 3–6 Hz band for explosion earthquakes, eruption tremors, and harmonic tremors. The difference in apparent velocity suggests variations in the depth of the excitation source within the conduit, or differences in the conversion processes from body waves to surface waves near the source region. We further analyzed seismic amplitudes along the circumferential for these three types of the earthquakes and tremors.

presentations.presentation_title: Insights Into the Hikurangi Subduction System and the Associated Deformation from Adjoint-state Double-difference Traveltime Tomography
presentations.abstract: The North Island of New Zealand is located at the southern terminus of the western Pacific subduction system. This region is a pivotal domain for accommodating the oblique convergence of the Pacific and Australian plates, where tectonic forces drive widespread geothermal activity and intense seismicity. Although existing models of the region have provided fundamental insights into the subduction dynamics and the associated deformation, there remains room for improvement, especially given the vast amount of data accumulated in recent decades. To better resolve the tectonic evolution of the complex plate boundary region, we collected the local earthquake traveltime data from GeoNet, spanning the period from 1980 to 2025. Following rigorous quality control, we obtained 3,741,736 high-quality traveltime data recorded by 594 stations. We applied an advanced adjoint-state double-difference tomography to iteratively invert the velocity structure of the North Island subduction system, starting from the previously published regional three-dimensional velocity model (adjoint-state waveform tomography model; NZATOM). Compared to the initial model, our final model exhibits substantial velocity perturbations. At shallow depths, we found a distinct low-velocity belt beneath the Taupō Volcanic Zone (TVZ) and the Hikurangi forearc, in agreement with previous models. Furthermore, our model reveals a notable low-velocity zone (Vp < 8.2 km/s) beneath the cold subducting slab, likely representing the asthenosphere of the subducting Pacific Plate. Particularly, beneath the TVZ at depths of ~150–200 km, we found that the subducting slab is truncated by a low-velocity anomaly. The location of this anomaly is remarkably coincident with the observed cluster of intense intermediate-depth seismicity. We suspect these features indicate a localized slab tear, potentially serving as a slab window for asthenospheric upwelling that feeds the volumetric volcanism along the central TVZ.

presentations.presentation_title: Rayleigh Wave Isotropic and Anisotropic Phase Velocity Tomography Suggests Slab Segmentation and Volcanism in the Sunda Banda Arc Transition Zone
presentations.institution: Taiwan International Graduate Program (TIGP)–Earth System Science Program(ESS), Academia Sinica and National Central University, Academia Sinica
presentations.abstract: In this study, we investigated isotropic and azimuthally anisotropic Rayleigh wave phase velocity variations beneath Sunda-Banda Arc Transition Zone (ATZ). We analyzed vertical-component seismograms recorded at 131 stations of the Indonesian Meteorology Climatology and Geophysical Agency (BMKG) seismic network from 2006 to 2024, spanning periods of 10-200 s. Interstation dispersion curves were measured using the two-station method for 6,642 paths from 7,214 tele-seismic earthquakes (M ≥ 5.5, depth ≤ 50 km, and epicentral distance 20°-170°) and were inverted for phase velocity maps and a 3D shear wave velocity model. Low phase velocity anomalies along the curved-Banda Arc, with trench-parallel anisotropy, likely indicate a strongly hydrated mantle wedge containing serpentinite. In contrast, the wedge interior shows higher phase velocities and trench-perpendicular anisotropy, consistent with corner flow within a relatively dry mantle. At larger periods beneath the arc and to the northwest, we observe high velocities with trench-perpendicular anisotropy, suggesting slab shearing. In the ATZ, seismic anisotropy exhibits an abrupt transition from trench-parallel to trench-perpendicular orientations near the ocean-continent boundary (around Sumba), indicating complex interactions related to the subduction of Australian continental lithosphere. In particular our maps suggest slab segmentation, including slab windows beneath Lombok and Sumbawa, likely associated with continental indentation. These gaps may promote mantle flow from the mantle beneath Indian Ocean to the mantle wedge beneath Sunda Arc, which could, in turn, influences magma generation and composition beneath anomalous volcanoes, such as Mt. Rinjani and Mt. Tambora, which produced major eruption in 1257 and 1815, respectively. We also infer lithospheric thinning and possible lithospheric detachment beneath Timor, consistent with collision of the Australian continental lithosphere beneath the arc, leading to partial jamming of the subduction process. Overall, these results provide new constraints on lithospheric structure, mantle dynamics, and subduction-related volcanism in the ATZ region.

presentations.presentation_title: Integrated Airborne Transient Electromagnetic and Aeromagnetic Survey for Delineating Prospective Areas of Copper-nickel Polymetallic Mineralization
presentations.institution: Institute of Geophysical and Geochemical Exploration,CAGS
presentations.abstract: As key geophysical methods, airborne transient electromagnetic (ATEM) and aeromagnetic surveys have consistently played a vital role in mineral resource exploration. This paper introduces innovative approaches to data preprocessing, processing, and correction for ATEM and aeromagnetic data, summarizing techniques to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio of airborne geophysical data. Methods such as LCI, SCI, and Gauss-Newton are applied to ATEM data inversion, with an analysis of the strengths and limitations of different inversion techniques when applied to measured airborne geophysical datasets. Taking a representative metallogenic belt in western China as a case study, an integrated interpretation of ATEM and aeromagnetic data is performed to investigate the distribution characteristics of basic–ultrabasic rock masses and fault structures, evaluate favorable geological indicators for copper‑nickel mineralization, and delineate prospective exploration targets. Large-scale, high-precision aeromagnetic surveys clearly delineate the structural framework of copper‑nickel metallogenic belts, revealing distinct rock-controlling and ore-controlling features. Furthermore, integrated inversion of ATEM and aeromagnetic anomalies provides critical guidance for copper‑nickel mineral exploration.

presentations.presentation_title: Deep Structural Characteristics of the Shuangjianzishan Polymetallic Mining Area: Constraints from Integrated Geophysical Data
presentations.institution: Institute of Geophysical and Geochemical Exploration, CAGS
presentations.abstract: The Shuangjianzishan Ag-Pb-Zn polymetallic deposit, located in the metallogenic belt of the southern Greater Xing’an Range, is the largest silver deposit in Asia. A series of large-scale polymetallic deposits are developed in its peripheral areas, including the Haobugao Ag-Pb-Cu-Sn deposit and the Baiyinnuo’er Pb-Zn-Ag deposit. However, a persistent lack of deep geophysical data has left our understanding of the deep metallogenic processes inadequate and thereby hindered further prospecting breakthroughs in this mining area. In this study, a ~139 km-long magnetotelluric (MT) profile trending NW-SE was deployed across the Shuangjianzishan polymetallic mining area. We constructed an 80-km-deep lithospheric electrical structure model for the study area by using multi-stage refined two-dimensional nonlinear conjugate gradient (NLCG) inversion method, and further performed comprehensive studies with the deep seismic reflection profile in the same strike direction adjacent to the MT profile. The results reveal that the crust-mantle structure of the study area is characterized by horizontal segmentation and vertically stratification as a whole. The Moho in the region is discontinuous and varies in depth from 36 to 40 km, showing a west-deep and east-shallow pattern. The upper crust of the main Great Xing’an Range displays high-resistivity characteristic, with numerous secondary faults developed within it. Two distinct low-resistivity zones are developed in the middle-lower crust, the Moho beneath these zones exhibits is offset, and deep large faults extend upward from their top to the shallow surface—a feature indicative of the source region and upward migration pathways for deep materials. Furthermore, A large number of secondary faults are developed around the large deep faults, and such faults may act as the terminals of ore-forming pathways or mineralized alteration zones, showing a spatial correspondence with the already discovered Shuangjianzishan Pb-Zn-Ag deposit and Haobugao Pb-Zn deposit at the surface.

presentations.presentation_title: Overview of the Network-MT Survey in Japan
presentations.institution: Earthquake Research Institute, The University of Tokyo
presentations.abstract: Electrical resistivity is one of the physical properties sensitive to the existence and connectivity of subsurface fluids such as interstitial water or melts. In order to elucidate a nation-wide 3-D deep electrical resistivity structure and to understanding the relationship between deep fluids and various tectonic activities, we developed an observation technique named Network-MT method (Uyeshima, 1991, Uyeshima et al., 2001, 2007). In this method, the telephone line network is fully used to determine horizontal distribution of voltage differences. Dipole lengths are typically several tens of kilometers. Since we deploy long dipoles, the S/N ratio of electrical records will be enhanced. This enhancement will enable us to extend the experiment both in space and frequency domain (especially toward the lower frequency range). We also obtain responses relatively free from the static effect.After the telluric voltage difference records are obtained, response functions in the frequency domain between each voltage difference and 2 component horizontal magnetic fields are estimated. Period range is from several to 10 5-6 s. By inverting those response functions with the aid of the inversion schemes specially designed for the Network-MT configuration (Siripunvaraporn, Uyeshima and Egbert, 2004, Usui and Uyeshima, 2025), we can estimate the 3-D resistivity structure.In this presentation, we first briefly introduce observations of the Network-MT method, several strategies to interpret the data to yield regional deep 2-D or 3-D structures. Then we will discuss on several resistivity structures obtained throughout Japan islands, in relation to the deep subduction of the Pacific and/or Philippine Sea slabs.

presentations.presentation_title: Estimation of Friction Parameters of the Source Regions of Slow Slip Events from Recurrence Intervals
presentations.abstract: Recurrence of slow slip events (SSEs) are generated in numerical simulations using a rate- and state-dependent friction (RSF) law to confirm that the recurrence interval of SSEs is consistent with the theoretical values of Ruina (1983) by correcting the ratio of effective stiffness k eff of a fault patch to the critical stiffness k c for unstable slip. Numerical simulations are conducted for two models: a single-degree-of-freedom spring-block model and a circular velocity-weakening patch embedded in a planar fault with velocity-strengthening friction in a 3D elastic medium. The simulations indicate that SSEs occur in cases that k eff is close to k c and the results for the two models are consistent with each other. The recurrence interval is approximately proportional to the characteristic slip distance divided by the loading velocity and a function of RSF parameters A (direct effect), B (evolution effect) and k eff /k c when the ratio of the peak slip velocity to the loading velocity is smaller than about 10. In the elastic continuum models, A−B in the velocity-strengthening region also affects the recurrence interval. For SSEs with higher slip velocities, A−B can be estimated from the peak slip velocity and the recurrence interval. The present results are applied to some observed SSEs such as the SSEs in the Bungo channel, southwestern Japan, and in the Boso peninsula, central Japan, to obtain friction parameters consistent with the estimates in previous studies. The present results can be used for constraining friction parameters in the source areas of SSEs, which are useful information for theoretical modeling of earthquake cycles.

presentations.presentation_title: Inelastic Crustal Deformation and Inland Seismogenesis of the Japan Islands
presentations.abstract: The generation mechanism of large inland earthquakes is an important scientific problem. However, there is no general understanding about it. This difficulty is attributed to the extremely slow loading process of inland earthquakes and the lack of knowledge about the mechanical properties of the crust. In March 2011, the Mw9.0 Tohoku earthquake occurred, causing large coseismic deformation in the surrounding areas characterized by instantaneous E-W extension, followed by significant postseismic deformation as gradually decaying E-W extension. Together with the interseismic deformation until 2011, these time-dependent deformations have been precisely documented by the permanent GNSS network in Japan, providing an opportunity to explore the mechanical properties of the Japanese island arc crust and thus the inland seismogenesis. The reversed deformation patterns before and after the Tohoku earthquake demonstrated that a localized shortening persists along the Japan Sea coast, implying the contribution of inelastic deformation in the lower crust, driven by the regional E-W compressive stress. We separated the crustal deformation of the Japanese islands into one caused by mechanical interaction at the subduction zones and the other caused by internal sources. It is demonstrated that the latter is persistent over different time periods and consistent with the seismologically determined regional stress field. Based on these observations, it is supposed that each crustal seismogenic fault is accompanied by a localized deformation in the lower crust that contributes to the tectonic loading of crustal faults. A numerical simulation considering the power-law behavior of the lower crust demonstrates the autonomous evolution of a mechanical feedback system between the upper and lower crusts, in which faulting in the upper crust causes localization of stress and strain in the lower crust while the localized lower crustal deformation builds tectonic stress in the upper crust.

presentations.presentation_title: Creeping But Capable: Evidence for Locked Asperities Along the Central Philippine Fault
presentations.abstract: We investigate coseismic slip release and interseismic strain accumulation along the central segment of the Philippine Fault system (PhF) from Masbate Island to Leyte Island using GNSS and InSAR observations. Our analysis focuses on recent moderate earthquakes and their relation to along-strike variations in fault slip behavior. In the Masbate region, we analyze coseismic deformation associated with the 2003, 2020, and 2023 earthquakes. The 2003 and 2023 events exhibit spatially coincident rupture areas, suggesting repeated slip on the same fault segment, while the 2020 earthquake appears to have occurred on a splay fault of the PhF, indicating a more complex fault geometry. The occurrence of these events suggests relatively rapid earthquake recurrence in Masbate, with an interval of approximately ~17 years for moderate-magnitude earthquakes. Interseismic modeling further indicates that the central to southern Masbate is characterized by low creeping rates and relatively high slip deficit rates of ~35–40 mm/yr. In the Leyte segment, interseismic deformation is dominated by high creeping rates in the northern and southern sections of the fault. However, a localized locking asperity is identified beneath central Leyte, coinciding with the source region of the 2017 Mw ~6.5 earthquake. Interseismic modeling indicates that the slip deficit rate in this central Leyte segment is comparable to that of southern Masbate, suggesting similar strain accumulation behavior despite differences in surface creep. Additional analysis of the 2017 Surigao earthquake indicates that coseismic rupture occurred along a segment characterized by high interseismic creep, extending from southern Leyte to the northern tip of Mindanao. This observation suggests the presence of another localized locking asperity along an otherwise creeping section of the fault. Overall, these results document pronounced along-strike variability in coseismic rupture behavior, interseismic slip deficit, and fault locking along the central PhF.

presentations.presentation_title: Foreshocks Evolution and the Seismic Nucleation Phase of an ML 5.6 Earthquake
presentations.institution: Shenzhen Research Institute, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
presentations.abstract: Understanding earthquake nucleation is fundamental for earthquake science. Using dense near-fault seismic observations, we investigate the nucleation of a shallow ML 5.6 earthquake at a hypocenter depth of 4.68 km, triggered by nearby hydraulic fracturing operations. High-resolution data reveal both a prolonged foreshock sequence and a weak seismic nucleation phase preceding the main rupture.The foreshock activity lasted approximately 11 months and evolved through three stages. (1) Fault destabilization stage (−11 to −3 months): foreshocks occurred in a stepwise manner and progressively migrated toward the mainshock hypocenter, indicating gradual fault weakening. (2) Precursory quiescence stage (−3 months to −3 days): seismicity markedly decreased, with reduced event rates and magnitudes and only sparse activity within 0.9 km of the hypocenter. (3) Immediate foreshock stage: seismicity reactivated near the hypocenter, highlighted by an ML 3.5 foreshock 0.6 km away six minutes before the mainshock, followed by several smaller events. Two very small events (ML −0.2 and ML 0.0) occurred 14 s before the mainshock in the immediate hypocenter vicinity, suggesting the possible role of preslip. A weak seismic nucleation phase lasting ~0.7 s was identified immediately before dynamic rupture. At near-fault stations, the initial impulse of the mainshock is weaker than that of the ML 3.5 foreshock and exhibits clear directivity, indicating rupture initiation within a confined area. With increasing distance, the mainshock initial impulse becomes stronger than the foreshock and shows enhanced low-frequency energy, implying distinct nucleation processes. Two additional subevents were identified during the nucleation phase, followed by cascading rupture after failure of a strong asperity. These observations suggest that earthquake nucleation involves long-term fault destabilization, a precursory quiescence period, and re-localization of seismicity near the hypocenter. The mainshock likely initiated within a low-strength zone adjacent to a strong asperity, producing a weak initial rupture before full dynamic failure.

presentations.presentation_title: Physics-informed Neural Networks Learn Precursory Behaviors of Slow-slip Events in the Nankai Subduction Megathrust
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Slow slips recur at the outermost layer of the megathrust asperities in the Nankai subduction zone, southwestern Japan. As a clue to its relationship with catastrophic earthquakes, this study reports a precursory behavior of slow-slip events (SSEs) in the Bungo Channel, the westernmost region of the megathrust. By employing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), we conduct a data assimilation analysis of onshore GNSS data recording the 2010 Bungo-Channel SSE with laboratory-derived physics of rate-and-state friction informed. PINNs begin to predict the remaining time to peak slip-rates, called time-to-failure, about a few months before reaching the peak slip rates, around which the estimated slip rates gradually exceed the plate loading rate. The estimated slip shows a simple acceleration curve of the slip rate inversely proportional to the time-to-failure, namely the inverse Omori law, that joins a fully coupled non-sliding plate motion to stress-releasing slip significantly faster than plate loading, which seemingly underlies the successful time-to-failure prediction. In support of this explanation, the trend of geodetic data near the epicenter transitions from preslip-like inverse-log to afterslip-like log around the estimated moment of peak slip rate. The above results imply that the preslip prospectively captured by PINNs is likely to reflect the actual behavior observed in the raw data rather than a bias arising from incomplete informed physics. Since those behaviors consistent with preslips have been expected, though not being directly detected thus far, as precursory phenomena of megathrust earthquakes, our detection of SSEs' preslip-like behaviors and their forecastability suggests that SSEs share the governing equation with fast earthquakes, conceptualizing the quasi-static self-similarity of earthquake ruptures. The 2010 Bungo-Channel SSE appears to be an aborted earthquake nucleation that traced the beginnings of ordinary earthquakes but terminated before radiating seismic waves.

presentations.presentation_title: Progressive Localization of Foreshocks Prior to Shallow Crustal Earthquakes
presentations.institution: Earthquake Research Institute, The University of Tokyo
presentations.abstract: On 6 January 2026, an Mw 5.7 shallow crustal earthquake occurred in Shimane Prefecture, SW Japan, characterized by right-lateral strike-slip faulting. Prior to the mainshock, a foreshock sequence was recognized near the mainshock hypocenter. To better resolve the spatiotemporal evolution of this sequence, we first relocate the associated earthquakes using a double-difference algorithm applied to differential travel-time data. The differential times are obtained from P- and S-wave arrival picks made on continuous waveform records by a deep neural network–based phase picker. We also used the differential arrival times obtained via the waveform cross-correlation method. We then apply a matched-filter detection approach, using the relocated events as templates, to identify additional earthquakes and construct an enhanced catalog. The foreshock activity began ~6 days before the mainshock within a tiny, localized spot. As the sequence progressed, the foreshocks intensified, including two M3-class events, and showed systematic migration toward shallower depths and westward. The foreshocks align within a ~500 m × 500 m planar structure that is nearly parallel to the aftershock distribution, interpreted as the mainshock rupture plane. Immediately preceding the mainshock rupture, an M ~1.0 event and an M ~4.0 event occurred in rapid succession, separated by less than 1 second. Overall, the observed foreshock evolution supports the progressive localization model proposed by Kato and Ben-Zion (2021).

presentations.presentation_title: Seismic-aseismic Interplay During the 2025 Mw 6.8 Sanriku-oki Earthquake Sequence Along the Japan Trench
presentations.abstract: The Mw 6.8 Sanriku-Oki earthquake of 9 November 2025 ruptured a Japan Trench segment characterized by inferred aseismic slip and recurrent Mw ~7 events, an area where offshore observations were previously limited. We utilize S-net seafloor data to examine the preparatory phase and early post-mainshock evolution of this sequence. Relocated seismicity reveals that activity began ~10 days prior to the mainshock, remaining clustered near the eventual rupture zone with a continuously low b-value (~0.5). This swarm subsequently migrated ~20 km, accelerating in the final ~2 days, exhibiting nucleation-like behavior near the creep–lock transition. Source inversions indicate that the mainshock and the largest aftershock initiated at opposite ends of the foreshock zone, propagating eastward and westward, respectively. Following the mainshock, aftershocks rapidly expanded ~75 km along strike within ~0.5 days, accompanied by the reactivation of repeating earthquakes. These observations collectively suggest a complex interplay between aseismic slip and seismic rupture on the shallow megathrust.

presentations.presentation_title: Records of Eocene Subduction Initiation in the Proto-south China Sea: Insights from the Volcanic Section of the Central Palawan Ophiolite, Philippines
presentations.abstract: Ophiolites exposed in the western Philippines and northern Borneo have been inferred to be related to the proto-South China Sea (pSCS). This fully consumed Mesozoic-Cenozoic oceanic basin played a crucial role in shaping the modern-day tectonics of southeast Asia. Despite its significance, the nature of the pSCS remains poorly constrained. Both Eocene and Cretaceous ophiolites in Palawan, Philippines were recognized to be related to the pSCS. In this contribution, we present novel geochemical and geochronological data from the volcanic section of the Eocene central Palawan ophiolite (CPO) to provide insights into the evolution of the pSCS. The volcanic sequence of the CPO records both explosive and effusive submarine volcanism, as indicated by the presence of pyroclastic breccias and lava flows, respectively. The lavas are composed of medium-Fe tholeiitic basalts with MORB-like signatures. In contrast, lapilli-sized glassy clasts within the pyroclastic breccias exhibit boninite series geochemistry. Both tholeiites and boninite series were likely derived from a depleted mantle source subsequently modified by subduction-related components. U-Pb geochronology of detrital zircons from a sandstone layer intercalated with boninitic pillow lavas yielded an Early Eocene age of 48.3±1.5 Ma. This not only suggests the possible maximum age of boninite volcanism, but also associates the boninite series with the CPO. The presence of boninite series provides an important tectonic constraint for the CPO, implying a possible subduction-initiation (SI)-related origin. Previous studies linked the metamorphic sole preserved in the northern CPO to subduction that was initiated near or along a spreading center within the pSCS. The results of this work highlight that SI in the southern portion of the CPO probably occurred along the interface between the Eocene and Cretaceous pSCS lithosphere. This interpretation explains the spatial distribution of lithologies across the CPO and underscores the complexity of the tectonic processes that occurred within the pSCS.

presentations.presentation_title: Novel Constraints on the Late Eocene–Miocene Island Arc Magmatism in the Southeast Asian Region: Insights from Western Philippine Arcs
presentations.abstract: Western Philippines comprises island arc and continent-derived terranes that record the complex interaction between the Indo-Australian and Philippine Sea Plates, and the migrating South China-derived slivers with its leading edge, the proto-South China Sea (pSCS). This study investigates magmatic products accross western Philippines to better understand the complex subduction, rifting-spreading, and arc-continent collision events that occurred in the region since Late Eocene to Miocene. In particular, geochronological and petrological analyses of volcanic and plutonic rocks in Marinduque (~22.1 ± 0.3 Ma) and Tablas islands (~20.3 ± 0.2 Ma), and in central Zamboanga (~24.0 ± 1.0 Ma), indicate magmatism in these areas in Early Miocene. Detrital zircons in sedimentary and metasedimentary units in Marinduque and central Zamboanga respectively, further hint at an Early Oligocene magmatism. At the same time, Late Eocene to Early Oligocene volcanism has also been recorded by previous works in other areas such as western Luzon, Panay, Negros, Palawan, Celebes Basin and southwestern Mindanao. We interpret the spatial and temporal distribution of these magmatic arcs in relation to regional tectonic events in Southeast Asia, supported by geochemical signatures of their magmatic products. The transitional arc-tholeiite affinities observed in Eocene-Oligocene arcs likely reflect a shift from oceanic spreading to subduction within and along the margins of the pSCS, driven in part by rifting in the South China Craton and the subsequent southward migration of continent-derived slivers. Progression toward calc-alkaline magmatism during the Miocene suggests continued subduction of the pSCS beneath these arcs, culminating in either its complete consumption or emplacement as ophiolitic sequences.

presentations.presentation_title: Importance of Detrital Materials in Mantle Peridotite Research
presentations.abstract: Heavy minerals and other detritus have been used for geological analysis of their provenance areas or their tectonic developments. Their importance for petrologic analysis of source bodies has been recognized to a very limited extent. We would like to show some examples to let you understand the importance of detrital materials to unravel more thorough petrologic characteristics of provenance peridotite complexes. They can be used: 1. To quickly understand petrologic characteristics of huge peridotite complex. Arai et al. (2006) used detrital chromian spinel in recent sediments to grasp petrologic character of the mantle section of the Oman ophiolite, which shows vast exposures and is, therefore, otherwise difficult to understand. 2. To obtain petrologic character of the part of peridotite complex, which has not been surveyed due to poor accessibility or thick vegetation. The Happo-O’ne peridotite complex in the Northern Japanese Alps was contact-metamorphosed by Ariake granite (~65 Ma). The contact metamorphic zonation has not been successful due to steep topography. Arai et al. (2024) examined metaperidotite cobbles in the creeks that cut the peridotite-granite boundary, and found opx-olivine assemblage, confirming the presence of opx-olivine zone at the contact. 3. To confirm the ABSENCE of chromitite in a peridotite body. The Happo-O’ne metaperidotite is mainly lherzolitic, and no chromitite pods are expected. To confirm this, the cobbles derived from the complex have been very carefully checked to find no chromitite. This is consistent with the idea of Arai and Abe (1995). 4. To unravel petrologic characteristics of highly sheared peridotite, which are otherwise difficult to obtain. The detrital chromian spinels from sheared peridotite mass are slightly higher in Cr# than those in peridotite blocks; high-Cr# spinels have not been reported from the latter. This indicates peridotites with high-Cr# spinel, which may contain more magnesian olivine, are preferentially destructed when sheared.

presentations.presentation_title: Precambrian Australia’s Fingerprint in Eastern Indonesia: P–T–t Constraints from Garnet–Sillimanite–Biotite Gneiss from the Banggai–Sula Microcontinent
presentations.abstract: The Banggai–Sula microcontinent, situated east of Sulawesi in eastern Indonesia, is interpreted as a continental fragment rifted from the Australia-New Guinea margin. However, its pre-Cenozoic basement history remains poorly constrained. We report the first evidence of Mesoproterozoic high-grade metamorphism from a garnet–sillimanite–biotite gneiss, providing a definitive link to the Australian cratonic interior. Garnet porphyroblasts containing sillimanite inclusions exhibit homogenous Mg-Fe-Mn profiles surrounded by high-Ca rims. Phase equilibria modeling constrains peak conditions at ~6.6 kbar and ~695°C, while conventional thermobarometry from garnet rims records 4–6 kbar and 580–650°C. The initial high-grade stage at ca. 1500 Ma is recorded by metamorphic zircon rims (Th/U < 0.1), while monazite geochronology revealed two distinct Mesoproterozoic tectonothermal events at ca. 1500 Ma and ca. 1400 Ma. Monazite inclusion in garnet (ca. 1396 Ma) suggests that garnet growth occurred syn- or post- the ca. 1400 Ma event. In contrast, zircon cores (Th/U > 0.1) record magmatic protolith crystallization at ca. 1600 Ma, with inherited populations at ca. 1750 Ma. The 1600 Ma population exhibits positive Hf(t) (0 to +6) and ages of 1.9–2.2 Ga, suggesting juvenile mantle-derived input into Paleoproterozoic crust. In contrast, the 1750 Ma inherited zircons show negative Hf(t) (0 to -2) and ages of 2.4–2.6 Ga, reflecting the recycling of ancient basements. The Proterozoic metamorphic "fingerprints" obtained from this study are distinct from the commonly reported Phanerozoic metamorphic ages in eastern Indonesia and suggest direct correlation with orogenic cycles in the North Australian Craton (e.g. Mt Isa, Georgetown, and Coen regions). These findings demonstrate that the Banggai-Sula basement represents a coherent fragment of the North Australian Proterozoic lithosphere rather than a distal sedimentary archive, offering a rare window into the billion-year evolution of Australian-derived microcontinents.
