presentations.presentation_title: Petrogenesis of Dunite-wehrlite Xenoliths from Oshima-Ōshima Volcano, Hokkaido, Ne Japan Arc: Implications for Sub-arc Uppermost Mantle Processes
presentations.abstract: Xenoliths in arc volcanics provide us with unrivaled constraints on the composition of the sub-arc lithosphere. Oshima-Ōshima volcano, Hokkaido, Northeast Japan arc, yields abundant ultramafic xenoliths for our information of arc mantle processes. Notably, the peridotite xenolith suite at Oshima-Ōshima is dominated by dunite and wehrlite, whereas lherzolite is absent and harzburgite is rare. This shows a sharp contrast to the xenolith suite of the Ichinomegata crater of Megata volcano in the same arc, where lherzolite-harzburgite are dominant and dunite-wehrlite xenoliths are rare. The key to elucidating this lithological contrast of peridotite xenoliths lies in the petrogenesis of the distinctive dunite-wehrlite dominating the Oshima-Ōshima xenolith suite. In this context, we present petrological data on these xenoliths to constrain their formation.These rocks occur as solitary xenoliths or frequently as composite xenoliths, either cut by veins or rimmed by selvages of clinopyroxenite to hornblende gabbro. Dunite and wehrlite are characterized by the absence of orthopyroxene and the presence of interstitial clinopyroxene, interpreted to have crystallized from a melt phase filling olivine interstices. Key mineral compositional features include: (1) olivine shows a gradual decrease in NiO (0.45–0.1 wt%) across a wide Fo range (93–78 mol%) and (2) spinel within interstitial clinopyroxene displays markedly higher TiO 2 (up to 3.6 wt%) than that enclosed in olivine, despite having a similar range of Cr# (0.3–0.6). These observed textural and geochemical features are explained by the invasion of silica-undersaturated alkali basalts into precursor orthopyroxene-bearing peridotites, causing incongruent melting of orthopyroxene and subsequent crystallization of clinopyroxene from the resultant secondary melt within olivine interstices. We suggest that this reaction proceeded extensively and intensely at the polygenetic Oshima-Ōshima volcano, driving pervasive dunite–wehrlite formation in the lithospheric uppermost mantle and generating the striking contrast with the monogenetic Megata volcano.

presentations.presentation_title: Temporal Changes in Mantle Wedge Geochemistry from the Early Cretaceous to the Paleogene in Japan: Constraints from the Crystallization Ages and Source Characteristics of the Iwafune Diorite
presentations.abstract: Crystallization ages and source characteristics of gabbroic and dioritic rocks are important for constraining the geochemical state of the mantle wedge and its temporal changes. Gabbroic and dioritic rocks in Northeast Japan show older crystallization ages and lower initial Sr isotopic ratios (SrI) than those in Southwest Japan, implying temporal changes in the mantle wedge from the Early Cretaceous to the Paleogene. To evaluate these changes, we examined gabbroic and dioritic rocks intruding into the Jurassic accretionary complex in easternmost Southwest Japan. In this region, both the gabbroic and dioritic rocks of Northeast and Southwest Japan intruded the same basement. This study focuses on the Iwafune diorite at the boundary between the gabbroic and dioritic rocks of Northeast and Southwest Japan. It consists of a main-diorite and a gabbroic diorite associated with granite. Whole-rock elemental compositions and SrI indicate that the gabbroic diorite is more primitive than the main-diorite. The elemental compositions of the Iwafune diorite show island-arc basalt characteristics (Pb and light rare earth elements enrichment and Nb, Ta, Ti, and heavy rare earth elements depletion). Zircon U–Pb dating indicates crystallization ages of ~65 Ma for the main-diorite, gabbroic diorite, and associated granite. Geochemical characteristics and mass-balance calculations indicate that the main-diorite was derived from the gabbroic diorite through an assimilation–fractional crystallization process. Elemental and Sr isotopic constraints suggest that the Iwafune dioritic magma originated from partial melting of a metasomatized mantle enriched in Sr and with higher 87Sr/86Sr than depleted mantle. The crystallization ages and SrI indicate that the Iwafune diorite belongs to the Southwest Japan suite. The temporal increase in SrI values from the gabbroic and dioritic rocks of the Northeast to Southwest Japan is interpreted to reflect changes in the mantle source rather than differences in the degree of crustal mixing.

presentations.presentation_title: Characterization of Serpentinite from Mt. Shirouma: Possibly the Highest-elevation Mantle Rock in Japan
presentations.abstract: The serpentinite exposed near the summit of Mt. Shirouma in the Northern Japanese Alps is possibly the highest-elevation mantle-derived rock in Japan (ca. 2800 m above the sea level). To confirm this, we examined the serpentinite in detail. The Shirouma serpentinite is one of the ultramafic bodies in the Hida Marginal Belt (Nakamizu et al., 1989). It occurs as a klippe thrust onto the Permian Shirouma-dake Formation (Takeuchi, 1998; Takeuchi et al., 2004). The Shirouma serpentinite body is overall highly sheared, but the massive part contains bastite after orthopyroxene. The bastite is around 10 volume % in mode, indicating a harzburgite or lherzolite protolith. Olivines and pyroxenes have been completely converted to serpentine (antigorite), talc, carbonates and magnetite. Chromian spinel is the only primary mineral preserved in part, and characteristically vermicular in shape. Its Cr# (Cr/(Cr+Al) atomic ratio) is about 0.37. The low to moderate Cr# of chromian spinel, combined with the estimated modal composition, indicates a protolith of lherzolite or clinopyroxene-bearing harzburgite (Arai, 1994). This is consistent with the predominance of lherzolite of the Happo-O’ne peridotite complex (Khedr and Arai, 2010), the largest mantle peridotite mass in this area. The vermicular shape of chromian spinel is common to lherzolite or harzburgite in peridotite complexes in the Japan-Sea side of Southwestern Japan (e.g., Matsumoto and Arai, 2001), where the extension of Hida Marginal Belt has been expected (Ishiwatari, 1989). The lherzolite as the protolith of the Shirouma serpentinite is possibly the mantle-derived peritodite of the highest elevation in Japan. The accumulative vertical elevation (possibly 9 km or more) is equivalent to that of the sediments exposed at Mt. Everest in the Himalayas. The Shirouma lherzolite may represent the active Japanese arcs, which has been mobile at the margin of the Eurasian continent.

presentations.presentation_title: Ultramafic Xenoliths in Andesite Lavas from Dinem Island, Philippines: Implications for the Subarc Mantle Beneath the Luzon Arc
presentations.abstract: Xenoliths entrained in ascending magmas provide important constraints on processes occurring at depth in the subarc region. In the Philippines, mantle xenoliths hosted by lava flows have previously been reported from Batan and Sabtang islands in the Batanes Group of Islands (BGI), northern Luzon. The BGI forms part of the Babuyan segment of the Luzon arc, which is associated with the subduction of the South China Sea basin along the Manila Trench. This work presents new petrological and geochemical data of the ultramafic xenoliths in the andesite lavas from Dinem island. Dinem is a triangular-shaped island located north of Batan and Sabtang islands. The xenolith suite consists primarily of spinel peridotites, mainly harzburgites and dunites, exhibiting protogranular to equigranular textures. Melt pockets composed of plagioclase and amphibole symplectite occur in the interstices of the spinel harzburgites, whereas secondary orthopyroxene is commonly observed in the dunites. Orthopyroxenite and hornblendite layers form reaction selvages between the peridotite xenoliths and the andesite host lavas. These textural relationships record the complex interplay between the entrained mantle fragments and ascending magmas. The geochemical data generated from these xenoliths provide new constraints on the physical and chemical conditions of the subarc conditions beneath this segment of the Luzon arc.

presentations.presentation_title: Spreading Modes at Slow-spreading Ridges Shifted by Mantle Heterogeneity of the Asthenosphere: A Case of Mid-Atlantic Ridge, 23°N
presentations.institution: Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources
presentations.abstract: Oceanic crusts at slow-spreading ridges are created either by symmetric spreading dominated by magmatic accretion or asymmetric spreading controlled by tectonic extension. Consecutive change in the spreading mode at the same ridge has been commonly attributed to variation in magma supply, but the mechanism controlling magma supply remains unclear. Here, we present geochemical analyses of peridotites and basalts from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge at 23°N, a region that has shifted from asymmetric spreading to symmetric spreading over the past 3.3 mi l lion years. Our results indicate that the asymmetric phase was characterized by a low magma flux, resulting from inherited ancient melt depletion in the asthenosphere. The subsequent increase in magma supply and shift to symmetric spreading corresponded with the arrival of more fertile mantle material. This work provides evidence of shifts between spreading modes driven by changing mantle compositions, highlighting the crucial role of asthenospheric heterogeneity in controlling the spreading modes at slow-spreading ridges.

presentations.presentation_title: Microseismicity of the Eastern Gakkel Ridge, Arctic Ocean
presentations.institution: State Key Laboratory of Submarine Geoscience, Second Institute of Oceanography, MNR
presentations.abstract: At ultraslow-spreading mid-ocean ridges, the formation and thickness of oceanic lithosphere are shaped by spreading rate, hydrothermal cooling, and magma supply. It is generally accepted that the lithosphere thickens significantly at spreading rates <20 mm/yr, driven by limited magma input and intense hydrothermal cooling. The Gakkel Ridge, the slowest-spreading ridge in the world, has been poorly studied due to harsh ice conditions and limited seismic data. The 2021 JASMInE cruise marked the first deployment of Ocean Bottom Seismometers (OBSs) along the eastern Gakkel Ridge. We detected 234 microearthquakes, with most occurring at depths of 0-10 km below the sea floor. This depth range is substantially shallower than the 20 km reported at other ultraslow-spreading ridges, but it is consistent with thermal models predicting the depth of the 750°C isotherm under ultraslow-spreading conditions. It is unexpected that no microearthquakes were recorded beneath the 1999 volcanic eruption site, which was substantially influenced by the large, hot volcano at 85°E. The majority of seismicity was concentrated near the ridge segment end at 88°E, where no volcanic cones or other volcanic features are observed in the bathymetric data. The deep seismicity, asymmetric spreading, and diverse stress pattern suggest the possible presence of an underlying detachment fault in this area. The deep-rooted fault system likely controls ridge segmentation by establishing strong rheological boundaries. Given the absence of large-offset transform fault systems at the Gakkel Ridge, the deep faulting system plays a more important role in ridge segmentation.

presentations.presentation_title: Slower Spreading Produces Thicker Crust at Sedimented Ultraslow-spreading Gakkel Ridge
presentations.institution: Second Institute of Oceanography,Ministry of Natural Resources
presentations.abstract: Crustal accretion at mid-ocean ridges is known to be spreading rate dependent, with relatively uniform crust at fast to slow ridges and progressively thinner crust at ultraslow ridges. Here we show, using integrated multichannel seismic data, two-dimensional gravity inversion and isostatic modelling, that crustal thickness along the eastern ultraslow Gakkel Ridge (70°E–125°E) increases as spreading slows. Average crustal thickness systematically increases from ~5.5 km at 10 mm/yr to ~7.5 km at 6 mm/yr, contrary to classical spreading–magmatism relationships. To explain this correlation, we propose that thick sediment cover (1.5-2 km) thermally insulates the ridge axis, prolonging magma production over a broader accretion zone, resulting in a thicker crust. Our model explains a fundamental difference in crustal accretion processes between thick sedimented ultraslow ridges and classical mid-ocean settings.

presentations.presentation_title: From Normal to Anomalous Seafloor: Long-baseline Geophysical Constraints on Spreading Dynamics West of the Australian–Antarctic Discordance, Southeast Indian Ridge
presentations.abstract: The Australian–Antarctic Discordance (AAD) is one of the most anomalous segments of the global mid-ocean ridge system, characterized by unusually deep bathymetry and rugged morphology despite an intermediate full spreading rate. While previous studies have suggested the presence of cold and compositionally distinct mantle beneath the AAD, the spatiotemporal evolution of seafloor spreading processes remains poorly constrained due to the lack of continuous, long-baseline observations. Here we present results from a three-year shipborne geophysical survey conducted during the 64th–66th Japanese Antarctic Research Expeditions (JAREs, 2022–2025), targeting the transitional zone west of the AAD along the Southeast Indian Ridge. Continuous measurements of three-component magnetic fields, shipborne gravity, multibeam bathymetry, and sub-bottom profiling were acquired along repeated north–south transects primarily aligned with the 110°E meridian and adjacent ridge-perpendicular lines. In total, more than 4,000 km of geophysical profiles were collected, covering a latitudinal range from 40°S to 60°S and crustal ages from present day to ~30 Ma. These data represent the first systematic geophysical coverage of this unexplored region, although adverse weather conditions and operational constraints occasionally required deviations from planned survey lines. Preliminary analyses reveal pronounced along-axis and off-axis variations in seafloor structures, indicating significant spatial heterogeneity in crustal thickness and magmatic accretion. Variations in the continuity of geophysical signals suggest temporal fluctuations in melt supply and asymmetric crustal formation over million-year timescales. In particular, the westward transition from “normal” seafloor spreading to anomalously deep and tectonized crust appears to be gradual rather than abrupt, implying evolving mantle thermal and compositional conditions beneath the ridge. These results provide new observational constraints on seafloor spreading dynamics in melt-poor ridge environments. Meanwhile, experience gained under persistently harsh Southern Ocean conditions underscores the importance of refining survey strategies to improve data continuity in future Antarctic investigations.

presentations.presentation_title: Crust-mantle Structure of the Southern Kyushu-palau Ridge: Implications for Magmatic Characteristics and Loading Processes
presentations.institution: Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources
presentations.abstract: The Kyushu–Palau Ridge (KPR) provides a natural laboratory for studying tectonic and magmatic evolution from subduction initiation to back-arc spreading, though the magma emplacement behind its structural variations remain unclear. Based on two wide angle seismic profiles, we imaged the crustal structure of the southern KPR. Results show that the KPR’s crust to the west is 6.0–7.6-km-thick with one summit at the basement and a flat Moho boundary at a 12-km depth; to the east, the crust has a thickness of 7.0–11.0 km, and three summits are observed at the basement sharing one depressed Moho boundary (12–15 km depth). These structural diversities indicate the presence of two independent seamounts, with distinct magmatic histories. We estimate that the western seamount formed through ~4 Myr of magmatism from a stable source, whereas the eastern seamount required two volcanic sources and ~10 Myr of episodic magmatism separated by a ~19-Myr period gap. Our analysis leads to two main conclusions: 1) multiple volcanic sources and episodic magmatism generated the along arc structural diversity at the KPR; 2) back arc spreading starting at ~26 Ma likely suppressed subduction related magmatism but may have induced partial remelting of the lower arc, creating new magma sources and leaving multiple conduits that reshaped the earlier island arc.

presentations.presentation_title: Hydrothermal Activity Along the Southwest Indian Ridge: Evidence from Hydrothermal Sulfide Geochronlogy
presentations.institution: Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources, China
presentations.abstract: Hydrothermal activities on the modern seafloor are critical for material and energy exchange between the lithosphere, hydrosphere, and biosphere. Seafloor hydrothermal sulfides are important deep-sea mineral resources which have been discovered in mid-ocean ridges, back-arc spreading centers and volcanic arcs (Hannington et al., 2005). The Southwest Indian Ridge (SWIR) has a full spreading rate of 14–18 mm/a, which is a typical ultraslow spreading mid-ocean ridge. The SWIR is characterized by a heterogeneous magma supply along the ridge axis, which is composed alternately of magmatic-enriched and magmatic-barren Segments. Since 2007, many hydrothermal fields (HFs) have been discovered in the SWIR, including Longqi, Duanqiao, Yuhuang, Suye, Tianzuo and Tiancheng (Tao et al., 2012; Liao et al., 2018, 2022; Ding et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2018). The 230 Th/ 238 U dating method was widely applied to determine the age of seafloor hydrothermal sulfides (Lalou et al.1985, 1993, 1995, 1998a, b). Chronology research can reveal multi-stage formation and superposition processes of ore bodies, as well as the formation and evolution history of sulfides, their growth and hydrothermal fluid activities. In this study, we used the 230Th/U dating method to constrain the sulfide formation history and the hydrothermal activity along the SWIR. In total, these 74 nonzero chronological data from hydrothermal sulfide samples provide the first quantitative characterization of the spatial and temporal history along the SWIR. The SWIR sulfide data indicate that hydrothermal events have been distributed unevenly through the time interval from 100 ka to 0.2 ka (Münch et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2018) .Hydrothermal events in the SWIR demonstrate that over the past 20 ka, hydrothermal activity in the SWIR has been relatively active. In contrast, between 40 ka and 100 ka, hydrothermal activity was relatively infrequent and short in duration.

presentations.presentation_title: Seismic Swarms in a Young Oceanic Transform Fault: Observations from the Zabargad Fracture Zone, Red Sea
presentations.institution: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Seismic swarms are commonly observed at oceanic plate boundaries, but their role in accommodating deformation along young oceanic transform faults is still not well understood. We examine seismic swarms at the Zabargad Fracture Zone (ZFZ) in the northern Red Sea. The Red Sea is classified as an ultra-slow spreading ridge, with a spreading rate of ~9 mm/year in the ZFZ. Recent high-resolution bathymetric mapping of the ZFZ, shows that deformation is focused along a ~50 km long transform fault that transitions into adjacent spreading segments. Our analysis is based on one year of ocean-bottom seismometer (OBS) data recorded between December 2021 and November 2022, together with data from land-based seismic stations. Earthquakes are detected using a machine-learning workflow applied to the OBS recordings, followed by manual phase picking and relative locations. The swarms exhibit a diffuse, cloud-like distribution rather than alignment on a single fault plane and elevated b-values. The earthquake focal mechanisms are predominantly strike-slip with a normal-faulting component, consistent with transtensional deformation along the transform system. The main swarms lasted for more than two months, extending from at least late 2021 to January 2022. Likely, the main swarm had already begun before the OBS deployment, preventing direct constraints on its initiation. To address this, ongoing work combines recordings from a small-aperture land-based seismic array located ~165 km away with several additional distant stations to investigate the earlier stages of the swarm. Instead of being released by a few large earthquakes, tectonic stress in this young transform fault appears to be taken up by many small events spread over a wide area, consistent with transtensional faulting and a structurally heterogeneous, possibly fluid-influenced crust.

presentations.presentation_title: Magnetic Signature of Oceanic Transform Faults and Their Fracture Zones
presentations.abstract: Oceanic transform faults (TFs) offset mid-ocean ridges, juxtaposing different-aged crust and causing fracture zones (FZ) crossing ocean basins. Recent studies challenge the consensus that TFs are conservative plate boundaries, instead supporting the existence of extensional tectonics and two-phases magmatism at TF systems. These processes should affect the magnetic signature of these systems, yet it is still a matter of debate. Here, we use magnetic data over Hayes and Oceanographer TFs and six archive datasets to explore the magnetization of TFs at a global scale. Magnetization at ridge-transform intersections and FZs is stronger than within transform valleys. Weak magnetization in valleys supports tectonic deformation. Strong magnetization, either normal or reversed, traced from the outside corner into the FZ, sometimes even overprinting the adjacent older seafloor, documents a second-phase of magmatism. Both features show a spreading-rate dependence. Magnetics comply with other data in supporting that TFs are more dynamic than previously considered.

presentations.presentation_title: Experimental Monitoring of Subsurface Structures Using Horizontal and Vertical Fiber Optic Array Observations
presentations.institution: National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience
presentations.abstract: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) is a technology that measures minute strains by irradiating laser pulses into optical fiber cables and measuring the phase of the backscattered light. We are focusing on DAS as a method for monitoring underground structures to predict seismic motion. Using DAS, it is possible to monitor vibrations along a cable approximately 50 km long at intervals of several meters. Furthermore, simultaneous observations using DAS that utilize the numerous communication cables laid underground are expected to enable three-dimensional estimation of subsurface structures.This study conducted observations aimed at developing a method for monitoring underground structures through combined horizontal and vertical optical fiber observations. DAS observations are currently underway in the Kinugawa River basin in Tochigi Prefecture. Simultaneous observations were made using approximately 25 km of optical fiber cable laid along the river embankment and optical fiber cable installed in the nearby Hi-net Moka deep borehole, which reaches a depth of 1648 m. These observations will be conducted about a one-month period from January to February 2026. During these periods, observations will be conducted using optical fiber cables and geophones installed along the embankment. Vibration records, including earthquakes and continuous microtremors, will be acquired, and cross-correlation analysis will be performed using these records. This presentation reports on the results of estimating the subsurface seismic velocity structure using these records.Acknowledgement:This research was funded by the Specified Critical Technologies Research Promotion Grants from the Cabinet Office, Government of Japan. Part of this research was conducted as a joint project between the NIED and the JGI, inc. The fiber optic observation along the embankment was conducted with the cooperation of the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism.

presentations.presentation_title: Feasibility Study for Estimating P-wave Attenuation at Shallow Depths from Borehole Das Observation
presentations.abstract: We propose a novel method to estimate P-wave quality factors (Qp) at shallow depths from borehole Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) observations and assess its utility using synthetic data. We assume a structure model composed of three horizontal layers. A plane P-wave pulse is normally incident on the free surface from below, and axial strain records are sampled at 512 channels along a vertical borehole between the surface and a depth of 2.56 km. Upgoing and downgoing waves are separated by applying a frequency-wavenumber (FK) filter to the records of all channels. That is a clear advantage of using borehole DAS records. Then, the downgoing wave is deconvolved with the upgoing wave. The obtained deconvolution record shows reflected waves from respective layer boundaries. Of these, the most prominent phase, the reflection at the free surface, is extracted and used for the spectral analysis. From the frequency gradient of the logarithmic spectral amplitude of the deconvolution record, the depth-averaged Qp value can be estimated once the round-trip travel time of the P wave from the surface to that depth is known. Furthermore, the depth-averaged Qp value for each channel is used as input to seismic tomography to estimate the depth distribution of Qp values. As a result, the Qp value is overestimated for the first layer at the shallow depths, but the Qp values ​​are restored for the second and third layers. The overestimation of the Qp value for the first layer is probably due to the too-short path length. We plan to examine oblique-incidence cases to understand the effects of the P-to-SV conversion.

presentations.presentation_title: Development of Seismic Monitoring System Using Distributed Acoustic Sensing Applying to Seafloor Cable Off Sanriku, Japan
presentations.abstract: A spatial density for a marine seismic observation can be increased by applying Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) technique to a fiber in a seafloor cable. Earthquake Research Institute deployed a seafloor seismic and tsunami observation system using an optical fiber cable off Sanriku, northeastern Japan in 1996. A total cable length is approximately 100 km. Short-term DAS measurements have proved a good performance for micro-earthquake observation. From March 2025, a DAS observation is continued to observe seismic activity. A quasi real-time data transmission system using the internet was developed for the successive observation. The system includes data decimation for spatial and temporal direction to reduce an amount of data. The HDF5 format of the data file is converted to domestic seismic data format (win format). Data with win format have advantage to apply various kind of established processing. Because we set the interrogator to generate data file every 30 seconds, the HDF5 file is read just after file generation and the system processes the data. As a result, data are transmitted with a delay of approximately 30 seconds. Identification of seismic arrivals in DAS data is needed to determine a hypocenter. First we picked up arrival times of P- and S-waves for Every 100 channel records on DAS data and data from close seismic stations on a computer display for local earthquakes. Results of location of earthquakes had smaller errors of location than those of the location without the DAS data. To expand the location method, we applied an improved automatic pick-up program using evaluation function from conventional seismic network data by seismometers, and we obtained precise arrivals time of P, S and converted PS waves. The location with higher resolution using all DAS data and surrounding ordinary marine and land seismic stations will be performed.

presentations.presentation_title: High-resolution Monitoring of Seismic Velocity Changes at Sakurajima Using Das-based Seismic Interferometry
presentations.abstract: Continuous monitoring of crustal seismic velocity using seismic interferometry is a powerful approach to detect stress changes and dynamic magmatic processes that are otherwise difficult to observe. Applying this technique to distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) data with thousands of channels enables unprecedented spatial resolution for subsurface structure monitoring. We analyzed continuous DAS data between September 2024 and October 2025 at Sakurajima volcano, Japan, using the optical fiber cable installed along a loop road around the volcano. Seismic ambient noise cross-correlation functions (CCFs) were computed for ~1.22 million channel pairs. The AOBA-S high-performance computing system at Tohoku University Cyberscience Center allowed us to drastically reduce the estimated computation time from 46 years to 26 days. Relative velocity changes were measured by applying the doublet method to 20-day stacked CCFs in the 0.25–0.5 Hz band.Significant coseismic velocity decreases and velocity recovery were detected. After the Mw 6.8 Hyuganada earthquake in January 2025, we observed a velocity decrease of 0.09%. Tomographic analysis revealed a pronounced velocity decrease (0.12%) around the crater. Smaller changes (0.01%) occurred during the Mw 6.0 Osumi earthquake in April 2025, and recovery after the Mw 7.0 Hyuganada earthquake in August 2024 was also identified. Recovery speeds after the January 2025 earthquake varied spatially, being slower along peripheral paths and faster across the crater. These results demonstrate that DAS-based seismic interferometry can resolve spatiotemporal velocity changes with exceptional detail, offering new insights into the response of volcanic systems to seismic shaking. Acknowledgments: We used fiber optic cables of the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism. We would like to thank the Osumi River National Highway Office for helping us with the DAS observation. We also thank the Tohoku University Cyberscience Center for providing access to the AOBA-S high-performance computing system for CCF calculations.

presentations.presentation_title: Weak Localization of Seismic Waves Detected with DAS at Sakurajima Volcano, Japan
presentations.abstract: Seismic waves undergo multiple scattering due to small-scale heterogeneities before reaching seismic stations. Weak localization (WL) is a phenomenon that provides evidence of multiple scattering. WL arises from constructive interference between scattered waves traveling along reciprocal paths, resulting in localized energy enhancement near the source. By observing WL, the mean free path (MFP) and mean free time (MFT), which characterize subsurface small-scale heterogeneities, can be estimated. Detecting this phenomenon requires spatially dense observation. As a method for ultra-dense spatial sampling, Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) using fiber optic cables provides a good opportunity to detect WL. Although WL has been well established for translational components recorded by seismometer, its observability in deformational components recorded by DAS has not yet been verified. This study aims to numerically verify the detectability of WL in strain-rate fields and apply the method to real DAS data.We conducted finite difference method (FDM) simulations of seismic wave propagation in 2D random heterogeneous media. The simulation results show that the WL signal is clearly observable in the strain-rate, with an energy peak comparable to that of acceleration.We analyzed real DAS data recorded along the Nojiri River in Sakurajima Volcano. An active seismic source was generated using a hammer, repeated 202 times at intervals of approximately 15 seconds. We applied a bandpass filter (19-23 Hz) and stacked the signals from all shots. The analysis successfully detected a localized energy enhancement near the source. The estimated MFP and MFT were approximately 240 m and 1.4 s, respectively, indicating strong scattering characteristics typical of volcanic regions.We gratefully acknowledge the cooperation of the staff of the Osumi River and National Highway Office and the Sakurajima Sabo Office, Kyushu Regional Development Bureau, Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, in conducting the DAS observations.

presentations.presentation_title: Relationship Between Geological Structure and Das-derived Site Amplification Factors Based on K-means Clustering at Sakurajima, Japan
presentations.abstract: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) is an emerging technique that enables dense spatiotemporal measurements of ground vibrations, including earthquakes, using existing fiber-optic telecommunication cables, which is difficult with conventional seismometer arrays. This study leverages DAS's unique capabilities to investigate site amplification factors at Sakurajima, Japan. In 2023, we conducted a DAS observation at Sakurajima volcano, located in Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan. Earthquake records obtained by DAS were used to analyze S-wave site amplification factors at 5 m intervals along the 40 km cable. Although our previous analyses revealed a negative correlation between site amplification factors and S-wave velocity estimated by coda wave interferometry in the overall trend, the amplification factors exhibit finer-scale spatial variations (Yonemori et al., 2024, VSJ). Sakurajima is covered by lava flow of various ages and sediments; therefore, we focus on spatial variations in site amplification characteristics in the frequency domain and investigate their relationship with geological structure using a clustering method to reveal the detailed mechanisms of site amplification. Site amplification factors were estimated using 10 s windows of S-wave arrivals from 23 earthquakes in eight frequency bands (1-16Hz). The estimated amplification factors were then classified into five clusters using the K-means++ clustering method. The results indicate that lava-flow and sedimentary regions are characterized by distinct dominant clusters. Moreover, clusters that dominate in lava flow regions show different peaks frequencies, and these differences may suggest the scale of heterogeneity. In addition, the channels belonging to specific clusters show no clear relationship with the surface geology of Sakurajima, suggesting that these clusters may be associated with artificial structures. In this study, we use an optical fiber cable belonging to the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, supported by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism Kyushu Regional Development Bureau Osumi River and National Highway Office.

presentations.presentation_title: Characterizing Fault Zone Structures in Urban Taiwan using Distributed Acoustic Sensing with Telecom Infrastructure and 3-D Fiber Arrays
presentations.abstract: Active faults buried beneath urban regions pose significant seismic hazards, yet their fine-scale geometries and physical properties often poorly constrained due to the resolution limits of conventional seismic observations. Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) addresses this challenge by converting optical fibers into ultra-dense sensor arrays, enabling unprecedented high-resolution imaging of near-surface structures. Here, we demonstrate the versatility of DAS in resolving complex fault zones through two complementary case studies in Taiwan: the Shanchiao Fault in the Taipei Metropolis and the Milun Fault in the Hualien city. By leveraging existing telecommunication cables across the Shanchiao Fault, we apply ambient noise beamforming to derive high-resolution 2-D shear-wave velocity profiles, delineating the east-dipping fault geometry and frequency-dependent site amplifications within the basin. In parallel, utilizing a 3-D DAS array (surface and borehole) across the Milun Fault in Hualien, we identified fault-associated reflected and refracted phases from local earthquake wavefields. Integrating synthetic wavefield simulations and travel time modeling allows us to place sharp constraints on the fault geometry and velocity properties. Collectively, these applications, ranging from repurposing urban telecom infrastructure to deploying dedicated borehole fiber arrays, highlight the capability of DAS to map detailed fault zone structures and ground motion characteristics, offering critical improvements for seismic hazard assessment in urban regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Preliminary Exploration of the Integration of Distributed Acoustic Sensing and Multichannel Analysis of Surface Waves
presentations.abstract: Near-surface shear-wave velocity (V s ) is a key parameter for evaluating subsurface conditions in engineering geology and earthquake engineering. Multichannel Analysis of Surface Waves (MASW) has been widely applied to shallow subsurface investigations due to its non-destructive nature and operational efficiency. However, conventional MASW is primarily developed based on discrete geophone measurements. Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS), which differs from geophones in measured physical quantities and data formats, cannot be directly integrated into existing MASW workflows. Moreover, the influence of DAS system parameters and the physical consistency of DAS-based MASW results remain insufficiently validated. In this study, a Python-based MASW processing workflow tailored for DAS data is developed. The proposed framework integrates data format conversion, cross-correlation analysis to estimate time delays between individual active-source impacts, and waveform alignment and stacking to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio, followed by dispersion analysis and shear-wave velocity inversion. Field experiments were conducted at multiple sites with different surface conditions using active-source DAS–MASW measurements, and different gauge length settings on waveform characteristics and dispersion images were systematically investigated. In addition, dispersion curves were performed to establish a closed-loop validation framework, in which dispersion curves derived from assumed subsurface models were compared with field-observed DAS–MASW dispersion results. The results indicate that increasing gauge length leads to DAS waveforms that closely resemble those recorded by conventional geophones, reflecting improved waveform stability and consistency. However, larger gauge lengths introduce spatial averaging effects, resulting in a reduction of high-frequency components and local waveform details. The observed dispersion trends show good agreement with theoretical predictions, demonstrating the validity of the proposed analysis workflow.These results clarify the influence of system parameters on dispersion characteristics and inversion outcomes. The study demonstrates the potential of DAS as a practical sensing approach for near-surface subsurface characterization at the engineering scale.

presentations.presentation_title: Estimation of Rayleigh-wave Scattering Mean Free Path from DAS Wavefield Coherence Along National Route 47, Japan
presentations.abstract: Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) on existing telecommunication fibers has enabled dense, kilometer-scale strain measurements and has been increasingly used for surface-wave–based near-surface characterization. However, the scattering properties caused by small-scale structural heterogeneities have not been quantitatively estimated from DAS wavefields. In this study, we estimated the Rayleigh-wave scattering mean free path (mfp) from wavefield coherence. Using ambient vibrations recorded by a ~31-km DAS array along National Route 47 (Osaki City, Miyagi, Japan), we computed cross-correlation functions (CCFs) between densely spaced channels (spacing ~6.38 m). Applying the stochastic method used by Chaput et al. (2015) to strain data, we estimated the coherent intensity as the time-averaged squared amplitude of the spatially averaged complex CCF waveform (averaged over channel pairs with the same inter-channel distance), and the total intensity as the time-averaged mean of squared amplitudes over the same set of channel pairs. The coherent-to-total intensity ratio decreased with inter-channel distance; fitting an exponential decay to this ratio provided the scattering mfp. The mfp was estimated for each 10-channel (~64 m) subsection. The estimated mfp ranged from ~0.1 to 1.0 km (mean 0.34 km) at 4-5.7 Hz and decreased (mean 0.21 km) at 5.7–8 Hz. The spatial pattern showed longer mfp on terrace segments and shorter mfp in floodplain segments. Our findings show that the Rayleigh-wave scattering mfp can be robustly constrained from DAS wavefield coherence using a stochastic method. The estimates closely match theoretical predictions from the near-surface Vs model of Yabu et al. (2025, IASPEI) obtained using a deterministic method. This consistency confirms that DAS enables effective near-surface characterization by jointly using stochastic and deterministic approaches. The scattering mean free path is a valuable metric for guiding DAS-based large-scale investigations of Vs structure.

presentations.presentation_title: Effect of Fluid on the Moment-Duration Scaling Laws of Slow and Regular Earthquakes: Analogue Modelling with Multiphase Flow
presentations.abstract: Slow earthquakes show a distinctive linear scaling law between their moment M 0 and duration T, M 0 ∝T, which differs from regular earthquakes with M 0 ∝T 3 [1]. Recently, we have found that the linear scaling of slow earthquakes is quantitatively followed by a mixture of soft hydrogel particles and viscous fluid [2]. In contrast, dry rigid glass beads exhibit a power-law scaling M 0 ∝T n with an exponent n. This implies that fluid modifies the relationship between slip amount and area by suppressing force-chain networking. In this talk, we will discuss the effect of fluid on the exponent of the moment-duration scaling M 0 ∝T n and also on the shear localization.——————————We have conducted rotary shear experiments on dry or fluid-lubricated granular media, which exhibit numerous intermittent slip phenomena. As an analogue material for fault gouges, we used a mixture of opaque spherical particles (hydrogel and glass) and a transparent, viscous heavy liquid (sodium polytungstate solution) for brittle particles and a pore fluid, respectively. While measuring the stress and strain rate both on the shear interface and within the sample, individual particle motion was also recorded in situ.——————————Using stress drop for each event, we calculated seismic moment M 0 , which follows a power-law scaling, M 0 ∝T n . The exponent exhibits n = 1.3 for the granular-fluid mixture, while it is larger without fluid. These results imply that a sufficient amount of pore fluid qualitatively alters the nature of fault self-similarity that regular earthquakes follow [3]. An order parameter controlling the phase transition between slow and regular earthquakes warrants further investigations.——————————[1] Ide & Beroza (2023) PNAS; [2] Sasaki & Katsuragi (2025) Nat. Commun.; [3] Kanamori & Anderson (1975) BSSA
presentations.session_title: The Spectrum of Fault Slip: Connecting Slow and Fast Earthquakes

presentations.presentation_title: Recurrent Earthquake Swarms and Transient Crustal Deformation Off the Tokara Islands, Southern Japan: Insights from the 2025 Swarm Sequence
presentations.abstract: Earthquake swarms are seismic sequences without a distinctive mainshock and are often coincident with transient crustal deformation. Such anomalous phenomena are interpreted to relate to magma intrusions, slow slips, or fluid supplies. Off the Tokara Islands, which are parts of the Nansei Islands, southern Japan, swarm activities have been recurrently observed, particularly since 2021. However, the driving mechanisms of these swarms had been unclear. Motivated by the aforementioned backgrounds, we investigate the latest 2025 episode using GNSS data on the islands operated by the Geospatial Information Authority in Japan and SoftBank Corporation. The 2025 episode initiated in late June 2025 off the Tokara Islands and continued for about one month. During the episode, a secondary swarm occurred in early July 2026, west of the primary one, with a three-day duration. The daily GNSS data at multiple stations exhibit transient displacement up to 5 cm until the secondary swarm initiation. During the secondary swarm, the direction and rate of displacements dramatically changed at stations near the swarm, compared with the previous phase. After the termination of the secondary swarm, the spatial pattern of displacements recovered to that before the secondary swarm. Given such variations during a single episode, we divide the 2025 episode into three phases: before, during, and after the secondary swarm, and estimate source models for each phase, assuming rectangular faults. In all phases, the shear slip models reproduce the observed displacements systematically better than the open crack model. Finally, based on the modeling results, we propose that a magma or fluid supply drives the earthquake swarms and coincident crustal deformation.

presentations.presentation_title: Heterogeneity and Temporal Change in Stress Due to Shallow Seamount Subduction Using Discrete Element Method
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: The topography of the incoming basement has a strong effect on the slip pattern of subduction zones. Shallow seamounts are believed to break through the upper plate and create complex fracture networks that can potentially host slow earthquakes. However, a clear spatial correlation between slow earthquakes and individual seamounts can not always be found from observations. In this study, we use a numerical rock-box model with discrete element method to investigate the effects of a subducting seamount on the accretionary wedge, in which the evolution of the fracture system can be captured. Our model shows that initial seamount subduction fractures the upper plate by creating a frontal thrust near the leading flank and multiple back thrusts from the landward tip, together with reactivation and formation of new thrusts within the wedge, which is consistent with sandbox analogue modeling. Seamount subduction is controlled by local deformation combined with reactivation of pre-existing thrusts, which may lead to slow earthquakes and mud volcano activity over a wide effective area.Seamount subduction can be divided into three stages based on the slip pattern. In the first stage, slip occurs only on the landward flank. Continuous ramping of back thrusts on the seamount flank results in stress heterogeneity and spatial and temporal variations. In the second stage, failure leads to intermittent slip on the seaward flank. Only in the later stage does the model show clear overstress on the landward flank and understress on the seaward flank, as reported in previous numerical studies. These results suggest that shallow seamounts at different stages of subduction may contribute to the observed complexity of regional slip patterns.
presentations.session_title: The Spectrum of Fault Slip: Connecting Slow and Fast Earthquakes

presentations.presentation_title: Observations and Characteristics of Shallow Slow Earthquakes Along the Nankai Trough
presentations.abstract: Slow earthquakes have been widely studied, especially in subduction zones, since pioneering discoveries (e.g., Dragert et al. 2001; Obara 2002). Shallow slow earthquakes occur at depths of 10 km or less. Because of permanent offshore instruments and extensive seismic surveys, the Nankai Trough subduction zone is the region where shallow slow earthquakes are most extensively studied worldwide. We briefly summarize the characteristics of shallow slow earthquakes along the Nankai Trough based on two reviews (Takemura et al. 2023, 2025). Shallow slow earthquakes along the Nankai Trough occur at three specific spots, which are transitional areas between strong and weak mechanical locking zones (Noda et al. 2018; Takemura et al. 2019c). In contrast, a belt-like, continuous but heterogeneous slip distribution of deep slow earthquakes along 30-40 depth contours of the Philippine Sea plate is observed in the Nankai Trough. Although the scaled energies are 10 –10 -10 –9 at both depths, shallow seismic slow earthquakes are more energetic (e.g., Takemura et al. 2024). As mentioned above, our understanding of shallow, slow earthquakes has deepened through extensive research in the Nankai Subduction zone. However, the role of slow earthquake regions during megathrust earthquakes is still an open question. Slow earthquake regions along the Japan Trench are considered barriers against the rupture of the 2011 Tohoku earthquake (e.g., Nishikawa et al. 2019). However, the microstructure near the Nankai Trough suggests that a shallow plate boundary has experienced both slow and fast deformations (e.g., Kimura et al. 2022). To understand how shallow slow earthquake regions will behave in future megathrust earthquakes along the Nankai Trough, it will be indispensable to continue monitoring and investigating shallow slow earthquakes from multiple perspectives.
presentations.session_title: The Spectrum of Fault Slip: Connecting Slow and Fast Earthquakes

presentations.presentation_title: Ultra-low-angle Faults Produce Giant Earthquakes
presentations.abstract: What controls the occurrence of giant earthquakes remains a central question in seismology. We reveal a strikingly simple—but previously overlooked—relationship between earthquake size and fault dip in subduction zones. Global earthquake statistics show a robust dependence of earthquake size on fault dip, with the probability of extreme events peaking on ultra-low-angle faults. Through three case studies, we demonstrate that earthquakes tend to grow larger when the fault geometry is aligned with the regional stress field. We further discuss how such favorable stress configurations are generated along subduction interfaces and emphasize the critical importance of monitoring the temporal evolution of stress in subduction zones to better forecast future mega-earthquakes.

presentations.presentation_title: Repeating Earthquakes Reveal Episodic and Symmetric Aseismic Slip Prior to the 14 April 2025 Ml 5.2 Earthquake on the Elsinore Fault, Southern California
presentations.abstract: Repeating earthquakes are sensitive indicators of fault slip behavior on creeping fault segments. Here we use repeating earthquakes to constrain the fault slip behavior that preceded the 14 April 2025 Ml 5.2 earthquake on the Elsinore Fault Zone in southern California, part of the San Andreas fault system, and to assess how surrounding aseismic slip may have contributed to the occurrence of this event. We find that repeating earthquakes occurred persistently on both the northern and southern flanks of the mainshock rupture zone during the two years prior to the mainshock, while the source region itself remained largely locked. Individual repeating sequences are short, consisting of only 2–3 events, yet display extremely irregular recurrence, with inter-event times ranging from several minutes to several months. Such burst-like behavior is inconsistent with steady aseismic creep and instead indicates episodic slip under heterogeneous frictional conditions. Slip inferred from repeating earthquakes reveals nearly symmetric cumulative loading on both sides of the locked patch, reaching ~109 mm on the southern flank and ~108 mm on the northern flank over the two-year observation period. Despite the intermittent nature of the inferred aseismic slip, this symmetry implies comparable long-term stressing rates acting on the locked patch from both sides. Episodic surrounding slip can therefore progressively increase shear stress on a velocity-weakening patch in the absence of clear continuous precursory acceleration. We interpret the 2025 Ml 5.2 earthquake as the failure of a locked patch that reached critical nucleation conditions due to sustained and symmetric loading from episodically slipping fault segments on both flanks. This study provides observational insight into the physical processes governing earthquake nucleation, demonstrating that cumulative stress buildup from intermittent aseismic slip can lead to rupture even in the absence of detectable systematic temporal acceleration in the surrounding slip rate.

presentations.presentation_title: Technical Improvements on the Japan Coast Guard’s GNSS-A Seafloor Geodetic Observation for Monitoring the Subduction Zone Activities
presentations.abstract: Along the Nankai Trough and the Japan Trench, the Japan Coast Guard (JCG) operates a seafloor geodetic observation array (SGO-A) using the GNSS-A technique. SGO-A monitors seafloor crustal deformation in a global reference frame, directly above the expected source regions of megathrust earthquakes. It can detect the internal deformation within an overriding plate associated with co-, post- and inter-seismic processes (e.g., Sato et al., 2011, Science; Watanabe et al., 2014, GRL; 2021, EPS; Yokota et al., 2016, Nature). Data accumulated over more than 10 years have also enabled us to capture temporal variation in interseismic crustal deformation in the Nankai Trough region (e.g., Yokota and Ishikawa, 2020, Sci. Adv.). Following improvements in GNSS-A procedures, including sound speed perturbation modeling (e.g., Watanabe et al., 2020, Front. Earth Sci.; 2023, J. Geod.; 2025, EPS) and instrumental bias correction methods (e.g., Yokota et al., 2024, EPS; Watanabe et al., under review), we can now monitor temporal changes in slip deficit rate distributions, which are strongly related to slow slip events and coupling erosion (Yokota et al., in prep). However, further improvements in precision are required to detect smaller or shorter-duration events. In addition, the analysis procedures need to be further refined to obtain high-quality positioning results more rapidly after each observation. In this presentation, we introduce our observation system and key results, followed by recent updates in GNSS-A analysis.

presentations.presentation_title: Late-stage Supershear Rupture in the 2021 Mw7.4 Maduo Earthquake
presentations.institution: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
presentations.abstract: Earthquake rupture propagation can undergo a speed transition to velocities exceeding shear-wave speed, thereby producing shear Mach cones that transport stress and ground motion over long distances. Positioning the transition and extent of supershear rupture are crucial not only for seismic hazard, but also on rupture mechanism. However, it often poses challenges for kinematic studies. Here we present a detailed analysis of rupture process for the 2021 Maduo Mw 7.4 earthquake that broke a slowly-slipping fault in the northeastern Tibetan Plateau. Using near-fault data and a novel algorithm that determines varying rupture speed through tracking the time of slip rate at various locations, our results identify a 40 km supershear extent. This rupture propagates at 4.4 km/s during the last half of eastward rupture, unveiling a unique late-stage supershear rupture. The supershear transition observed at a gentle bend marking the fault orientation from main strike to the branch strike, could be explained by the barrier-induced supershear mechanism. Despite characterized by the mirrored morphology and uniform tectonic regime, the westward rupture just experiences a stable-to-slow-to-fast subshear process associated with a sharp bend severing as barrier. These findings underscore the role of critical size of barrier capable of triggering the supershear transition, which may further affect the rupture behaviors of immature faults.

presentations.presentation_title: Lawsonite Blueschist in a Dehydration-limited State Undergoes Semi-brittle Deformation That Triggers Intermediate-depth Earthquakes: Evidence from Acoustic Emission Experiments
presentations.abstract: Intermediate-depth earthquakes in cold subduction zones occur at the depths of 70-100 km where rocks are not expected to fracture because of high pressure-temperature (P-T) conditions. Fluid release associated with dehydration reactions in subducting blueschist has been presumed as a mechanism of intermediate-depth earthquakes. Previous experimental studies have mainly tested this hypothesis using powder samples of minerals in blueschist under P-T conditions relevant to earthquake hypocenters, but no consistent conclusion has been reached. Moreover, because the oceanic crust is composed of consolidated rocks, it is essential to test intact rock samples rather than powders. In this study, we conducted high-pressure (1-2 GPa) deformation experiments on intact lawsonite blueschist using a new Griggs-type apparatus at Tohoku University. During deformation, temperature was ramped from 473 K to 973 K (from 200℃ to 700℃) across the dehydration boundary, while acoustic emissions (AE) were monitored in situ. This allowed us to directly examine whether dehydration reactions trigger seismic failure. At different strain rates (10 -6 -10 -4 s -1 ), under P-T conditions where dehydration is expected to be completed, the rock first weakened by ductile flow without AE and subsequently transitioned to AE-accompanied seismic slip. Rock strength transition and AE data suggest semi-brittle behavior, in which ductile deformation and brittle fracture proceed simultaneously. However, no microstructural evidence for dehydration reactions was observed in the recovered samples. This indicates that faulting occurred under disequilibrium conditions, in which the reaction did not catch up with temperature ramping and the rock remained metastable. Our results suggest that semi-brittle deformation of dehydration-limited blueschist may be a viable mechanism for intermediate-depth earthquakes.

presentations.presentation_title: Spatiotemporal Controls on Cenozoic Magma Genesis in eastern West Java
presentations.abstract: Java Island forms part of the Sunda Arc, generated by Indo-Australian Plate subduction beneath Eurasia since ~45 Ma. This study presents zircon U–Pb geochronology, Hf isotopes, and whole-rock geochemistry from 54 igneous samples across nine eastern West Java volcanoes (Ciremei, Guntur, Galunggung, Cikuray, Papandayan, Malabar, Patuha, Tangkuban Parahu, Southern Mountains). Cenozoic magmatism divides into four stages: early Miocene (20.9–5.6 Ma, εHf (t) +17.0 to +13.5), late Miocene (5.6–3.7 Ma, εHf (t) +8.4 to +6.4), Pliocene (3.7–1.2 Ma, εHf (t) +17.0 to +11.0), and Pleistocene (1.2–0.2 Ma, εHf (t) +14.5 to +0.4). All stages exhibit subalkaline basalt to rhyolite compositions with LREE enrichment and HFSE depletion (Nb, Ta, Ti), which are typical island-arc signatures. Magmatism migrated south-to-north during stages 1–3 and became widespread in stage 4. Pleistocene Tangkuban Parahu shows elevated K 2 O and incompatible elements due to deeper Benioff zone melting, identifying it as back-arc compared to southern volcanic-front volcanoes. Guntur Volcano displays andesite-dominated west (back-arc; high LREE/HREE) versus basalt-dominated east (volcanic front). Galunggung samples match primitive tholeiites from the 1982–1983 eruption phase 3. Low εHf (t) at Cikuray (+8.4 to +6.4) reflects Garsela Fault-related crustal assimilation. Patuha's low εHf (t) (+6.7 to +0.4) results from slab tear-induced asthenospheric upwelling and sediment melting between Sumatra and Java.

presentations.presentation_title: Mountain Building Mechanism of the Taiwan Orogeny - Along Strike Variability
presentations.abstract: Taiwan is situated within an active arc–continent collision zone and represents one of the most rapidly exhuming orogens on Earth, characterized by complex structural architecture. In our previous work, we developed a comprehensive thermomechanical model that incorporates the depth-dependent transition from brittle to ductile deformation, lithology-controlled erosion, and observed geometries of the basal decollement and backstop. The model successfully reproduces the key structural features of the northern Taiwan orogen and is consistent with metamorphic temperature profiles, thermochronological constraints, spatial patterns of strain, and the observed rates of exhumation and cooling. The results further demonstrate the critical roles of ductile deformation and ramp structures in the formation of the Hsuehshan Range and the Western fold-and-thrust belt. Structural styles, however, vary systematically from north to south across the Taiwan orogen. Notably, the Hsuehshan Range is absent in southern Taiwan, and total crustal shortening decreases significantly toward the southern tip of the island. Here, we apply the same thermomechanical framework under varying boundary conditions to reconstruct the along-strike evolution of mountain building across Taiwan. Our results indicate that the timing of orogenic onset is comparable along strike, whereas the rate of shortening decreases progressively from north to south. The basal decollement extends to approximately 20 km depth and exhibits variable ramp–flat geometries, leading to distinct structural styles along the orogen. The model successfully captures the development of the Pingtung Basin and the structural evolution of the Hengchun Peninsula, providing a unified framework for understanding the along-strike variability of Taiwan’s orogeny.

presentations.presentation_title: Provenance and Tectonic Setting Through Whole Rock Geochemistry of Sedimentary Sequences, Marinduque Island, Philippines: Insights Into Arc-continent Collision
presentations.abstract: Marinduque Island’s proximity to the arc-continent collision zone in Central Philippines makes it ideal for testing whether its sediments preserve records of the collision event. Major and trace element compositions of a Cenozoic sedimentary sequence are used to discriminate provenance (mafic, intermediate, felsic) and tectonic setting (e.g., oceanic island arc vs. continental arc/margin) using established discrimination diagrams. Geochemical proxies indicate mixed mafic-felsic sources in an oceanic island arc setting. Detrital zircons from the sedimentary unit record a Late Eocene magmatic event, linking sediments to regional arc magmatism. These data constrain sedimentary response to collision, supporting tectonic evolution models for the Philippine Mobile Belt. Results indicate that Marinduque may hold vital data for reconstructing Cenozoic arc-continent interactions.

presentations.presentation_title: Crustal Architecture and Fault-controlled Deformation in the Central Philippine Arc–continent Collision Zone
presentations.abstract: The tectonic architecture of the West Central Philippines records the cumulative effects of several interacting geodynamic processes, including arc–continent collision and strike-slip deformation associated with the Philippine Fault Zone. The northern part of the central Philippines, situated within the Philippine Mobile Belt and the Palawan Microcontinental Block, is a zone of particularly complex plate interaction where these processes overlap. As a result, the region exhibits diverse structural styles ranging from contractional uplifts to extensional basins, reflecting spatial and temporal variations in the prevailing stress regime. Major fault systems, such as the Verde Island Passage Fault and the Sibuyan Sea Fault, cut across both onshore areas and marginal seas, accommodating significant lateral displacement and exerting strong control over crustal deformation. This study reexamines the geologic framework and crustal structure of the West Central Philippines by integrating regional geophysical datasets. Mantle residual gravity anomalies derived from the WGM2012 global gravity model were analyzed using Euler deconvolution to estimate Moho depths and characterize first-order variations in crustal thickness. These gravity-based interpretations were evaluated in conjunction with available magnetic data, bathymetry, and seismic strain rate to assess patterns of active deformation and their geodynamic implications. The resulting models reveal pronounced lateral variations in crustal thickness that systematically correspond to zones of transtension and transpression. These observations highlight the fundamental role of internal fault systems in shaping crustal architecture within a convergent-margin setting. By linking crustal thickness variations with present-day strain, this study provides new constraints on the tectonic evolution of the West Central Philippines and underscores its implications for seismic hazard assessment in this highly dynamic region.

presentations.presentation_title: Cenozoic Tectonic Evolution of Southeast Korea Since the Opening of the East Sea (Japan Sea).
presentations.abstract: The Cenozoic geology of SE Korea preserves the key records for reconstructing the evolution of the East Sea (Japan Sea). During the late Oligocene to Middle Miocene (ca. 25-15 Ma), the southeastern part of Korean Peninsula was belonged to dextral shear stress in response to the NNW-trending back-arc extension of the East Sea. This resulted in the development of the Miocene pull-apart basins in SE Korea, governed by NNW-striking dextral strike-slip faults (PDZs: Principal Displacement Zones) and the associated NE-striking normal faults. The basin fills comprise Early Miocene dacitic and basaltic volcanogenic rocks interbedded with terrestrial sediments (ca. 23-18 Ma), conformably overlain by Middle Miocene terrestrial to marine sequences (ca. 17-10 Ma). The Early Miocene volcanic rocks are mostly sub-alkaline, whereas the Middle Miocene basaltic rocks (ca. 15-13 Ma) are sodic alkaline phono-tephrites. As indicated by stratigraphic and structural datasets, parallelogram-shaped basins formed between the NNW-trending PDZs during the Early Miocene, accompanied by northwestward tilting and clockwise horizontal rotation of the blocks. Since 17 Ma, dextral strike-slip movement of the NNW-trending Yeonil Tectonic Line (YTL) and associated NNE-trending normal faults led to the formation of wedge-shaped Middle Miocene basins, characterized by northward migration of depocenters and southwestward rift propagation. However, following the collision between the Philippine Sea Plate and southwestern Japan at approximately 15 Ma, vigorous basin extension ceased. This subsequently triggered basin inversion, leading to the contraction of pre-existing extensional structures and crustal uplift in the SE Korea. Following the tectonic inversion, crustal magmatism shifted from sub-alkaline to alkaline, and the basin fill sedimentation eventually terminated around 10 Ma. Since approximately 5–3.5 Ma, the regional stress field of Korea has been dominated by E–W to ENE–WSW compression, primarily driven by eastward motion of the Amurian Plate and westward low-angle subduction of the Pacific Plate.

presentations.presentation_title: Seismogenesis of Earthquakes in the Yellow Sea and Their Tectonic Implication
presentations.abstract: Relatively large earthquakes of magnitude 5 have occurred in the central Yellow Sea in a north-south direction, with a 10-year cycle over the past 30 years: 1993–1994, 2003–2004, and 2011–2013. Areas with high seismicity include west of Heuksando (35°N, 124°E) and Baengnyeongdo (38°N). In 2021, three earthquakes of magnitude greater than 4 occurred in the Gunsan Basin. Although they can be considered as a continuation of the 10-year cycle in terms of timing, the 2021 earthquakes occurred in a completely different location, in the sedimentary Gunsan Basin. The focal depths of 10 km for 2021 earthquakes suggest that they occurred in the bedrock beneath the sedimentary basin. While large earthquakes in the central Yellow Sea align north-south, the relocated earthquakes reveal that they ruptured on east-west striking planes. This is confirmed by the locations of earthquakes near Heuksando and Baengnyeongdo. Most earthquake clusters in the region appear to have occurred in uplift zones, although a small number of earthquakes occurred within sedimentary basins. Most large events exhibit strike-slip faulting on near-vertical nodal planes striking NE or ESE. Some earthquakes also show normal faulting. The stress field consists of compression with a maximum principal stress (σ 1 ) trending NE-SW with a plunge of 20°, and extension with a minimum principal stress (σ 3 ) trending N-S. The stress field in the central Yellow Sea is typically transtensional. This stress field aligns with the horizontal stress direction in the Korean Peninsula, but its 20º plunge angle can induce normal faulting. We analyze earthquakes in the region in detail to examine whether the old tectonic elements, the collision of the north- and south-China blocks, remain as an ambient geologic fabric beneath the Yellow Sea and to elucidate their tectonic implications.

presentations.presentation_title: Tracing Macroscopic Supercritical Fluid Release In Deeply Subducted Continental Crust: Insights From The Sulu Orogenic Belt
presentations.institution: Shandong University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Supercritical fluids (SCFs) are increasingly recognized as highly efficient agents of mass and element transfer in subduction zones, yet their presence in natural rock systems is commonly inferred from high-pressure experiments or microscopic fluid inclusions, rather than from direct field observations. In particular, macroscopic evidence for SCF activity in deeply subducted felsic continental crust has remained elusive. Here we present the first field-scale record of fossilized supercritical fluid channels preserved within an ultrahigh-pressure (UHP) gneissic system from the Sulu orogenic belt, eastern China. The SCF channels are expressed as laterally continuous, phengite-rich vein networks composed of phengite, quartz, feldspar, garnet, epidote, and titanite, which either crosscut or follow the foliation of the host UHP gneisses. These veins are internally derived and differ fundamentally from externally sourced infiltration veins or melt leucosomes. Integrated U–Pb geochronology of zircon, garnet, and titanite, combined with quantitative thermobarometric calculations, constrains vein crystallization at pressure–temperature conditions exceeding the granite second critical endpoint. These conditions require direct precipitation from a supercritical fluid, rather than formation from immiscible aqueous fluids or hydrous silicate melts. Geochronological data indicate that SCF channel formation occurred at ca. 227 Ma, synchronous with the initial exhumation of deeply subducted continental crust in the Sulu UHP terrane. Our results provide a critical link between microscopic records of supercritical fluids and crustal-scale mass transfer processes, demonstrating that SCFs can form discrete, channelized transport networks within continental subduction systems.

presentations.presentation_title: The Generation and Enhancement of the Adakite Signature in the Ultra-high Sr Intermediate-silicic Rocks from Colo Volcano, Sulawesi, Indonesia
presentations.abstract: Adakitic rocks are important because they are often linked to the formation of early Archaean continents and associated with Cu-Au mineralisation processes. Although originally interpreted as the products of slab melting, many studies indicate that adakitic rocks can arise from various petrogenetic processes. Here we present whole-rock major and trace elements data along with Sr, Nd, and Pb isotopic ratios of eruption products from Colo Volcano, Sulawesi, Indonesia - a system with exceptionally high Sr/Y (up to ~200). Colo's eruptive products range from basaltic-trachyandesite to trachydacite and display very high Sr (~2000 ppm) and moderately low Y (10 to 15 ppm), resulting in very high Sr/Y (~100 to 200). Radiogenic isotopic ratios and LILEs (including Sr) show no systematic variation with indices of differentiation, indicating that the radiogenic and adakite signature are inherited from primary melt rather than crustal assimilation and fractionation. Decreasing HREE and Y with increasing SiO 2 suggest the importance of amphibole-dominated fractionation during crustal-level evolution. We propose a two-stage model for the origin of the adakite signature in the Colo eruptive products: (1) generation of primary melt with exceptionally high Sr (and other LILEs and Pb), producing initial adakite signature with Sr/Y around 100, followed by (2) crustal-level amphibole -dominated fractionation that decreased HREE and Y, enhancing Sr/Y to around 200. The production of this high-Sr primary melts reflects mantle enrichment processes related to the complex tectonic configuration of North Sulawesi that might be related to a combination of (i) multiple subducting slabs, (ii) involvement of pre-metasomatized mantle source, and/or (iii) metasomatism by hydrous melt or supercritical fluids.

presentations.presentation_title: Origin of Magnetite Aggregates in the Happo-O’ne Metaperidotite, Central Japan: Toward Understanding of Mantle-wedge Fluid Activities
presentations.abstract: Slab-derived fluids have been known to be active in the mantle wedge although details of their activity have been left unclear. We found magnetite aggregates in a serpentinized dunite-rich zone, which is possibly representative of a fluid conduit in the mantle wedge above the slab. We examined the magnetite rock to understand the mobility and concentration of Fe and other elements via slab-derived fluids. The Happo-O’ne metaperidotite complex, the largest ultramafic body in the Hida Marginal Belt, central Japan, is lherzolite-dominant and associated with Renge high-P/low-T metamorphic rocks (300 Ma) (Nakamizu et al., 1989; Nozaka, 2005; Khedr and Arai, 2009). Magnetite aggregates were found in a dunite-dominant layer (~40 m thick) within meta-lherzolite. Most magnetite aggregates occur as seams or lenses, >1 cm, up to 10 cm across, with well-developed pull-apart structures. A representative chemical composition of magnetite aggregates is (Fe 2+ 0.905 Mg 0.074 Ni 0.012 Mn 0.005 Co 0.004 ) Σ1.000 (Fe 3+ 1.996 Cr 0.004 ) Σ2.000 O 4 . Elemental distribution mapping further revealed the presence of unidentified mineral assemblages containing Na, Cl, and C in the host serpentinite. The Happo-O’ne metaperidotite complex was derived from the mantle wedge. The dunite-rich zone in lherzolite has been selectively hydrated (antigoritized) and probably had served as a conduit of fluids provided from underlying slab, represented by the Renge high-P/low-T metamorphic rocks. The pull-apart structure suggests high stress for formation of the magnetite aggregates prior to deformation of the peridotite during emplacement. The magnetite aggregates are interpreted to have formed in the mantle wedge under a high fluid/rock ratio along the fluid conduit. The presence of Na-, Cl-, and C-bearing mineral assemblages around the magnetite aggregates suggests that the mantle-wedge fluids contained NaCl and CO 2 . Iron and other elements were mobile in aqueous fluids by forming complexes. This study was supported by the fund of Association for Nagano Prefecture for the Advancement of Science.

presentations.presentation_title: Serpentinite Boron Isotope Dilemma: Dehydration Proxy or Fluid Overprint?
presentations.abstract: Serpentinites are major reservoirs of fluid-mobile elements in subduction zones. Boron (B) is readily enriched during serpentinization, and its isotopic composition (δ 11 B) is highly sensitive to fluid sources and reaction histories. However, it remains debated whether serpentinite δ 11 B primarily records isotope fractionation during dehydration (deserpentinization) associated with subduction, or whether it is commonly overprinted by later addition and redistribution of B by externally derived fluids, including seawater-derived components, forearc pore waters and crustal fluids, and sediment-derived fluids.This ambiguity arises because serpentinites can experience multiple stages of open-system fluid–rock interaction from seafloor hydration through prograde metamorphism and exhumation. Seafloor serpentinization may impart relatively heavy δ 11 B together with elevated B contents, whereas subsequent devolatilization, channelized fluid flow, and localized reaction fronts can modify both B concentrations and δ 11 B at various scales. Recent work highlights two partly competing views: (i) boron isotope fractionation during serpentinite dehydration is systematically large and thus potentially diagnostic; versus (ii) δ 11 B variability cannot be explained by simple phase-equilibrium models alone and instead reflects heterogeneous fluid ingress, spatially variable reaction progress, and strong kinetic and textural controls.In this presentation, we synthesize current B–δ 11 B systematics of orogenic serpentinites and evaluate when serpentinite δ 11 B can be used as a robust proxy for subduction-zone dehydration. We emphasize the need to interpret δ 11 B together with B contents, mineralogical context, and complementary fluid-mobile and trace-element indicators to distinguish dehydration-related signatures from late-stage overprinting.
