presentations.presentation_title: Direct of Evidence of Dehydration Embrittlement in Subducted Continental Crust in the Upper Mantle; Pseudotachylite in Uhp Metamorphic Rocks
presentations.abstract: In order to understand the origin of intra-slab earthquakes in the upper mantle, dehydration embrittlement was proposed based on stability of hydrous minerals in cold subducting plate . There are numbers of research which described brittle deformation from eclogites although few of them unraveled solid evidence of dehydration embrittlement. Here I report pseudotachylites after phengite in UHP eclogites. It indicates that there was dehydration embrittlement due to fluid-absent melting in subducted continental crust in the upper mantle. Borehole samples from UHP rocks are one of the best specimens to identify pseudotachylites because outcrop surfaces are often weathered. CCSD eclogites were used for in the present investigation. The eclogite is characterized by the presence of coesite, garnet, omphacite and minor hydrous phases such as amphibole, epidote/zoisite and phengite. It is notice that phengite is commonly present in the eclogite because the protolith of the eclogite is K-rich basaltic rocks. Peak pressure–temperature (P–T) conditions from the assemblage of phengite-garnet-clinopyroxene-(coesite) as P = 3–4 GPa, and T = 650–780°C. Polished slab surface oof the specimens clearly indicates that pseudotachylite veins are present. Under thin sections of the eclogite, part of the pseudotachylite vein was described as melt after phengite decomposition (Okamoto et al, 2013, Island Arc, 22, 25-36). Presence of the K-feldspar in the vein suggests that the vein was formed by dehydration melting. In the vein, large garnets are in angular shape with brittle deformation features. Small idiomorphic garnets are also present in the vein, suggesting that pseudotachylite vein was formed at UHP condition or early retrograde condition at lower crustal depths. The present study suggests that origin of pseudotachylite of deeply subducted eclogite is fluid-absent melting of phengite. It is consistent with review research by Dobson et al. (2020 G 3 ).

presentations.presentation_title: Fluid-assisted Brittle Fracturing Triggers Ductile Deformation and Foliation Development in Antigorite Serpentinite in the Nomo Metamorphic Rocks
presentations.abstract: Mantle wedges exhibit a systematic transition in slip behavior along the slab–mantle interface with increasing depth. This transition is commonly associated with ductile deformation of antigorite (Atg) serpentinite, yet the dominant deformation mechanisms under fluid-rich conditions remain poorly constrained. Serpentinites from the Nomo Metamorphic Rocks (Nagasaki, Japan) record intense deformation at the slab–mantle interface under peak conditions of ~1.5 GPa and ~540 °C. At outcrop scale, the serpentinites exhibit a well-developed foliation defined by the alignment of bastite grains. However, microstructural observations reveal a distinctive block-in-matrix texture, in which coarse-grained, interpenetrating Atg blocks are embedded in a fine-grained, strongly aligned Atg matrix. The matrix shows a pronounced concentration of [001]axes oriented perpendicular to the foliation. The absence of intracrystalline deformation features (e.g., subgrain boundaries and undulatory extinction), together with grain-boundary indentation, implies that deformation was dominated by dissolution–precipitation creep rather than dislocation creep. We interpret the block-in-matrix texture as the result of repeated fault–fracture mesh formation under supra-lithostatic fluid pressure, consistent with a previous study (Hirauchi et al., 2025, Commun. Earth Environ.). Elevated fluid pressure induces microcracking within coarse-grained Atg serpentinites, increasing permeability and reducing effective grain size, thereby promoting dissolution–precipitation creep. Continued fluid infiltration under low differential stress promotes oriented Atg precipitation and growth along the microcracks, and this cycle leads to the development of the observed microstructure. These observations provide a conceptual model in which initial brittle failure creates conditions favorable for subsequent ductile deformation, driving a progressive transition from brittle to ductile behavior. Such a transition may support the shift from slow earthquakes to stable sliding along the slab–mantle interface.

presentations.presentation_title: Boron Isotopes Record Fluid Activity and Anatexis in the Himalayan Orogen
presentations.abstract: Himalayan fluid activity-anatexis links remain unclear (LHS fluid-saturated melting vs GHS dehydration melting). Boron isotopes trace fluid sources/melting roles, yet LHS fluid constraints are lacking. We present in situ B isotope data of tourmaline/muscovite from LHS/GHS samples (chlorite schist, quartz-tourmaline rock, leucogranites, etc.). Tourmaline δ¹¹B ranges -18.3‰ to -8.2‰ (varying by rock type), muscovite δ¹¹B is -23.3‰ to -15.4‰. Isotope variations stem from source differences, devolatilization, fractionation, fluid exsolution and metasomatism. LHS is ¹¹B-depleted; its 600℃ dehydration fluids have δ¹¹B -15.2‰ to -12.0‰, while GHS metamorphic fluids show -11.8‰ to -4.8‰. LHS hydrous mineral dehydration generates light-B fluids, making LHS fluid-triggered hydration-melt leucogranites light-B isotopic (vs GHS dehydration-melt ones). Muscovite devolatilization modeling reveals significant B fractionation (δ¹¹B >7‰), with mica-lost B accounting for heavy B in GHS leucogranites. We propose a model: LHS dehydration fluids migrate upward, triggering GHS melt channel edge hydration melting (tourmaline inherits LHS light-B); melt channel interior mica dehydration melting produces tourmaline with higher δ¹¹B.
presentations.session_title: Signals of Fluid–rock Interaction in Subduction Systems: Petrological and Geochemical Perspectives

presentations.presentation_title: Seismic Hazard Assessment in the Sumatran Subduction Zone: PGA Exceedance Mapping for Mitigation Applications
presentations.abstract: This research models the likelihood of ground shaking exceeding 50 gals over a 50-year interval in the Sumatran subduction region. It provides an estimate of the probability of exceedance (PoE) for a given peak ground acceleration (PGA) along the Sumatran subduction zone in Indonesia. Using shallow earthquake data from that area, the seismicity rate model is developed for the years 1963 to 1999. Since the focus is on understanding the area around the earthquake source, the radii of 50, 75, and 150km are used in this study to estimate PoE of PGA around 50 gals in 50 years. The b-value used in this study is based on spatial variation, with a constant number of 100 events and the maximum likelihood method. The algorithm for developing the best-fit seismicity rate model is based on the results of a previous study of the Sumatran subduction zone. The results of the PoE model based on radius estimations of 50, 75, and 150km are then used to estimate the total probability of PGA greater than or equal to 50 gals, which is then mapped. By analyzing seismicity rates and spatial variations in b-value from 1963–1999, the study identifies high-risk zones that closely align with historical earthquake records. The resulting hazard maps are important for supporting earthquake mitigation and, perhaps, the earthquake insurance study. It offers actionable data for urban planning, infrastructure resilience, and the insurance industry, aiming to reduce the socio-economic impacts of future seismic activity.

presentations.presentation_title: Simultaneous Rupture of Primary and Secondary Faults Based on Paleoseismological Evidence Along the Surface Ruptures of the 2016 Kumamoto Earthquake
presentations.abstract: During the 2016 Kumamoto earthquake, distinct surface ruptures appeared along the primary Futagawa fault. Simultaneously, wide-ranging minor displacements were detected by InSAR and confirmed by field surveys. Determining whether these secondary faults rupture in synchronization with the primary fault is critical for fault displacement hazard and for understanding the evolution of tectonic landforms, especially where triggered displacements occurred on previously identified active fault traces. Paleoseismological investigations since the 2016 event have identified four events along the Futagawa fault since the K-Ah tephra (7.3 ka), with the penultimate event constrained to approximately 2,000 years ago. Evidence of this 2,000-year-old event is also recorded on secondary faults. Furthermore, archaeological sites in the Aso caldera exhibit open cracks and lateral spreading from this period, mirroring phenomena observed in 2016. These results strongly suggest that the penultimate Futagawa fault rupture triggered widespread secondary deformation similar to the 2016 event. Regarding the other two events since K-Ah, simultaneous activity is likely along the Idenokuchi fault, which accommodated slip partitioning. While these findings suggest a recurring pattern of widespread simultaneous rupture, radiocarbon dating has limitations, typically involving uncertainties of several hundred years. Therefore, establishing absolute synchronicity based on chronology remains challenging. Future research focusing on the geophysical mechanisms behind triggered displacements will be essential for improving displacement hazard assessments and fault segmentation.
presentations.session_title: From Active Tectonics to Seismic Hazards of Southeast and East Asia

presentations.presentation_title: Tectonic Geomorphological Analysis Along the Central Segment of the Ulsan Fault, Southeastern Korea
presentations.abstract: The Ulsan fault system, located in southeastern Korean Peninsula, is an east-dipping active fault system characterized by reverse-dominated motion with relatively minor right-lateral component, and poses significant seismic hazard potentials for the region. Despite being one of the most active fault systems in Korea, the precise location of its fault traces and their Quaternary activity remain poorly constrained. In this study, we integrated high-resolution LiDAR digital elevation model (DEM) analysis, detailed field mapping, and shallow geophysical surveys (ground penetration radar, GPR, and electric resistivity tomography, ERT) to delineate the active fault traces along the central segment of the Ulsan fault. We identified a complex imbricated thrust system consisting of at least 7 reverse-dominated branches and minor strike-slip strands. Most notably, a newly identified frontal branch exhibits continuous tectonic scarps on Quaternary alluvial fans with likely corresponding knickpoints along current river valleys, indicating young activity of the fault branch. Along this branch, higher fault scarps are consistently observed on higher and older terraces, indicating accumulated deformation over time. Subsurface discontinuities revealed by GPR and ERT surveys further support the existence of this active strand. Moreover, the spatial distribution of lithologic units of the terrace bedrocks, with granitic rock and older alluvium in the east and younger alluvium in the west, suggests a tectono-stratigraphic model of westward fault propagation. These findings imply that the active strands of the Ulsan fault have migrated into the populated plain area, with higher seismic risks to the infrastructures than previously thought. Future work will focus on paleoseismological trenching, with optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) and radiocarbon dating along these newly recognized frontal branches to constrain their slip rates and earthquake recurrence intervals.

presentations.presentation_title: InSAR-based Kinematic Analysis of the West Valley Fault (WVF), Philippines
presentations.institution: University of the Philippines Resilience Institute
presentations.abstract: The West Valley Fault (WVF) exhibits complex kinematic behavior that strongly influences deformation across eastern Metro Manila and adjacent provinces in the Philippines. InSAR time-series analysis reveals vertical velocities ranging from subsidence of -14.5 mm/yr and uplift of +2.3 mm/yr within and near the vicinity of Marikina Valley, a graben bounded by the WVF to the west and the East Valley Fault (EVF) to the east. A sharp contrast in motion is observed along the WVF trace: the eastern block shifts westward at rates up to –4.8 mm/yr, while the western block moves eastward at rates up to +5.4 mm/yr. This differential displacement reflects a transpressive strike-slip regime, where horizontal shear is coupled with compression, producing localized uplift and subsidence. Further south, near Biñan (Laguna) and Carmona (Cavite), InSAR deformation maps highlight elongated northeast–southwest subsidence zones that align with left-stepping en echelon fault structures. These features mark a releasing stepover segment of the WVF, where extensional fractures and subsidiary splays accommodate differential settlement. For the first time, by integrating InSAR observations with fault kinematic analysis of the WVF, this study demonstrates how segmentation, stepover geometry, and secondary shear structures govern localized deformation of this major fault in the Philippines. The millimeter-scale precision and broad spatial coverage of InSAR enable the characterization of both its transpressive and transtensive regimes, underscoring its critical role in seismic hazard assessment and in strengthening urban resilience planning within fault-controlled areas.

presentations.presentation_title: Engineering Applications of Fault Displacement Hazard Analysis
presentations.institution: National Center for Research on Earthquake Engineering, National Institutes of Applied Research
presentations.abstract: For buildings located near or crossing active faults, seismic design and analysis must consider two major seismic characteristics: ground motion and surface fault displacement. Intense ground motion may exceed the design basis earthquake, causing structures to reach performance limit states and resulting in damage or even collapse. Significant surface fault displacement can induce differential settlement, leading to structural deformation, tilting, or instability. Current seismic design codes generally include specific provisions for near-fault ground motion; however, explicit requirements for design fault displacement along principal fault traces remain limited. This study aims to identify the key components of Fault Displacement Hazard Analysis (FDHA), including seismic sources, empirical models, and uncertainties in hazard results. By identifying these critical aspects, the study seeks to enhance the feasibility of FDHA for engineering applications and to provide a technical reference for the seismic design and evaluation of buildings located near or across active faults.

presentations.presentation_title: Probabilistic Seismic Hazard Assessment for Taiwan: Updates and Improvements in Tem Psha2025
presentations.abstract: The Taiwan Earthquake Model (TEM) has previously released two probabilistic seismic hazard assessments (PSHA) for Taiwan, TEM PSHA2015 and TEM PSHA2020. Building on these efforts, this study develops TEM PSHA2025, which incorporates substantial updates in earthquake catalog completeness, source characterization, and ground motion prediction equations (GMPEs). The new model expands the study area from only the region surrounding Taiwan to encompass a radius of 320 km, integrates multiple international earthquake catalogs, refines on-land and offshore seismogenic structures with multiple-structure rupture models, and adopts time-dependent recurrence through the Brownian passage time model. In addition, recent Taiwan-specific and global GMPEs are systematically selected and weighted, while site effects have been reassessed using an updated database. Compared to previous versions, TEM PSHA2025 provides a more rigorous treatment of epistemic uncertainties and produces updated hazard maps for Taiwan. These advancements offer a robust scientific foundation for seismic disaster mitigation, regulatory compliance, and engineering applications.

presentations.presentation_title: Does Singapore Have Active Faults? Emerging Geomorphic, Sedimentological, and Coral Microatoll Evidence for Recent Coseismic Rupture
presentations.abstract: Singapore is commonly believed to be tectonically stable, with seismic hazard thought to arise solely from distant Sumatran earthquakes. This view, however, overlooks two M ≥ 5 earthquakes in 1922, less than ~140 km away in neighboring Johor, and a 1948 event reported only from southern–central Singapore that produced EMS intensities IV–V at multiple closely spaced sites, consistent with a local source and M ≈ 4. Although recent mapping has identified numerous bedrock faults across the island, their activity and seismic potential remain largely unexamined. The Downtown Core of Singapore is underlain by the low-lying Kallang Basin and adjacent reclaimed land, where sediments — likely MIS 5e (~120 ka) and younger — reach depths exceeding 40 m. Immediately to the west, Cretaceous to Pliocene bedrock rises to ~50 m above sea level. We interpret the steep, east-dipping contact between bedrock and basin-fill sediments as a potentially active, predominantly normal fault, possibly forming part of a transtensional stepover within a longer, northwest-trending dextral fault system. Analysis of legacy borehole data reveals that the thalwegs of at least two east-flowing buried paleochannels exhibit apparent drops of >10 m across this contact and may show southward deflection, though resolution is limited by borehole spacing. Southward projection of this structure may intersect Lazarus Island, where mid-Holocene (~7 ka) in situ coral microatolls on the eastern half of the island are systematically ~30 cm higher than coeval microatolls to the west, consistent with post-growth vertical displacement. Many other microatolls on Lazarus Island are tilted northeastward, suggestive of strong ground motion. Taken together, these geomorphic, sedimentological, and coral-based observations are consistent with geologically recent coseismic deformation, challenging the assumption that Singapore is tectonically quiescent and motivating renewed evaluation of local seismic hazard.

presentations.presentation_title: Recycling of Ancient Slab Components in High-Nb Basalts from Baja California, Mexico
presentations.institution: Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: High-niobium basalts (HNBs; Nb > 20 ppm) and niobium-enriched basalts (NEBs; 10–20 ppm Nb) are volumetrically minor but important components of subduction zones. They are often spatially associated with adakites and regarded as key indicators for ridge subduction or slab detachment. A leading petrogenetic model suggests that HNBs form from melting of a mantle wedge metasomatized by adakitic melts, while an alternative hypothesis links them to contributions from ancient recycled oceanic crust in the asthenospheric mantle.We examined the classic Santa Clara HNB–adakite suite and San Quintín HNBs (Baja California, Mexico) using an integrated Mo–Sr–Nd–Hf–Pb isotopic approach. The results reveal distinct sources: the Santa Clara adakites exhibit depleted isotopic signatures akin to East Pacific Rise basalts, consistent with melting of stalled subducted oceanic crust. In contrast, both HNB suites display enriched radiogenic isotope compositions and elevated δ 98 Mo (up to –0.12‰), indicating a genetic link to ancient (>1 Ga) recycled oceanic crust and serpentinite components.Under reducing conditions buffered by serpentinite-derived fluids, heavy Mo isotope signatures can be preserved in altered oceanic crust—likely hosted in Ti-bearing phases such as humite. We propose that HNBs acquire their isotopic characteristics through interaction between such ancient recycled materials and serpentinite fluids. Subsequently, hot asthenospheric upwelling thermally induces melting of the stalled slab, generating the spatially associated adakites. This framework reconciles deep recycling, fluid–rock interaction, and slab melting in a unified subduction-zone process.
presentations.session_title: Interaction of Mantle Plume with Subduction System

presentations.presentation_title: Interactions Between Spatial-dislocated Mantle Plumes and Subduction Plates
presentations.abstract: Plumes ascending from deep mantle and subducting plates sinking from lithosphere play vital roles in the recycling of the Earth system. Although mantle plumes and subduction zones are considered independent in their spatial distribution, many geophysical and geochemical investigations suggest frequent interactions between them (Fletcher & Wyman, 2015; Saki et al., 2024). Furthermore, increasing tomography research have shown globally widespread low-velocity anomalies beneath the subduction zones (Amaru, 2007; Lu et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2025). These observations and evidence lead us to a conjecture: Is there a mutual attraction between mantle plume and subducting plates?To verify our hypothesis, we use geodynamic modeling to investigate the long-distance interactions between the spatial-dislocated plume and subduction zones. The results show that plate subductions will always try to capture upwelling plumes, even with an evident spatial dislocation. The main insights from the numerical experiments are as follows: (a) Attraction between subducting plate and mantle plume is mainly achieved by the horizontal movement of the upwelling plume, which will result in tilted upwelling channels of them. (b) Interactions between the spatial-dislocated plumes and subduction zones show different patterns depending on whether the plate motions of the subduction plates have evolved. (c) Stronger plume (with greater volume or excess temperature) and faster plate subduction will enhance the interactions between them. And therefore, change their geodynamic processes and responses.The geodynamic models present fine agreements with the tomography investigations in different subduction zones, which can be used to interpret the morphological characteristics of both the plumes and the slabs. The mechanism revealed by our research suggests a widespread attraction between mantle plumes and subduction plates, which also proposes a possible contributing factor of the spatial distribution for certain hotspots.

presentations.presentation_title: Progressive Sub-arc Mantle Oxidation Modulated by Sediment Melt
presentations.institution: Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: The redox state of the sub-arc mantle beneath volcanic arcs is typically oxidized but exhibits substantial variability, with oxygen fugacity (fO 2 ) variations reaching up to 1–2 log units. While it is generally accepted that the incorporation of slab-derived components alters both arc magma compositions and the mantle redox state, the dominant component responsible for these changes remains a subject of intense debate. By compiling global Cenozoic primitive arc basalt and olivine-hosted melt inclusion data, we demonstrate that sediment melt — predominantly of terrigenous origin — plays the controlling role in modulating sub-arc mantle oxidation. Our compilation reveals that the progressive influx of sediment melts into the sub-arc mantle results in a gradual enrichment of K 2 O and most incompatible elements (such as LILEs, Th, and LREEs) in arc magmas. This chemical enrichment strongly correlates with rising fO 2 values, as recorded by whole-rock V/Sc ratios and olivine-melt inclusion V-partitioning, highlighting the potent oxidizing potential of sediment melt over other slab components like serpentinite fluids. Moreover, we found that the high K 2 O, high fO 2 arc magmas spatially correlate with the distribution of Cenozoic porphyry Cu-Au deposits, showing that the sediment melt influx not only elevates the sub-arc mantle fO 2 but also enhances the metallogenetic potential for porphyry deposits

presentations.presentation_title: Material Recycling Associated with the Interaction Between the Mantle Plume and the Subduction System in the South China Sea
presentations.institution: Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: The South China Sea (SCS), a significant marginal basin in the Western Pacific, represents a critical natural laboratory for investigating mantle dynamics and material recycling. The integration of multi-isotope tracers (Sr–Nd–Hf–Pb–Mg–Mo isotopes) with seismic observations underscores the essential role of recycled materials in generating mid-ocean ridge basalts (MORBs) and shaping the geodynamic evolution of the SCS. During continental breakup, metasomatism induced by fluids from the subcontinental lithosphere and subducted sediments reduced the mantle solidus, facilitating efficient lithospheric thinning and rupture. Subsequent seafloor spreading processes established a geochemically heterogeneous mantle source, distinct from the typical upper mantle. This heterogeneity further arises from the interaction between mantle plumes and stagnant slabs within the mantle transition zone, which is pivotal to material recycling. Seismic observations and geochemical modeling indicate that stagnant slabs acted as barriers, bifurcating ascending plumes. Magnesium isotopic evidence reveals a layered distribution of recycled materials, with serpentinite-derived components dominating the shallow mantle (less than 200 km) and carbonated eclogites influencing deeper mantle sources (greater than 200 km). In the southwestern sub-basin, stagnant slabs impede plume ascent, preserving a greater abundance of serpentinite signatures, whereas in the eastern sub-basin, plume penetration facilitates the transport deeper carbonated components into the upper mantle. These recycling processes distinguish this marginal sea from open oceans, as the SCS displays more pronounced geochemical anomalies and dynamic topographic responses due to its proximity to subduction zones and limited mantle convection.
presentations.session_title: Interaction of Mantle Plume with Subduction System

presentations.presentation_title: Mantle plume formation away from the LLSVPs
presentations.abstract: The origins of mantle plumes are often related to large low-shear-velocity provinces (LLSVPs) at the core-mantle boundary (CMB). However, some plumes (e.g., Hainan and Yellowstone plume) lie far away from Pacific and African LLSVPs. They can not be explained using classical plume initiation models. These plumes are found not only connected with hot anomaly, but also with chemical heterogeneity. As a representative plume distant away from the LLSVPs, Hainan plume locates at the edge of a high-velocity anomaly at the CMB beneath East Asia, which is interpreted as a "slab graveyard" from long-term accumulation of ancient slabs(He&Wen, 2011; Maruyama, 2007). Therefore, chemical heterogeneity near Hainan Plume is proposed as a potential thermo-chemical source for its initiation(Wang et al., 2013). To test this hypothesis, we established a thermo-mechanically coupled numerical model to investigate the initiation of the chemical related plume away from LLSVPs. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that heterogeneous slab accumulation drives the initiation of isolated chemical mantle plumes. Key results revealed by our numerical experiments are: (1) Asymmetric distribution of basaltic components appears when the plume reaches the base of the lithosphere, with most of the basalt distributed on the accumulation side. (2) Plume initiation rate correlates positively with height variations, chemical component and boundary layer thickness. This study investigates the initiation of chemical mantle plumes away from LLSVPs, and proposes a novel dynamic model. It identifies independent slab graveyards at the core-mantle boundary (CMB), characterized by slab accumulation height variations resulting from multi-episode subduction, as key incubators for isolated chemical plumes (e.g., Hainan) far from large low-shear-velocity provinces (LLSVPs). This mechanism provides a new geodynamic explanation for global mantle plume formation. References He Y M, Wen L X. 2011. Seismic velocity structures and detailed features of the D'' discontinuity near the core-mantle boundary beneath eastern Eurasia. Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors. 189: 176 - 184. Maruyama, S.; Santosh, M.; Zhao, D. 2007. Superplume, Supercontinent, and Post-Perovskite: Mantle Dynamics and Anti-Plate Tectonics on the Core–Mantle Boundary. Gondwana Research, 11 (1–2): 7–37. Wang X C, Li Z X, Li X H, et al. 2013. Identification of an ancient mantle reservoir and young recycled materials in the source region of a young mantle plume: Implications for potential linkages between plume and plate tectonics. 377 - 378: 248 - 259

presentations.presentation_title: Seismic Gap Breached by the 2025 Mw 7.7 Mandalay (Myanmar) Earthquake
presentations.institution: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Seismic gaps are fault sections that have not hosted a large earthquake for a long time compared to neighbouring segments, making them likely sites for future large events. The 2025 Mw 7.7 Mandalay (Myanmar) earthquake, on the central section of the Sagaing Fault, ruptured through a known seismic gap and ~160 km beyond it, resulting in an exceptionally long rupture of ~460 km. Here we investigate the rupture process of this event and the factors that enabled it to breach the seismic gap by integrating satellite synthetic aperture radar observations, seismic waveform back-projection, Bayesian finite-fault inversion and dynamic rupture simulations. We identify a two-stage earthquake rupture comprising initial bilateral subshear propagation for ~20 s followed by unilateral supershear rupture for ~70 s. Simulation-based sensitivity tests suggest that the seismic gap boundary was not a strong mechanical barrier in terms of frictional strength, and that nucleation of the earthquake far from the gap boundary, rather than its supershear speed, allowed the rupture to outgrow the gap and propagate far beyond it. Hence, we conclude that the dimension of seismic gaps may not reflect the magnitude of future earthquakes. Instead, ruptures may cascade through multiple fault sections to generate larger and potentially more damaging events.
presentations.session_title: Lesson Learned from the 2025 Mandalay/sagaing Earthquake:

presentations.presentation_title: Strong Ground Motions of the 2025 Mw 7.7 Myanmar Earthquake
presentations.institution: National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience
presentations.abstract: The 2025 Mw 7.7 Myanmar earthquake was a shallow earthquake with unusually long rupture propagation over 400 km. The earthquake caused widespread damage to buildings and infrastructure, resulting in more than four thousand fatalities. Impulsive records at short distances and long-lasting records at basin sites were typical features of the strong motion records. We analyzed the accelerograms from five stations located within approximately 5 to 370 km of the causative fault. Our analysis revealed that the peak values were generally consistent with the range of values predicted by typical ground motion prediction equations for crustal earthquakes in Japan. These observations may provide a useful basis for future evaluations of probabilistic seismic hazard maps in the Myanmar region.
presentations.session_title: Lesson Learned from the 2025 Mandalay/sagaing Earthquake:

presentations.presentation_title: Community-based Macroseismic Assessment of the 2025 Mw 7.7 Mandalay/Sagaing Earthquake
presentations.abstract: On 28 March 2025, an Mw 7.7 earthquake struck central Myanmar, with its mainshock epicenter situated close to the country’s second-largest city, Mandalay. While the earthquake caused extensive damage and was widely felt across Myanmar and its neighboring regions, the scarcity of local instrumental observations limited our understanding of its damage pattern and ground motion characteristics, especially immediately after the earthquake. To address this data gap, this study assesses the earthquake's impact and macroseismic intensity using crowdsourced data gathered from community responses, including online questionnaires, photos, videos, and text descriptions posted on social media. Despite significant logistical challenges resulting from internet blockages and firewall restrictions in Myanmar, these data provide timely and critical ground motion and damage information for rapid macroseismic assessment. Our results reveal an approximately 500-km-long continuous zone of severe and moderate damage in towns and cities adjacent to the Sagaing fault, extending from 22°N in the north to in the south. This matches the extent of surface rupture observed during the earthquake event. In addition to the area along the rupture, the Inle Lake area was also severely damaged due to site effects and liquefactions within the basin. Our data suggest that the overall ground motion pattern of the 2025 Mandalay/Sagaing earthquake does not match well with predictions from empirical intensity prediction models, this discrepancy is likely caused by the rupture characteristics and the rupture directivity effect of this earthquake, further amplified by the crustal heterogeneity across Southeast Asia. Such effects could also affect the ground motion patterns of other large and long strike-slip fault ruptures, causing unexpected damage and ground motions to settlements close to the fault rupture.
presentations.session_title: Lesson Learned from the 2025 Mandalay/sagaing Earthquake:

presentations.presentation_title: Source Model and Magnitude of the Great 2025 Mw 8.8 Kamchatka Earthquake Constrained by High-rate Gnss Observations
presentations.abstract: The Great Mw 8.8 Kamchatka earthquake occurred on July 29, 2025 at 23:24:52 UTC, approximately 110 km off the eastern coast of the Kamchatka Peninsula, near the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench in the Pacific Ocean. This region is one of the most seismically active in the world. The event's source region nearly coincides with that of the Great 1952 Mw 9.0 Kamchatka earthquake. The mainshock was accompanied by several strong foreshocks and aftershocks with magnitudes ranging from Mw 7.4 to 7.8. In this study, we processed high-rate GNSS data (with sampling rates of 1 Hz and 30 seconds) from over 100 stations belonging to several regional continuous geodetic networks in the Russian Far East. We employed the PPP-technique, utilizing both real-time and final orbit and clock products to obtain high-temporal-resolution coordinate time series for the period from 21:00 to 24:00 UTC on the day of the mainshock. Using the final products, we estimated coseismic displacements at GNSS sites located up to ~1500 km from the epicenter. Based on these data, which are unaffected by postseismic effects, we developed a source model using the SDM software (Wang et al., 2009). The model yields a moment magnitude of Mw 8.62 and a maximum slip of 13.5 m, with the largest slip localized ~100 km to the northeast of the southern edge of the Kamchatka Peninsula.Furthermore, we derived peak ground displacements (PGD) and seismic waveforms from the 3D high-rate position time series at GNSS sites within 3000 km of the seismic source. The moment magnitude was independently estimated using both the direct PGD approach (Melgar et al., 2015) and a classical seismological methodology, where the high-rate GNSS displacement time series were converted to velocities and processed as seismic data. Both methods yielded a magnitude close to Mw 8.8.

presentations.presentation_title: Trans-Oceanic Propagation of Tsunami Reflection Wave from the 1952 and 2025 Kamchatka Earthquakes and Its Implications for Real-Time Forecasting of Tsunami Later Waves
presentations.institution: Meteorological Research Institute, Japan Meteorological Agency
presentations.abstract: Prediction of later tsunami waves is important for tsunami warnings. Following the 1952 Kamchatka earthquake (moment magnitude Mw 9.0), the significant increases in water level changes were observed at coastal tide gauges in Japan approximately 48 hours after the earthquake. During the 2025 Mw 8.8 Kamchatka earthquake, the similar water-level changes were recorded by ocean-bottom pressure gauges deployed off the Japanese archipelago, as well as by tide gauges. The moving root mean square (MRMS) amplitude of these water-level changes, averaged across the multiple stations, reached approximately half the maximum MRMS amplitude throughout the entire tsunami process. In this work, we investigated the cause of the characteristic water-level changes. Numerical tsunami simulations for 84-hour integration time was performed, indicating that the characteristic amplitude increases were reproduced well in both earthquakes. Snapshots of the simulated tsunami propagation showed that the amplitude increase was caused by trans-oceanic reflection waves from the Pacific coast of South America. These results demonstrate that tsunami waves arriving ~48 hours after an earthquake can behave as significant later waves and that such waves are reproducible with the present tsunami simulation techniques.We additionally performed tsunami simulations assuming Mw 8.7 megathrust earthquakes along the Pacific Rim subduction zones. The result showed that significant later tsunamis would reach the Japanese coast 30 to 50 hours after the initial tsunami arrival when earthquakes happen in the following three subduction zones: the North Kuril Trench including off the Kamchatka Peninsula, the East Aleutian Trench, and the Tonga-Kermadec Trench. These results were consistent with actual observations from tide gauges in Japan during the 1957 Mw 8.6 and 1965 Mw 8.7 Aleutian earthquakes, as well as the 1952 and 2025 Kamchatka earthquakes. These demonstrate that the long-duration tsunami simulation can contribute to predicting later tsunami waves for future earthquakes.
presentations.session_title: Lesson Learned from the 2025 Mandalay/sagaing Earthquake:

presentations.presentation_title: Propagation Characteristics of the 2025 Kamchatka Tsunami Off Eastern Japan Revealed by Wave Gradiometry
presentations.institution: Meteorological Research Institute, Japan Meteorological Agency
presentations.abstract: Thanks to the recent deployments of dense ocean-bottom pressure gauge (OBPG) arrays such as DONET, S-net, and N-net, we have been able to investigate detailed propagation characteristics of tsunamis using observed ocean-bottom pressure records. The tsunamis generated by the 2025 Kamchatka earthquake (Mw 8.8) were well recorded by these OBPG arrays. We apply wave gradiometry, one of the array analysis methods, to the S-net OBPG records to reveal propagation characteristics of the tsunamis in the region of the array. The initial tsunamis, which arrived at the S-net OBPG array approximately 1.3 hours after the earthquake origin, were characterized by long-period pressure disturbances, whereas the secondary tsunamis contained both long- and short-period disturbances. Therefore, we conducted the wave gradiometry analyses in two period ranges: 40–90 min and 10–30 min. Our results show that the long-period components of the tsunamis propagated from the northeast during the time window of the initial tsunamis; however, we were unable to detect the propagation of long-period tsunamis during the time window of the secondary tsunamis. In contrast, coherent tsunami propagation was detected in the short-period components of the tsunamis during both time windows. By comparing the observations with synthetic tsunamis, we interpret that both long-period and short-period tsunamis were generated at the source region and propagated as the initial tsunamis. The long-period components of the tsunamis during the time window of the secondary tsunamis appear to have been trapped off eastern Japan, whereas the short-period components were composed of tsunamis reflected from the Kamchatka Peninsula and scattered by the Emperor Seamounts, both of which propagated from the northeast of eastern Japan.Acknowledgement: We thank the National Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience for providing the S-net OBPG records (https://doi.org/10.17598/NIED.0007).
presentations.session_title: Lesson Learned from the 2025 Mandalay/sagaing Earthquake:

presentations.presentation_title: Preliminary Rock Magnetic Results of the Nickel Laterite Deposit in Santa Cruz, Northern Zambales, Philippines
presentations.abstract: Nickel laterite deposits are generally formed by the weathering of ultramafic rocks in tropical to subtropical climates. The physical and chemical characteristics of nickel laterite deposits are controlled by various factors, including parent rock composition, climate, tectonic setting, and topography. The Philippines is the second-largest producer of nickel ore in the world, and the nickel laterite deposits in Santa Cruz, northern Zambales, were formed by the weathering of ultramafic rocks in the Zambales Ophiolite Complex. This complex is located within the Philippine Mobile Belt, an actively deforming region bounded by subduction zones associated with the Eurasian Plate and the Philippine Sea Plate. In this study, rock magnetic results are reported for the limonite, saprolite, and bedrock samples collected from several laterite profiles and drill cores in Santa Cruz. The aim is to characterize the rock magnetic properties of each zone and to evaluate whether these properties can be used to estimate degrees of weathering or pedogenesis. Magnetic susceptibility measurements show higher values in limonite and saprolite samples than in the bedrock samples, with a more scattered distribution in the weathered zones. Based on stepwise isothermal remanent magnetization acquisition tests, the predominant magnetic minerals in all zones are low-coercivity minerals, with little contribution from high-coercivity minerals. Thermomagnetic analyses indicate that maghemite is the major magnetic mineral in limonite and saprolite samples, whereas magnetite and maghemite are present in bedrock samples. Furthermore, low-temperature magnetic analyses indicate different degrees of maghemitization among the zones. These results suggest that rock magnetic analyses can provide useful constraints on oxidation processes and weathering intensity in nickel laterite deposits.

presentations.presentation_title: Adakitic Alkaline Rocks and Associated Gold-copper Mineralization in Cordon (Luzon, Philippines): Magmatic and Tectonic Controls
presentations.abstract: The Cordon alkaline rock complex hosts gold – copper mineralization. Intermediate sulfidation (IS) epithermal gold – base metal and porphyry copper deposits (PCD) are mapped on the surface and encountered in drill cores. The IS mineralization includes sulfidic veins, quartz veins and mineralized silicified lithologies. The PCDs exhibit sericitic to potassic alterations. Chalcopyrite, sphalerite, pyrite, minor galena and tellurides are present. Reddening associated with hematite is noticed mostly in the inner propylitic zone. Siliceous lithocaps contain alunite, dickite, diaspore and minimal pyrophyllite. In the Sr/MnO vs Sr/Y diagram, samples plot in the prospective field with the elevated Sr, low Y and Mn acting as PCD vectors. The high V/Sc (>10) signifies an oxidizing condition (at least FMQ+1). The host rocks, mostly shoshonitic, are composed of syenite, monzonite and lusitanite. The rocks are metaluminous in the A/NK vs A/CNK diagram. The Sr/Y vs (La/Yb) n indicates the rocks are adakitic and supposedly melted subducted oceanic crust products. Adakitic rocks, being siliceous, oxidized and hydrous, are linked with gold-copper mineralization. On the other hand, alkaline rock-hosted mineral deposits are usually low-tonnage but high-grade. The relatively low-K shoshonitic rock mineralization is a product of crustal processes, whereas the higher-K shoshonitic rock-hosted ore deposits had tapped a metasomatized mantle. The formation of the Cordon gold-copper deposits is consistent with a relatively thin oceanic arc setting. The oceanic arc complex had undergone rifting that initiated the alkaline rock formation. The adakitic alkaline rock chemistry could be the product of the interplay of melt fractionation, subducted slab fluid contribution and metasomatized mantle melt. This process may explain the observation in Cordon and in similarly situated mineralization globally.

presentations.presentation_title: Characterization and Formation of the Phayaung Taung Mesothermal Orogenic Gold Deposit, Central Myanmar: Constraints from Raman Analysis of CO2-bearing Fluid Inclusions and Supergene Enrichment Processes
presentations.abstract: Myanmar hosts a diverse range of ore deposits, including several structurally controlled orogenic gold systems. The Phayaung Taung gold deposit, located in the northeastern Mandalay Region of central Myanmar, is an important example of gold mineralization within the Mergui Belt. The deposit is hosted by interbedded quartzite and phyllite units of the Late Proterozoic Chaung Magyi Group. Although its geological setting and ore mineralogy have been previously described, detailed fluid inclusion constraints based on Raman spectroscopy have remained limited. This study presents new Raman spectroscopic data on CO 2 -bearing fluid inclusions, combined with pressure–depth estimates derived from CO 2 density and temperature constraints. Raman analyses indicate extremely low H 2 O contents in CO 2 -rich inclusions, with CO 2 densities ranging from 288.82 to 969.68 kg/m³ and only trace amounts of N 2 . Recrystallization entrapment pressures are estimated at ~7 MPa (≈0.26 km) for low-density inclusions and up to ~34 MPa (≈1.28 km) for high-density inclusions. The low-pressure assemblages are interpreted to record uplift and deformation events associated with the tectonic evolution of the Mergui Belt. Bi-phase liquid-rich fluid inclusions yield salinities of 3.4–12.9 wt.% NaCl equivalent and homogenization temperatures between 218°C and 450°C, consistent with mesozonal orogenic gold systems. Gold mineralization is preferentially concentrated within quartzite units due to their brittle behavior, which enhances fracture development and fluid permeability, making quartzite–phyllite contacts key exploration targets. The deposit also exhibits local supergene enrichment, where hypogene gold was remobilized during sulfide oxidation by meteoric fluids and redeposited with secondary copper sulfides such as covellite, digenite, and djurleite. These results classify the Phayaung Taung deposit as a structurally emplaced, mesozonal orogenic gold system and provide new constraints on ore-forming processes and exploration potential within the Mergui Belt of central Myanmar.

presentations.presentation_title: New Natural Pyrite and Sphalerite Reference Materials for in Situ S, Fe and Zn Isotope Microanalysis
presentations.institution: Institute of geology and geophysics, Chinese academy of sciences
presentations.abstract: Zinc, iron, and sulfur isotope geochemistry serves as a powerful tool for investigating a wide range of geological processes across igneous, metamorphic, sedimentary, hydrothermal, and biological systems. Pyrite, a ubiquitous iron- and sulfur-bearing mineral, and sphalerite, a common zinc- and sulfur-bearing phase are among the most prevalent sulfides in diverse rock types and dominate many hydrothermal ore deposits. Pyrite frequently precipitates throughout successive stages of hydrothermal mineralization. The coupled Zn–Fe–S isotopic systems in pyrite and sphalerite provide critical constraints on fluid sources, fluid–rock interactions, and the physicochemical and redox conditions during mineral precipitation. In contrast to conventional bulk analytical methods, in situ microanalytical techniques—particularly laser ablation multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-MC-ICP-MS) and secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS, primarily for S isotopes)—enable high-spatial-resolution characterization of Zn–Fe–S isotopic variations and fine-scale heterogeneities. Such capabilities are essential for deciphering complex, multistage hydrothermal systems. However, the broader application of these techniques is currently limited by the scarcity of matrix-matched reference materials with well-characterized Zn, Fe, and S isotopic compositions. Here, we evaluate two natural sulfide samples—pyrite (IGGPy-1) and sphalerite (IGGSph-1), both handpicked from a Balmat sphalerite specimen—for their Zn–Fe–S isotopic homogeneity. Bulk analyses by elemental analyzer–isotope ratio mass spectrometry (EA-IRMS) yield δ 34 S VCDT values of +17.09 ± 0.30‰ for IGGPy-1 and +16.35 ± 0.26‰ for IGGSph-1. Solution nebulization MC-ICP-MS (SN-MC-ICP-MS) yields δ 56 Fe IRMM-014 = -1.31 ± 0.06‰ and δ 66 Zn JMC-Lyon = +0.17 ± 0.04‰, respectively. These results demonstrate that IGGPy-1 and IGGSph-1 are promising candidate reference materials for in situ Zn–Fe–S isotopic microanalysis of pyrite and sphalerite.

presentations.presentation_title: Lithological and Geochemical Characteristics of Hydrothermal Alteration Associated with Porphyry Copper System in Wild Boar Prospect, Andong Meas, Ratanakiri, Cambodia
presentations.institution: Dept. of Earth Resources Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, Kyushu University
presentations.abstract: The Wild Boar prospect is located in Ratanakiri province, Northeastern Cambodia. Several explorations are being conducted in this country, and the research area is one of them. There are the Canada Wall, Gossan Hill, and South Creek copper prospects nearby. Geophysical exploration, trench investigation, and diamond drilling are conducted in the areas. In order to reveal the characteristics of hydrothermal alteration associated with mineralization in the Wild Boar prospect, we conducted mineralogical observations and geochemical analyses using samples from drill core LKWB-10. The rock observed in this drill core consists of diorite, granodiorite, and tonalite, as well as andesitic-basaltic dykes. Quartz vein and epidote stockworks are observed in intrusive rocks, and quartz and calcite veins are observed in the dykes. Based on the thin section observation and X-ray diffraction analysis, the dykes are composed of plagioclase, chlorite, quartz, hornblende, and augite. Intrusive rock is mainly composed of quartz, plagioclase, biotite, and hornblende. In addition, K-feldspar is observed only in the deeper part of the drill core. Moreover, it is found that plagioclase and biotite in intrusive rock are altered to sericite and chlorite, respectively. Epidote and calcite are observed as alteration minerals, which suggests that the alteration in this area is categorized as phyllic alteration. Associated with the phyllic alteration, magnetite, pyrite, sphalerite, and chalcopyrite are observed as opaque minerals in the form of veinlets and disseminations. All these characteristics are discussed to describe the ore formation system.

presentations.presentation_title: Geological Structure Analysis for REE and U-Th Mineralization Using Gravity Data and Morpho-structural Interpretation of SAR Imagery in Mamuju, West Sulawesi
presentations.abstract: Rare Earth Elements (REE) and U - Th mineralization in the Mamuju area, West Sulawesi,are hosted by volcanic rocks of the Adang volcanic complex and occur in stratabound, structure-bound, and volcano-sedimentary settings. Geological structures play a fundamental role in controlling permeability, fluid migration pathways, and the localization of radioactive mineralization, particularly Uranium-Thorium enrichment along faults and fractures. This study aims to delineate surface and subsurface geological structures and to evaluate their relationships with REE and U-Th mineralization through an integrated analysis of gravity data and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery, supported by mineralogical investigations. Global Bouguer Anomaly Data from WGM2012 were processed using upward continuation to enhance deep-seated structural features related to fault and fracture systems. Surface geological structures were extracted from ALOS PALSAR-1 imagery using automated lineament extraction with directional and topographic correction. these datasets were integrated within a Geographic Information System (GIS) framework to identify structurally controlled mineralization zones. Mineralogical analyses, including optical microscopy, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), and X-ray Diffraction (XRD), were conducted to verify the occurrence of REE- and U-Th bearing minerals. The Ahu, Tampalang, Rantedoda, Botteng, and Pangasaan areas exhibit high surface lineament density and coincide with gravity-defined structural corridors, suggesting a structural influence on fluid migration and mineral occurrence. Structure-bound U-Th mineralization is expressed as veinlets and fracture fillings containing uranium–thorium minerals, including davidite and thorianite, within volcanic host rocks. REE occur as accessory phases associated with the same structurally controlled zones. The results provide a framework for delineating targets for further detailed exploration in the Mamuju area.

presentations.presentation_title: Characterization of Hydrothermal Alteration and Mineralization in Drill Hole Brc-57, Guinaoang Porphyry Cu-Au Deposit, Mankayan, Northern Luzon, Philippines
presentations.institution: Dept. Earth Resources Engineering, Graduate School of Engineering, Kyushu University
presentations.abstract: The Philippines hosts numerous porphyry Cu copper deposits because of its tectonic setting along an active convergent margin. In northern Luzon, the Mankayan Mineral District (MMD) contains several well-studied porphyry-epithermal systems. The Guinaoang porphyry Cu–Au deposit is located in the southeastern part of the district. In contrast to other deposits in the MMD, detailed studies on the Guinaoang deposit remain limited. To address this gap, this study examines the drill core BRC-57 provided by Cresent Mining and Development Corporation to characterize the hydrothermal alteration and ore mineral assemblages of the Guinaoang deposit.Petrographic observations, whole-rock X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis, and vein characterization were conducted on selected samples collected from BRC-57. Point-counting analysis of thin sections from the host rock samples indicated a tonalitic composition, with recalculated QAP (Quartz - Alkali feldspar – Plagioclase) modal abundances of Q = 42–59%, A = 0.5–3.3%, and P = 45–57%. Whole-rock XRD analysis revealed alteration mineralogy dominated by quartz and anhydrite, with common occurrence of chlorite and illite. Minor kaolinite, halloysite, and pyrophyllite were also present, whereas gypsum was only observed in the shallow part of the core.Cross-cutting relationships of veins defined a paragenetic sequence beginning with early magnetite-quartz veins, followed by quartz-dominant veins, quartz–sulfide veins, and lastly pyrite-dominant veins. Copper-bearing minerals, including chalcopyrite and bornite, occurred mainly in the quartz–sulfide veins, with minor occurrences in the early magnetite–quartz veins. Most of the gold grains observed were hosted in the pyrite-dominant veins and occur as Au-rich electrum (Au = 73.3 At. %, Ag = 25.7 At. %) associated with petzite and native gold (Au = 85.9 At. %, Ag = 14.1 At. %).The results from drill core BRC-57 documented the alteration evolution and mineralization sequence of the Guinaoang porphyry Cu–Au system.

presentations.presentation_title: Alteration, Vein Paragenesis, and Fluid Evolution of the Guinaoang Porphyry Cu–Au System, Mankayan Mineral District, Northern Luzon, Philippines
presentations.abstract: The Mankayan Mineral District in northern Luzon, Philippines, is one of the country’s highly endowed mineral provinces, hosting well-known deposits such as the Lepanto high-sulfidation epithermal and Far Southeast porphyry deposits. Southeast of Lepanto lies the Guinaoang porphyry Cu–Au deposit, a blind system concealed beneath post-mineral volcanic and sedimentary units and thick soil cover. Despite prior studies, vein paragenesis and mineralization timing at Guinaoang remain poorly constrained, highlighting the need for further investigation.The host rocks at Guinaoang comprise basement units of the Cretaceous Lepanto Metavolcanics, syn-mineral diorite–quartz diorite, and intra-mineral diorite–dacite porphyry. Petrographic analysis identifies three principal alteration assemblages: (1) pervasive magnetite–secondary biotite replacing mafic minerals in basaltic and dioritic units at deeper drill-core levels; (2) chlorite–illite; and (3) sericite–pyrite, which affected all lithologies. The chlorite–illite and sericite–pyrite assemblages occur at different depths and overprint each other. Cross-cutting relationships revealed different veinlet types. Stage 1 magnetite–quartz veinlets were cut by Stage 2 wispy quartz-rich veinlets, both containing trace chalcopyrite and bornite. These were subsequently crosscut by Stage 3 quartz–sulfide veinlets with sulfide centerlines, within which anhedral native gold occurs as inclusions in chalcopyrite, along chalcopyrite–bornite grain boundaries, and as free gold in quartz. These were overprinted by Stage 4 chalcopyrite-dominant veinlets which also host anhedral native gold, followed by Stage 5 pyrite-dominated veinlets with associated sericitic halos. Quartz-hosted fluid inclusions comprise vapor-rich and halite-bearing polyphase assemblages. Their coexistence indicates fluid immiscibility during porphyry-stage mineralization. These observations provided constraints on the hydrothermal evolution and vein paragenesis of the Guinaoang porphyry Cu–Au system.

presentations.presentation_title: Artificial Water Reservoir Triggered Seismicity (rts): a Global Review
presentations.abstract: Triggering of earthquakes can occur due to anthropogenic activities, such as gold/coal mining, natural gas/oil production, harnessing geothermal energy, filling artificial water reservoirs etc. Among all these anthropogenic activities, RTS is most prominent having been reported from hundreds of sites. At least at 5 sites, earthquakes exceeding M 6 have occurred. The most important correlate for RTS is the height of water column in the reservoir. The common characteristics of RTS are useful in ascertaining whether the observed seismicity in the vicinity of an artificial water reservoir is RTS or natural seismicity. The lack of knowledge of physical properties of rocks and fluids in the fault zone does not permit comprehending the genesis of RTS. The Koyna Dam site in India is found to be a very suitable location for putting a deep borehole to learn the physical properties in the earthquake source zone before, during and after the occurrence of the seismic event. Among the salient findings is understanding of the nature of the stress field in the source zone in the Koyna region.

presentations.presentation_title: Paleogeographic History of Paleozoic Proto-Japan: From Gondwanan Affinities to Tectonic Evolution along the Western Paleo-Pacific Subduction Zone
presentations.abstract: The Paleozoic geological units of Japan provide a critical archive for reconstructing the origin and early evolution of proto-Japan.Metamorphic rocks derived from Lower Paleozoic accretionary complexes in the South Kitakami Belt of NE Japan yield detrital zircon U–Pb age spectra that display prominent Pacific Gondwana signatures. The zircon populations are characterized by major peaks at 510–500, 480–470, and 450–440 Ma. These patterns are consistent with derivation from the Terra Australis Orogen, which extended from eastern Australia to Antarctica. This evidence demonstrates that proto-Japan represented a segment of the Ordovician–Silurian Terra Australis Orogen developed along the northeastern margin of Gondwana.Devonian to Carboniferous strata in the Hida Gaien Belt of SW Japan and similarly in the South Kitakami Belt, record a major transition in dominant lithologies from clastic rocks and limestones to widespread volcanic sequences. Provenance analyses and detrital zircon U–Pb ages demonstrate that Devonian sandstones were derived from uplifted arc-related basements and Precambrian sources, including Mesoarchean and Grenvillian components, reflecting a Gondwanan affinity. In contrast, Early Carboniferous strata document a shift to bimodal volcanism. Comparable bimodal volcanic rocks occur not only in Japan but also along the southeastern South China margin and within the eastern Central Asian Orogenic Belt (CAOB).This paleogeographic trajectory indicates that the Japanese Paleozoic belts, while sharing a Gondwanan lineage, began to evolve independently during the Carboniferous as rifting detached proto-Japan from Gondwana. In the Permian, Japanese volcano-sedimentary sequences show provenance from both contemporaneous arc volcanism and recycled early Paleozoic sources, and closely resemble coeval strata in the Jilin area of Northeast China. These similarities suggest that proto-Japan and the eastern CAOB evolved together within the same subduction system along the western Paleo-Pacific.

presentations.presentation_title: Constraints on Lithospheric Properties from Dynamical Models of Continental Collision
presentations.abstract: Dynamical models of lithospheric deformation in the India-Asia continental collision are well constrained by high-resolution geodetic data from global navigation satellite systems and by radar interferometry from repeat satellite orbits. The observations imply that large-scale deformation of the continental crust occurs by a combination of discontinuous displacement on a few major faults that separate regions within which differential motion is slower and appears to vary continuously. To enable high displacement rates on the large active fault systems, compatibility of motion at greater depths requires creep within a relatively narrow ductile shear zone which extends downward beneath the seismogenic fault. The existence of such ductile shear zones is one aspect of a more general conclusion about lithospheric deformation: that the lithosphere deforms coherently, with horizontal velocity independent of depth within the lithosphere. For the major active faults identified from InSAR maps of strain-rate we assume that depth-averaged traction on the fault is equal to slip rate times a fault-resistance coefficient. Between the major faults, the relatively low rates of strain can be represented by distributed ductile creep and modelled using a viscous constitutive law with a viscosity coefficient that may vary with location. Two-dimensional models of the velocity and stress are then obtained by balancing the horizontal forces everywhere in the model region subject to boundary conditions obtained from global plate motion models. Comparing the model velocity field to the observed geodetic velocity field, the variable model parameters (viscosity and fault resistance coefficients) can be adjusted to optimise the fit of model to data. The extent to which deformation is localised on the major faults is controlled by the fault resistance coefficients which thereby constrain the properties of the fault and associated ductile shear zone, and also the magnitude of shear stress in the neighbouring regions.

presentations.presentation_title: New and Published Paleomagnetic Data Constraining Tectonic Rotation and Latitudinal Displacement of Southwest Yunnan and the Indochina Block
presentations.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: The India–Asia collision and formation of the Tibetan Plateau are arguably the most important geological events of the last 100 Ma in Earth's history. The collision directly reshaped large part of Asia and changed regional climate and biodiversity. Yet the tectonic consequences and geodynamic models are widely different and have been long debated. Paleomagnetic data have long been used to hypothesize that the Cenozoic extrusion of the Indochina Block along the left-lateral Aliao Shan-Red River fault, as a result of the India-Asia collision, may have been associated with southward paleolatitude movements and vertical-axis rotations. However, the detailed rotation and latitudinal displacement of blocks of SE Asia remain controversial. In this study, we report results of our paleomagnetic study on the Jurassic-Eocene sedimentary and volcanic rock from the western Yunnan and critically review the available paleomagnetic data from the southeast margin of the Tibetan Plateau, NW part of the South China Block, as well as those from Myanmar and Indochina. Paleomagnetic declinations from our study as well as those from blocks in the SE Tibetan margin and the northern Indochina reveal large coherently clockwise rotations for blocks in the SE Tibetan margin and the northern Indochina. These blocks are bounded by fold-thrust belts and strike-slip faults, which may have accommodated these block rotations during the Cenozoic. On the other hand, there is no paleomagnetically resolvable southward motion of the Indochina Block with respect to Eurasia based on the published paleomagnetic data.

presentations.presentation_title: Importance of Eclogites from Cratonisation to the Phanerozoic Explosion of Onshore Life
presentations.institution: Zhejiang Deep-time Digital Earth International Research Center
presentations.abstract: High-pressure, low-temperature eclogites are believed to be rare in cratons, but we identify large amounts of eclogitic lower crustal rocks in the Baltic Shield 1 . Such eclogites in various metamorphic grade explains the high topography of the NW Scandinavian mountain range 2 . Our findings suggest that the amount of sub-Moho eclogite can be generally underestimated globally!Eclogitization also plays a major role in plateau formation in Tibet. New mafic underplate immediately transforms into eclogite, which founder each time the eclogite layer exceeds a critical thickness 3 . Therefore, the crust in central Lhasa Block is felsic down to the Moho at 80 km depth, explaining half the present topography by isostasy. However, underplating and crustal partial melt are also required to explain the high elevation of the Tibetan Plateau and other major plateaux 4 .By interpretation of >18,000 km of seismic profiles, we document that a mafic crustal layer is generally preserved in Proterozoic orogens but absent in Phanerozoic orogens 5 ., which indicates massive eclogitization and foundering of lower crust in Phanerozoic orogens. The resulting buoyant felsic crust lifted continents above sea level, which enabled onshore life to develop, thus explaining the Neoproterozoic oxidation event and the explosion of life in the Phanerozoic. 1. presentations.presentation_title: The 2008 Mw 7.9 Wenchuan, China Earthquake Was Not Triggered by the Zipingpu Reservoir
presentations.abstract: The devastating Wenchuan Mw 7.9 earthquake occurred in China on the 12 May 2008, claiming about 70,000 human lives. For a long time, it has been debated whether it was triggered by the nearby Zipingpu Reservoir. We find that the region is tectonically active and has hosted 5 earthquakes of magnitude 7 and larger since 1920 within 300 km radius of the location of Wenchuan earthquake. Detailed studies have established that the artificial water reservoir triggered earthquake sequences fall in Type 2 of Mogi’s classification of earthquake sequences. While the Wenchuan earthquake sequence fell in Type 1 of Mogi’s classification. In addition, the tectonic nature of this earthquake was also confirmed from the observed foreshock and aftershock ‘b’ value of 0.47 and 1.15. It is also pointed out that the thrust fault environment is not conducive for the occurrence of RTS. As a matter of fact, there was a reduction in the frequency of earthquakes occurring in the vicinity. This leads us to conclude that the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake is not a case of RTS, putting to rest a long-time debate.

presentations.presentation_title: Triple Oxygen Isotope Paleoaltimetry – an Emerging Tool in Tectonic Reconstructions
presentations.abstract: Triple oxygen isotopes of hydrothermally altered minerals from crystalline rocks, sediments and clays can be used to determine past elevations of mountain ranges. In this work I summarize the utility of using all three stable isotopes of oxygen ( 16 O, 17 O, and 18 O) to create data trends in 17 O/ 16 O vs 18 O/ 16 O that are extrapolated back to the meteoric water line. I present the application of this method to the early uplift of southern Tibet. The timing and magnitude of the early Cenozoic surface uplift of the Tibetan Plateau is controversial due to a scarcity of unaltered terrestrial sediments required for paleoaltimetry techniques. Such information is critical, however, for constraining the geodynamic and paleoclimatic evolution of the Indian and Eurasian continents, and for interpreting global climate, biodiversity and biogeochemical cycles since the Cenozoic. Our recent work proposes that substantial uplift occurred by 63 to 61 million years ago, prior to the collision of the Indian and Eurasian continental plates, based on comparison of triple oxygen isotopes of modern meteoric waters with epithermal Ag-Pb-Zn deposit quartz veins from the Paleocene Gangdese Arc in southern Lhasa. Suggesting that by 63 to 61 Ma the Gangdese Arc reached an elevation of ~3.5 km, achieving >60% of its current elevation prior to continent-continent collision. This early high paleoelevation estimate for the Himalaya-Tibetan system challenges previous assumptions that southern Tibet uplift required continent-continent collision to achieve substantial topography. In this talk I will interrogate the assumptions of such reconstructions and outline tools for determining the robustness of such calculations for future and ongoing work. The application of triple oxygen isotopes as a tool for paleoaltimetry reconstructions is nascent but provides complementary information to be used in conjunction with more traditional isotope-based paleoaltimetry approaches.

presentations.presentation_title: A Tale of Two Volcanoes in East Java: the Bromo Tengger Semeru Complex and the Lamongan Monogenetic Volcanic Field
presentations.abstract: This study compares the magmatic plumbing characteristics of the Bromo Tengger Semeru (BTS) volcanic complex and the Lamongan Volcanic Field (LMVF) in East Java to evaluate how the tectonic regime influences magma ascent pathways and crustal storage patterns. The analysis integrates gravity and magnetic data through Bouguer anomaly modelling, source-depth estimation using three-dimensional Euler deconvolution and two-dimensional Werner deconvolution, gravity constrained inversion, and lineament extraction from magnetic anomalies using edge detection. Beneath BTS, the results indicate a high-density body developed within the mid-crust at depths of about 5 to 20 km, forming a relatively continuous geometry, together with evidence of a spatial connection between Semeru and Bromo that aligns with north–south structures under a compressional setting. In contrast, the LMVF response is dominated by shallow intrusions of dyke type, generally shallower than 2.5 km, dispersed and segmented, and controlled by northwest–southeast and northeast–southwest fault sets that also correlate with the distribution of maars and scoria cones. These differences suggest that the compressional regime at BTS is more favourable for the development of deeper, relatively connected magma accumulation zones, whereas the extensional regime at LMVF preferentially facilitates shallow, strongly structure-controlled intrusions. This framework provides a basis for developing regional segmentation analyses across East Java and can be applied to other volcanic-arc settings.

presentations.presentation_title: Thermal State and Lithosphere Thickness in Asia
presentations.institution: Zhejiang Deep-time Digital Earth International Research Center, China
presentations.abstract: Thermal structure of the lithosphere reflects its long-term evolution and controls its rheology, expressed in crustal and mantle anisotropic layering as observed in many seismic tomographic models globally and for Asia. Estimates of lithosphere thermal thickness, which defines lithospheric geotherms, show significant differences depending on the method and the employed lithosphere definition (Artemieva, 2011). While lithosphere thermal structure is often constrained by borehole heat flow values, the approach requires, among other critical things, exclusion of tectonic provinces with non-steady-state thermal state and areas with active tectonics (young magmatism and hots springs) (Artemieva & Mooney, 2001). These requirements are not satisfied for ca. 75% of the Asian continent. Due to data limitations and intrinsic complexity of lithosphere structure and composition, the existing models for lithosphere thermal structure are either of low resolution, or poorly constrained, or unreliable.This new study fills this knowledge gap by presenting lithosphere thermal model for the entire Asia continent (15-50 N/70-135 E) based on an alternative approach (Artemieva, 2019a,b, 2022; Artemieva & Shulgin, 2019; Xia et al., 2023). The results are discussed in relation to regional geological ages (Artemieva, 2006) and geodynamic processes that shaped the region from Archean to present. References:Artemieva, I.M., 2011. presentations.presentation_title: Rupture Process of the 2016 Kumamoto Earthquake and Its Effects on Near-fault Ground Motions
presentations.abstract: Strong ground motion near the source fault of an earthquake is one of the biggest causes of seismic disasters, and the rupture process of the earthquake has a major impact on it. Therefore, detailed analysis of the rupture process and the evaluation of near-fault ground motion based on the results of the analysis are essential for mitigating seismic disasters. The 2016 Kumamoto earthquake was what first drew attention to near-fault ground motion, so we reanalyze this earthquake. Disaster-causing earthquakes have wide source faults, and their models have a significant impact on the analysis results, so the aftershock distribution, which is the main information for fault modeling, is precisely redetermined. In addition, since the Green's functions used in the analysis is highly dependent on a velocity structure model, a comprehensive search is carried out to precisely adjust the model using observed records of several medium-sized aftershocks as data. Then, using the obtained fault model and velocity structure model, we will perform source inversions with different methods on a dataset containing all major observations near the source fault. We will discuss and examine in detail common points in the results of each method to see if there are any special features not found in previous studies. If there are any discrepancies, the causes will be discussed and examined in detail. These discussions and examinations will be summarized to provide an outlook on the relationship between the rupture process and near-fault ground motion.

presentations.presentation_title: Insights Into Faulting and Seismic Hazard Along the Indo-burman Margin from a New Focal Mechanism Catalog in Northeastern Bangladesh
presentations.abstract: The active tectonics and seismic hazard of Bangladesh remain poorly constrained despite geodetic evidence suggesting the accumulation of elastic strain capable of generating a large-magnitude (M~8–9) earthquake along the Indo-Burman margin (Steckler et al., 2016), compounded by sparse long-term seismic observations and a complex plate boundary setting between the Indian Plate and the Indo-Burman margin. In this study, a focal mechanism catalog for northeastern Bangladesh is presented using broadband seismic data recorded by the TREMBLE (Temporary REceivers for Monitoring BangLadesh Earthquakes) network. Focal mechanisms are determined using the HASH algorithm (Hardebeck & Shearer, 2002) , which incorporates P-wave first-motion polarities and uncertainty-based sampling to obtain robust solutions for moderate earthquakes and their aftershock sequences. This work builds directly upon previous seismic hazard assessments in Bangladesh based on ambient noise analysis, horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio (HVSR), and fragility index mapping, which revealed strong site-dependent amplification and vulnerability related to thick sedimentary basins (Bin Abdul Rahman et al., 2024). The focal mechanism catalog is used to investigate faulting style and regional stress conditions, with particular emphasis on the 2017 Tripura earthquake sequence. The mainshock and subsequent aftershocks exhibit consistent focal mechanisms characterized by near-vertical nodal planes and rake values close to 180°, indicating dominantly strike-slip faulting. The strong similarity between mainshock and aftershock mechanisms suggests that aftershocks occur on the same fault or on closely aligned fault segments under a stable regional stress field, implying coherent stress release along a mature fault structure rather than distributed deformation. The observed strike-slip faulting is consistent with tectonic models that accommodate oblique convergence through lateral shear within the Indo-Burman Fold-and-Thrust Belt. Together with earlier HVSR- and fragility-based hazard analyses, the results underscore the importance of integrating source mechanics and site effects for improved seismic hazard assessment.
