presentations.presentation_title: Detailed Hypocenter Determination Associated with Submarine Volcanic Activity Using Teleseismic Body Waves
presentations.abstract: We conduct detailed hypocenter determinations associated with submarine volcanic activity using Pn and Sn waves. In such problems, there are no nearby observation stations, and a major challenge is to accurately extract source information from seismic waveform data that are strongly disturbed by scattered waves caused by oceanic plates.In this study, we performed detailed hypocenter determinations of swarm seismicity associated with volcanic activity at the Getsuyo Seamount in 2006. At that time, a temporary broadband ocean-bottom seismometer array, deployed for deep structural studies, was installed to surround the source region, and teleseismic data with good azimuthal coverage were recorded. We developed a detailed hypocenter determination method suitable for such problems (Aoyama et al., 2024). Using Pn double-pair double-difference times and Sn–Pn times as input data, this method successfully demonstrated accurate relative hypocenter estimation.In addition, we have also conducted hypocenter determinations of seismicity associated with submarine volcanic activity near Torishima in 2023. In this case, data from permanent observation networks in and around the Japanese Islands are available. Although azimuthal coverage is limited, dense observation data can be utilized. For this problem, we are currently developing a method to estimate detailed relative hypocenters using Pn and Sn double-difference travel-time data. Such methods will be useful for future analyses of ongoing submarine volcanic activity.In this presentation, we plan to report the detailed temporal evolution of swarm seismicity at the Getsuyo Seamount and the accuracy of the hypocenter determinations. We will also introduce the methodology and results of detailed hypocenter distribution estimation for the Torishima region.

presentations.presentation_title: Spatial Pattern in Stress Drops of Small Earthquakes Reveals Heterogeneous Shear Strength on Faults Around Japan
presentations.institution: Faculty of Basic Natural Science, Ibaraki University
presentations.abstract: Source parameters of earthquakes, including stress drop, provide important information on physical conditions of seismogenic areas. Here, we analyzed stress drops of more than 2000 earthquakes (4.0 <= M <= 5.0) that occurred between 2003 and 2024 around Japanese islands focusing on four regions; (1) off the south-east coast of Hokkaido, (2) off the east coast of Honshu, including the source region of the 2011 Tohoku earthquake, (3) off the west coast of northern Honshu, and (4) off the east coast of Kyushu. The results showed clear spatial heterogeneity and strong correlation to source characteristics of historical large earthquakes, that is, small earthquakes at edges of source regions of historical large earthquakes had larger values of stress drop. Because the stress drop can be treated as a proxy of the difference between the shear strength and the dynamic stress level, our results suggest that further ruptures had been prevented by areas with a high shear strength during these historical earthquakes. In addition, stress drops of small earthquakes in some of the areas inside the source region of the 2011 Tohoku earthquake likely decreased after the main shock. This indicates that the frictional strength decreased at the areas due to the following aftershocks of the 2011 Tohoku earthquake, consistent with a high aftershock activity. This also supports that the frictional properties ona subducting plate interface can be monitored by stress drops of small earthquakes.

presentations.presentation_title: Modelling of Site Effects on Radiation Characteristics Observed in Seismic Recordings
presentations.abstract: The statistical Green's function method is a widely adopted approach for simulating ground motions based on fault models. In this method, the accurate evaluation of radiation characteristics is a critical issue. Conventionally, dominant parameters are considered to be the take-off angle, azimuth, frequency dependence, and the propagation path from the hypocenter. However, an analysis of observation records from earthquakes occurring off the coasts of Miyagi and Fukushima reveals that local site characteristics also exert a significant influence. This study summarizes the impact of site characteristics on radiation characteristics and attempts to model this effect.The analysis utilized observation records obtained from 18 stations along the Pacific coast, including Miyagi and Iwate Prefectures, focusing on 28 offshore earthquakes. To evaluate seismic radiation characteristics, the A T value defined by Takemura et al. (2009) was employed: A T = |T|/sqrt(R²+ T²). For each record, an A T ratio was calculated for every earthquake-station pair, defined as the ratio between the theoretical radiation coefficients and the observed values. This ratio served as an indicator of the discrepancy between theoretical predictions and actual observations.We quantitatively evaluated the influence of site characteristics by examining the correlation between the A T ratio and site profile parameters. Specifically, we analyzed V S30 and the sediment layer thickness D1400 (the depth to the layer with an S-wave velocity of 1.4 km/s). For earthquakes with magnitudes of 6.8 and above, the data showed a negative correlation between the A T ratio and V S30 , and a positive correlation with D1400 . These results demonstrate that site characteristics significantly modulate radiation characteristics. Consequently, the A T ratio was modeled as a function of V S30 and D1400 to facilitate quantitative evaluation.

presentations.presentation_title: Basin Amplification in Numerical Simulation: Study Case in Greater Jakarta
presentations.abstract: Basin amplification reveals earthquake complexity, where basin structure could cause intense ground motion. This could lead to higher risks if basin amplification occurs in Jakarta, Indonesia’s largest city in an active seismic zone that lies on a sedimentary basin. Both the geological setting and the city’s economic impact push for improved ground motion modelling (GMM). However, there has not been an Indonesia or Jakarta-specific Ground Motion Prediction Equation (GMPE) that incorporates local geology. We employed physics-based numerical modelling by using the best available model of the Jakarta Basin to simulate multiple events from nearby active faults. Numerical simulations of Jakarta showed that basin amplification is theoretically possible because the structure could support entrapment of seismic energy, leading to constructive seismic interference and stronger ground motion. Complex basin structure also creates irregular distributions of Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) that reflect seismic-basin interaction. Some events above Mw6.0 could create “belt zone”, a narrow zone of accumulated seismic energy in southern Jakarta that reaches up to MMI XI (violent). In contrast, hazard assessment using the global GMPE set does not show a belt zone for the same events because of the absence of a complete basin model in GMPE. Numerical simulation could improve ground motion models because the empirical method still lacks special attention to local effects in Jakarta, capturing amplification as a local effect that is useful beyond hazard assessment, like catastrophe modelling.

presentations.presentation_title: Structure and Deformation Mode Across the Narrow Fault-bounded Block in Southwestern Taiwan from Dense Microtremor Observations
presentations.abstract: A narrow, km-long, fault-bounded zone with a high strain rate of 2-3 × 10 -6 /yr causes severe damage to nearby infrastructure, such as highways and tunnels, in southwestern Taiwan. The NE-SW-trending fault-bounded zone, with the Chekualin Fault on the west and the Chishan Fault on the east, consists mainly of highly-deformed mudstone. The fault-bounded zone is characterized by about 50 mm/yr of fault-perpendicular, WNW-striking horizontal motion and 20-80 mm/yr of vertical uplift within the overall NW-SE tectonic convergence regime, based on GNSS and precise leveling measurements. We determined the velocity models of this area using four seismic array data, and our analyses indicate a distinct low-velocity zone between the two faults. Moreover, we investigate the seismic response of the area by using microtremor horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratios (MHVR) and time-frequency polarization analysis on four fault-perpendicular profiles to reveal the seismic characteristics of the highly deformed fault-bounded mudstone area. The MHVSR profile indicates notable subsurface structural discontinuities influenced by the Chekualin and Chishan Faults, with steep dip angles consistent with the region's established high-angle stratigraphic features. Additionally, there is no apparent amplification ratio between the two faults, suggesting a lack of pronounced velocity layering in the underlying strata. This implies that the strata within the fault zones have undergone significant fracturing due to fault activity, resulting in a highly disrupted geological structure. Polarization results show that near the fault, the direction is at a high angle or perpendicular to the strike (NE-SW) of the faults. In contrast, the polarization direction within the two faults is mainly parallel to the fault strike, matching characteristics of fault-trapped waves in low-velocity zones. Our study indicates that the microtremor analyses can be used to identify fault locations, mechanical properties, and the slip direction of the underlying stratum.

presentations.presentation_title: Resolving Misestimates of Vertical Tectonic Motion by Quantifying Large Sea-level Variations Caused by Sediment Redistribution
presentations.abstract: Relative sea-level histories are fundamental tools for quantifying vertical tectonic motions and assessing structural activities and seismic hazards in coastal areas. However, sediment isostatic adjustment (SIA) induced by erosional unloading and depositional loading can significantly perturb local relative sea level. Traditional approaches often neglect these effects, relying instead on global or regional eustatic curves, which can lead to biased tectonic interpretations. In this study, we used Taiwan as a natural laboratory due to its extreme sediment redistribution rates, to quantitatively assess the effects of SIA on the relative sea-level changes over the last glacial-interglacial cycle (122 ka to present) and the resultant misestimations of tectonic coastal uplifts in this region. We first reconstructed a comprehensive, time-varying sediment transfer history by integrating over 1,000 empirical erosion and deposition measurements. This history was then utilized to drive a gravitationally self-consistent sea-level model to quantify SIA effects. Our simulations reveal that SIA is a primary driver of the spatial variation of relative sea level in Taiwan, causing crustal and sea-level responses that vary drastically over short distances (<100 km). Specifically, erosional unloading along the eastern coast of Taiwan drives isostatic uplift and sea-level fall exceeding 200 m, while depositional loading in the southwest induces crustal subsidence and sea-level rise of ~70 m. Finally, we demonstrate that ignoring SIA leads to substantial errors in estimating tectonic uplift rates, with >50% overestimate in areas that have experienced SIA-induced uplift and >100% underestimate along coasts that have undergone SIA-induced subsidence. We highlight the global importance of incorporating SIA corrections for accurately estimating tectonic motion and fault slip rates, particularly for orogenic belts or regions with rapid sediment redistribution, such as Japan, the Philippines, and western Myanmar.

presentations.presentation_title: Stratigraphic Records from the Pacific Coast of Central Japan Indicate Variable Tsunami Recurrence Intervals Along the Nankai Trough
presentations.abstract: We reconstructed the tsunami inundation history along the Pacific coast of central Japan facing the Nankai Trough over the past several thousand years. We collected sediment core samples from two coastal wetlands in Mie Prefecture (Toba City and Shima City) and conducted detailed radiocarbon dating. In the Toba cores, 18 sand layers interpreted as tsunami deposits were identified, while 8 such layers were found in the Shima cores. All of the layers contain marine microfossils, such as foraminifera and marine diatoms, as well as fragments of bivalves and gastropods. In addition, changes in diatom assemblages below and above some of the sand layers suggest that subsidence occurred in the area associated with those events. Using OxCal, we estimated the depositional ages of the sand layers and found that the ages of the upper three sand layers at both sites overlap in age with historical tsunamis generated along the Nankai Trough: the Meio (1498 CE), the Eicho (1096 CE), and the Hakuho (684 CE) earthquake tsunamis. Damage caused by the Meio and the Eicho earthquake tsunamis had been documented in this region, and archaeological evidence suggests that the rupture zone of the Hakuho earthquake extended to this region. On the other hand, no clear historical or geological evidence has been obtained indicating that earthquakes and tsunamis originating from the Nankai Trough occurred in this region between these events. Furthermore, by applying the difference function in OxCal, we examined the recurrence intervals of these tsunami events. The recurrence intervals varied between approximately 100–800 years. The results of this study indicate that the Nankai Trough does not have regular tsunami recurrence intervals of 90–150 years as has been widely assumed.

presentations.presentation_title: Dominance of Structural Inheritance on the Seismogenic Potential and Segmentation of the Deformation Front in northern Taiwan Orogen
presentations.abstract: The active deformation front (DF) in NW Taiwan has extended to the offshore, presenting a rare case of how a shallow orogenic propagation is segmented by pre-existing structure and basement architecture. In particular, the deformation front in NW Taiwan extends from land to sea and is close to densely populated metropolises and cluster of global semiconductor companies , such as the headquarters of TSMC. To characterize the involvement of the basement high of the passive margin on the active DF, we collected high-resolution Sparker seismic data. Our results show the DF has been segmented into Miaoli, Hsinchu, and Hukou domains. The Miaoli domain features W–E trending fault-propagation folds driven by fold hinge migration, associated with higher uplift rates (~0.67–1.0 mm/yr), indicating an efficient thrusting. In contrast, the Hsinchu domain exhibits a ~N70°E-trending fault-propagation folds driven by limb rotation, associated with lower uplift rates (~0.33–0.67 mm/yr). Numerous transtensional faults exist along the fold ridges and cut the seafloor, indicating that the strain is partitioned into block rotation and constrictional deformation. Thus, these features are interpreted as a locked rotational mode forced by a basement buttress, rather than tectonic inactivity. Further north, the Hukou domain becomes blind fold structures as rotation reaches its limit. From a seismic hazard perspective, the transition from high-angle thrusting to rotation suggests that segments with lower uplift rates may represent locked zones with higher stress accumulation. These complex structures and historical earthquakes, such as the M 7.1 Hsinchu-Taichung earthquake in 1935, underline a high seismogenic potential of the DF in northern Taiwan Orogen. This study demonstrates that basement geometry is a dominant factor controlling orogenic propagation and should be integrated into regional seismic hazard assessments.

presentations.presentation_title: Geodetic and Tsunami Constraints on the Rupture Zone of the 2025 Mw 8.7-8.8 Kamchatka Megathrust Earthquake
presentations.abstract: The Kamchatka subduction zone marks one of the most tectonically active regions in the world, accommodating a shortening of ~80 mm/yr between the Pacific and Okhotsk plates. On 29 July 2025, a Mw 8.7-8.8 earthquake occurred offshore Kamchatka, generating a tsunami that traveled across the Pacific. The 2025 epicenter lies less than 40 km from that of the 1952 Mw 8.8-9.0 megathrust earthquake and is accompanied by a comparable aftershock distribution. Here, we analyzed coseismic deformation of the 2025 Kamchatka earthquake using InSAR and GNSS. InSAR images show deformation concentrated in the southern Kamchatka Peninsula, with amplitudes increasing from inland areas toward the coast. The GNSS station on Paramushir Island recorded the maximum GNSS displacement, with seaward horizontal and downward vertical motions of ~1.7 m and ~0.2 m, respectively. Slip inversions suggest that the rupture propagated unilaterally to the southwest for ~480 km, consistent with the aftershock distribution. The coseismic slip extended downdip to a depth of ~46 km, where the geodetic data provide sufficient resolution. However, geodetic data are insensitive to near-trench slip. Therefore, we generated three geodetic slip models with extreme, moderate, and zero shallow slip, and used DART tsunami observations to evaluate them. As a result, the model with zero shallow slip best reproduces the tsunami arrival times at DART stations, supporting the absence of large near-trench rupture. The rupture zone was confined to depths of 13-46 km, with a peak slip of ~9 m and a geodetic moment magnitude of 8.7. The updip shallow portion of the 2025 rupture zone and the northern adjacent section may pose an elevated tsunami risk due to stress transfer. We highlight the crucial role of seafloor observations, as inland data offer limited insight into the shallow slip of subduction interfaces.

presentations.presentation_title: The Orientation of Marine Sediment Cores Using a Submersible Equipped with a Cross-line Laser
presentations.abstract: The paleomagnetic directions of two marine sediment cores were used to assess the effectiveness of the cross-line laser method for azimuthal orientation. Sediment cores, several tens of centimeters long, were collected using SHINKAI 6500 from a site in the Okinawa Trough. Ten paleomagnetic cubes were collected from the sediment cores. Results of 14 C dating indicated that the bottom ages of the cores were approximately 7.2 ka. The collected paleomagnetic samples were subjected to stepwise alternating-field demagnetization, and their characteristic remanent magnetization directions were determined using principal component analysis. The downcore variations of our sediment cores were compared with the paleomagnetic secular variations of Lake Biwa sediments in Japan, and corresponding patterns were observed. This result indicates that the cross-line laser method was nearly successful in determining the azimuthal orientation of the sediment cores.

presentations.presentation_title: An Exceptionally Long Eocene Geomagnetic Reversal Recorded in IODP Site U1408 Sediments
presentations.abstract: In 2012, Integrated Ocean Drilling Program (IODP) Expedition 342 was conducted with the primary objective of investigating multiple extreme climate events during the Eocene. Sediment cores recovered from Site U1408 exhibit pronounced variations in chemical composition and lithology, which enabled the construction of a high-precision age model through the incorporation of sedimentary climate rhythms related to Earth’s orbital forcing. Within the core, we identified an approximately 8 m interval that preserves an exceptionally detailed record of a geomagnetic reversal dating to ~40 Ma. High spatial and temporal resolution sampling was therefore carried out at 2 cm intervals for comprehensive paleo- and rock-magnetic analyses. The results reveal two distinct intervals recording polarity transitions. These intervals are interpreted as reliable records of the geomagnetic field, as the primary carriers of remanent magnetization are identified as biogenic magnetite. Astronomical time calibration indicates that the durations of these transitions were approximately 18 kyr and 70 kyr, substantially longer than the ~10 kyr durations commonly reported in previous studies, which have focused primarily on geological materials from the past ~17 Myr. Such long-duration transitions are reproduced in numerical geodynamo simulations, suggesting that variability in reversal duration is an intrinsic feature of the geodynamo.

presentations.presentation_title: A Preliminary Report of Archeointensity in 1800 Years Ago Estimated from Yayoi Pottery of Kokujaku, Fukuoka, Japan
presentations.abstract: The archeological magnetic field intensity (archeointensity) is essential to elucidate geodynamo process and archeomagnetic dating in archeology. Recently, the large secular variations of archeointensity have been reported, called Levantine Iron Age “geomagnetic spikes” (e.g., Ben-Yosef et al., 2017, PNAS). Besides, a candidate of such geomagnetic spike large archeointensity variations were reported from Japanese archeointensities in 175 CE (Tema et al., 2023, GJI). To validate such large archeointensity variations in Japan, we conducted archeointensity experiments using Yayoi pottery fragments made from 50 CE to 200 CE excavated at the Kokujaku site in Onojo City, Fukuoka Prefecture. The Kokujaku site is a complex remain from the end of the Jomon period to the Kamakura period, and is a very close, only about 1 km north of the Gokuden site. 10 pottery fragments about 5 ~ 20 cm in size are provided to us from the Board of Education of Onojo City, Fukuoka Prefecture. We carried out archeointensity experiments on a total of 11 specimens from six pottery fragments made from 200 CE to 250 CE. The Tsunakawa-Shaw method was carried out in air and archeointensities of 37.1 and 83.6 µT were obtained from six pottery fragments. These are comparable to or stronger than the archeointensity of 50 CE already determined from the Gokuden Yayoi potteries (Yoshimura et al., 2025, ESSOAr). Although the results in this study are preliminary, we can observe that the geomagnetic intensity increased from 250 BCE to 225 CE and show a large variation from 75 to 250 CE when our archeointensities from the Kokujaku and Gokuden sites are arranged in chronological order. Its maximum is about 1.7 times the present geomagnetic field intensity at Onojo City. The results tentatively suggest that the geomagnetic intensity increased greatly in a short period of time in the Yayoi period.

presentations.presentation_title: DeformMS: A Simple Toolbox for Modelling Magnetic Fabric Evolution During Rock Deformation
presentations.abstract: The magnetic fabric, studied mainly by means of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS), has become one of the well-established, fast, and reliable rock fabric proxies applied in many branches of Earth sciences. The magnetic fabric of rocks reflects the crystallographic or shape preferred orientation of all rock-constituent mineral grains; each mineral grain contributes to the overall fabric according to its single-grain anisotropic properties and its orientation.Because magnetic fabric is very sensitive to strain, a simple tool box is presented to model its evolution as a results of rock deformation. The toolbox works with a set of uniformly distributed model particles deformed following the so-called line/plane model which assumes that the particles behave as if they formed lines or planes in the deforming rock matrix; their shapes do not change in response to the imposed deformation but their orientation does. The pre-deformational and deformational magnetic fabrics are considered, both having originated through combined pure shear and simple shear acting in the pre-defined directions.The resultant magnetic fabric tensor is calculated by integrating the combined contribution of the entire set of modelled particles. The results are presented in terms of the principal AMS directions, degree of anisotropy, and shape of anisotropy ellipsoid. The presented toolbox is an integral part of Anisoft6 software which enables the instant visualization of how magnetic fabric gradually changes as a function of progressive deformation.The research was in partially conducted within the research plan RVO 67985831 of the Institute of Geology of the Czech Academy of Sciences.

presentations.presentation_title: Building a Credible Magnetofossil Record Into Deep Geological Time: Evidence for Magnetotactic Bacterial Presence Through the Jurassic
presentations.abstract: Understanding how and when life on Earth began remains a great open question. The first three billion years of life was entirely microbial; finding traces of this ancient microbial world is extraordinarily difficult. Microbial soft tissue or organic molecules rarely survive in the rock record. This preservation challenge could be overcome by finding the remains of magnetotactic bacteria (MTB)—microbes that biomineralize chains of magnetic nanoparticles to orient themselves with Earth’s magnetic field to avoid chemically toxic waters. Molecular clock evidence suggests that MTB first appeared at ~3,400-3,200 Ma, which makes them potential contributors to life’s earliest chapters. Unlike most microorganisms, when MTB die, they leave behind detectable evidence in the form of magnetic particles known as magnetofossils. These particles provide sedimentary rocks with distinctive magnetic properties that can be detected using rock magnetic techniques. Once the magnetic signatures due to magnetofossils are identified, credible magnetofossil identification requires confirmation of the size, shape, crystallinity, and stoichiometry of biogenic magnetic particles using transmission electron microscope observations (or equivalent). Over the last 15 years, a credible magnetofossil record has been built through the Cenozoic and into the Cretaceous. This complements a few existing credible Mesozoic and older magnetofossil occurrences. Despite the overall sparse global magnetofossil record, the potential to explore Earth’s earliest microbial record remains, which we seek to extend by working systematically back in time. Here we present results from Italian marine carbonate sequences in which we document the consistent presence of magnetofossils. Our results indicate that MTB were present through the Cretaceous (66-145 Ma) and Jurassic (145-201 Ma), with further limited evidence for Triassic (~240 Ma) magnetofossils. Much systematic work remains to build a record of microbial life and environments into deeper geological time.

presentations.presentation_title: Archaeomagnetism in Japan
presentations.abstract: Paleomagnetic measurements of archaeological materials, such as artifacts and structures, in Japan began in the 1940s and 1950s. In the 1960s and 1970s, large-scale residential development in Osaka resulted in the excavation of numerous climbing kilns, providing additional paleomagnetic data that revealed detailed information about geomagnetic secular variation. After Hirooka published the standard curve in 1971, 1977, and 1983, archaeomagnetic directions became a widely used chronological tool in archaeology. This state persisted for a long time. However, spurred by progress in large-scale archaeomagnetic projects in Europe during the 2000s, a revival project aimed at developing geomagnetic secular variation models and dating methods began, and it continues to this day. Regarding archaeomagnetic intensity measurements, however, the number of measurements in Japan was quite low because the destructive analysis of pottery shards and similar artifacts was not widely accepted in the archaeological community. Encouraged by the development of measurement equipment and improvements in the absolute paleointensity measurement methods, as well as the increasing acceptance of the analysis of archaeological artifacts, the number of measurements has increased in the 2010s. Currently, momentum is building with the launch of multiple projects conducting intensity measurements dating back over 2,000 years. In this presentation, we will provide an overview of this trend and introduce the current challenges in archaeomagnetism and archaeo-rock magnetism research in Japan.

presentations.presentation_title: Building a Case for Frequent, Rapid Geomagnetic Field Instabilities and Their Wider Implications Over the Last Glacial Cycle
presentations.abstract: Knowledge of Quaternary geomagnetic field behaviour has traditionally hinged on paleomagnetic analysis of (i) volcanic and (ii) sedimentary sequences. Both archives have well-known resolution limitations associated with (i) chronological precision and eruption frequency and (ii) smoothing due to magnetization lock-in effects. Despite these limitations, such archives provide evidence for frequent large-scale Quaternary geomagnetic excursions. Speleothems provide an excellent additional paleomagnetic archive because magnetizations are locked in rapidly via carbonate cementation, with high temporal resolution provided by precise radiometric dating. These advantages have been used to demonstrate large-scale geomagnetic field changes on unexpectedly rapid multi-decadal to centennial timescales, which provide further evidence of frequent and rapid Quaternary geomagnetic excursions. Cosmogenic isotope records from ice cores provide further temporally well resolved evidence for dipolar geomagnetic field changes. Compilation of results from the most highly resolved sedimentary, speleothem, and ice core records supports a view that frequent dipole field strength changes are associated with directional geomagnetic excursions. The temporal precision of these records enables comparison between geomagnetic field and climate changes, including from the same record (e.g., ice core), to assess long-discussed links between climate and geomagnetic field behaviour. Such comparisons can be extended to include well-dated records of genetic changes in populations of organisms. These diverse records are explored here to start to assess inter-relationships between geomagnetic field, climate, and population genetic changes.
presentations.session_title: Magnetism Across Time and Space: Unlocking Earth and Planetary Histories

presentations.presentation_title: An Adaptive Anisotropic Filter to Enhance Grace/grace-fo Signal Retrieval Via Directional Noise Smoothing
presentations.institution: Hubei University of Arts and Science
presentations.abstract: The Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and its successor GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) missions have significantly advanced our understanding of Earth’s time-variable gravity field, providing critical insights into Earth mass transport processes. However, the presence of stripe noise in the level-2 data limits the accuracy of geophysical interpretations. To address this issue, we propose a novel Adaptive Anisotropic Smoothing (AAS) method, which can dynamically adjust its directional smoothing strength based on a combination of two-dimensional Gaussian smoothing and longitudinal gradient characteristics, designed to suppress stripe noise directly in the spatial domain. Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) and Noise Reduction Ratio (NRR) are used to evaluate AAS's performance by comparing it to commonly used smoothing techniques. AAS demonstrates an average improvement of ~28% in SNR and ~55% in NRR over the DDK3, and ~34% in SNR and ~48% in NRR over the G300+P3M10. Furthermore, AAS exhibits superior retention of hydrological and cryosphere signals, yielding more consistent trends and annual amplitude estimates relative to the Level-3 data at both global and basin scales. Simulated experiments also confirm the advantages of AAS. By adaptively smoothing based on the spatial distribution characteristics of stripe noise, AAS minimizes over-smoothing especially in high-latitude regions, whereas filters designed solely from the correlation of spherical harmonic coefficients tend to overemphasize higher-degree components, leading to excessive smoothing. Given its demonstrated capability in both noise suppression and signal preservation, AAS represents a superior alternative to conventional filtering techniques for the data processing of GRACE/GRACE-FO time variable solutions.

presentations.presentation_title: Space Gravimetric Constraints on the Gravitational Coupling Between the Inner Core and the Mantle
presentations.abstract: The Earth’s solid inner core (IC) possesses an oblate shape with certain topographic features at its surface. Because of the presence of density anomalies in the mantle, the IC orientates its topographic surface in order to reach its equilibrium shape. This gravitational readjustment induces an IC reorientation that oscillates at a period depending on the strength of the mantle inner-core gravitational coupling. The largest contribution comes from the degree-2 density anomalies generated by the Large Low Velocity Provinces (LLVPs) below the Pacific Ocean and Africa. The induced surface gravity signature of the IC reorientation depends on a few parameters that are the amplitude of the topography at its surface, the tilt angle between the IC and the degree-2 density anomalies in the mantle, and the IC viscosity. The IC rotation also generates a gravitational torque on the mantle, counteracting the electromagnetic torque at the core mantle boundary, resulting in a net torque creating some variations in the Earth's daylength. These geodetic signatures are challenging to detect and interpret, particularly due to the difficulty of distinguishing them from surface processes. Albeit, numerical simplified models suggest that the long-term westward drift of the mantle resulting from the gravitational coupling between the IC and the mantle could be as high as 0.25° per year (15 km/year) close to what has been observed over the last few hundred years, implying a negligible long-term IC differential rotation resulting from the electromagnetic coupling at the core boundaries. In this work, we show how geodetic observations can constrain the gravitational coupling between the IC and the mantle in terms of a simplified model involving the hereabove mentioned parameters.

presentations.presentation_title: A Previously Unrecognized Coupling Between Groundwater and Interannual CO2 Growth Rate
presentations.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Terrestrial ecosystems have long acted as a major buffer against rising atmospheric CO 2 , yet the key terrestrial factors control on year-to-year fluctuations in the atmospheric CO 2 growth rate remain incompletely understood. While climatic factors such as temperature and surface water availability are widely recognized as important regulators of land carbon uptake, current explanations primarily emphasize temporal co-variability and give limited attention to how hydrological processes shape large-scale spatial coupling between land and atmosphere. In this study, by jointly using gravity satellite observations and hydrological model simulations, we demonstrate that groundwater storage plays a previously underappreciated role in modulating carbon cycle dynamics across both time and space. Beyond short-term surface moisture conditions, deep water reserves provide persistent hydrological support to ecosystems, enabling redistributed carbon responses under climate variability. We find that this groundwater–carbon coupling exhibits contrasting behaviors across latitude bands, forming a bipolar pattern in which global groundwater showing two opposite but dynamically connected modes of fluctuation. This spatially organized compensation suggests that groundwater functions not merely as a local water source, but as a stabilizing element in the Earth system that redistributes hydroclimatic impacts on ecosystem carbon exchange. Such regulation becomes increasingly relevant under intensifying droughts and precipitation extremes, where surface indicators alone may fail to capture ecosystem resilience. Our findings highlight the necessity of moving beyond surface-based representations of water–carbon coupling and call for next-generation modeling frameworks that explicitly account for subsurface hydrological memory and cross-regional interactions. Incorporating these processes is likely essential for improving projections of terrestrial carbon sinks in a changing climate.

presentations.presentation_title: Integrated Analysis of Climate Change-Driven Crop Migration and Groundwater Storage Anomalies Across China
presentations.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: GRACE and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) satellite gravimetry observes the Earth’s time-variable gravity field, providing a unique constraint on changes in terrestrial water storage and enabling the inference of groundwater storage anomalies (GWSA) in space and time. Building on this gravity-satellite information, this study is set in the context of changing crop spatial patterns across mainland China and focuses on composite pressure areas where rising agricultural water pressure and groundwater change overlap. From a national-scale perspective, we propose an integrated analysis framework that brings together crop distribution, climatic background, and GRACE/GRACE-FO-constrained groundwater change to identify potential groundwater-risk areas and to provide baseline information for subsequent interpretation and management decisions. We synthesize multi-source datasets on crop dynamics, climate, and GWSA, conduct regional comparisons, and summarize key features from temporal evolution and spatial differences. Overall, several regions show a co-occurrence of increasing agricultural water pressure and persistent groundwater decline, suggesting that human water use may be involved in groundwater depletion processes.

presentations.presentation_title: Multi-source Observation–constrained Long-term Reconstruction of Terrestrial Water Storage Variations
presentations.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Terrestrial water storage (TWS) is a key integrative indicator of the global water cycle and hydrologic extremes, yet generating long, internally consistent reconstructions remains challenging because of the limited observational record and the scarcity of constraints in the pre-GRACE era. Here we present a multi-observation–constrained framework for long-term TWS-change reconstruction. Our approach uses a high-spatial-resolution machine-learning product based on a CNN–BiLSTM architecture to represent the spatiotemporal structure of TWS variability, and leverages the extended record of satellite laser ranging (SLR) gravity-field solutions to impose a physically consistent constraint and correction on low-frequency, decadal-scale variations. Over the overlap period, we further benchmark the low-frequency adjustment against an independent reference dataset to ensure robust performance. The framework is designed to preserve the fine-scale spatial detail captured by the machine-learning reconstruction while stabilizing its low-frequency behaviour through complementary observational constraints, accompanied by consistency checks using multiple external datasets and an explicit assessment of uncertainty. The resulting long-term TWS-change record provides a data foundation for a broad range of Earth-science applications, including improved closure of global water budgets, stronger constraints for the evaluation of hydrological models, deeper insight into coupled climate–carbon–water processes, and evidence to inform water-resources management.

presentations.presentation_title: The Importance of Quantitatively Evaluating Geodetic Signals to Reduce Gravitational Redshift Uncertainty in the Continuous Operation of Optical Atomic Clocks
presentations.institution: National Institute of Information and Communications Technology
presentations.abstract: The National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (NICT) is advancing the development of strontium lattice clocks and indium ion clocks to support the calibration of International Atomic Time (TAI) and the steering of Japan Standard Time (JST). To ensure the long-term stability of optical atomic clocks, we apply accurate corrections for geodetic and geophysical effects. In the tectonically active western Pacific region, including Japan, we must quantify gravitational redshift uncertainty arising from crustal deformation linked to volcanic and seismic activity, solid Earth tides, ocean tide loading, and related geodynamic processes. Through this assessment, we aim to establish rigorous correction strategies that minimize clock-related uncertainties and enable high-precision chronometric levelling. Chronometric levelling, in turn, offers a promising approach for realizing the International Height Reference System (IHRS) by integrating global geoid modelling, GNSS observations, and advanced satellite gravimetry.Since 2021, we have conducted geodetic observations near the optical clocks at NICT headquarters in Koganei, Tokyo. With support from the National Institute of Polar Research (NIPR), we carried out absolute gravity measurements in August 2019 and May 2022, and with cooperation from the Earthquake Research Institute (ERI) of the University of Tokyo, we performed an additional campaign in March 2025. We obtained an absolute gravity change of −17.6 μGal. Using the in-situ vertical gravity gradient, this change corresponds to 6.35 cm of uplift. GEONET station 93019 indicates 7.02 cm of uplift over August 2019–March 2025, consistent with the gravity-inferred estimate. We continuously monitor Earth tide signals using a Micro-g LaCoste gPhoneX gravimeter installed adjacent to the clock facilities. We analyze the observed tidal variations with BAYTAP-G and compare them with predictions from ETGTAB, GOTIC2, and TIDE4N to evaluate their influence on gravitational redshift uncertainty. We will present recent activities and preliminary findings.

presentations.presentation_title: Towards Monitoring and Quantifying Subsidence Evolutions Using Multiple Geodetic Observables in Central Valley, California
presentations.abstract: It is estimated that by 2025, five billion people worldwide will live in water-stressed regions. The worldwide water stresses have been exacerbated by more frequent and more severe droughts resulting from an increasingly warmer Earth. Severe spatially and temporally heterogeneous land subsidence is highly correlated with excessive anthropogenic groundwater pumping for human consumption and agricultural irrigations leading to depleted and under-recharged aquifers, anthropogenic mineral extractions in the coastal deltaic or other regions leading sediment compaction/loading. In addition, increased frequency and magnitudes from cyclone-induced storm surge, and atmospheric river-driven land subsidence over aquifers and other regions, necessitates the knowledge and origin of land deformation, for timely and efficient disaster responses. Here, we postulate that multiple and distinctly different satellite based geodetic observables could be exploited together towards timely and monitoring at adequate spatiotemporal scales towards improved quantification of land subsidence and its hydro-geophysical origins to aid climate actions over agricultural and coastal regions. Our study region of Central Valley, California, USA contributes to the State of California’s agricultural economic income estimated at $61.2 billion in 2024, fourth largest in the world. Central Valley is under severe land subsidence since the 1902s, due primarily to anthropogenic groundwater pumping, causing collapses of aquifers and prolonged/serve droughts, and more recently atmosphere river-driven severe storm caused large floods. In this study, we used satellite gravimetry data, postprocessed to have enhanced temporal resolution, satellite altimetry over low gradient terrains (solid Earth), Sentinel-1A synthetic aperture radar interferometry (InSAR) land deformation time series, and deformation from available GNSS, and incorporating deep-learning analytics to process selected observables. We present primary results on our objective to quantify land subsidence, groundwater evolutions, storage changes, and their hydrogeologic state with potential applications for water resources management and disaster response in Central Valley, California, USA.

presentations.presentation_title: Yundukala Area Hydrothermal Au-Cu-Co Deposit, East Junggar, Xinjiang, Northwest China
presentations.abstract: The East Junggar terrane, a crucial component of the Central Asian Orogenic Belt (CAOB), is bounded by the Altai orogens. This region hosts diverse mineral systems, including subduction-related porphyry Cu and Fe-Cu-Au deposits, post-collisional Cu-Mo and Cu-Ni systems, and epithermal Au-Cu deposits. Recent exploration investments in Northwest China led to the discovery of the Yundukala Au-Cu-Co deposit on the northern margin of East Junggar. This diorite-related hydrothermal vein deposit features average grades of 0.2-16 wt% Cu, 0.1-21 g/t Au, and 0.01-0.78% Co.Mineralization is concentrated in three main alteration zones (700–2000 m long, 50–600 m wide) surrounding diorite and gabbro-diorite intrusions. The Au-Cu-Co mineralization occurs predominantly at the exo- and endo-contacts of diorite, especially along diorite-basalt interfaces. The mineralized zone comprises several ore bodies, including a principal Cu-Au-Co body and Cu-Au bodies. These NW-SE trending, vein- and stratiform-like bodies extend to 700m depth, with mineralization styles ranging from veinlet and stockwork to disseminated and locally massive structures, closely associated with silicification.The dominant ore structures are veinlet, stockwork, and disseminated, with metallic minerals primarily consisting of pyrite, chalcopyrite, and cobaltite, accompanied by subordinate pyrrhotite, native gold, electrum, and magnetite. Gangue minerals include K-feldspar, plagioclase, quartz, biotite, and chlorite.Chronological and geochemical studies indicate that the ore-bearing diorite and gabbro-diorite share similar origins. LA-ICP-MS zircon U-Pb dating yields Early Devonian ages of 401.3 ± 3.8 Ma and 401.6 ± 4.5 Ma, respectively. Integrated whole-rock Sr-Nd and zircon O-Hf isotope data suggest these magmas formed from the mixing of mantle-derived and crustal melts (10-30% crustal component). This mixing process likely provided essential sulfur and metals for mineralization. The geochemical signature supports an island arc setting for both the intrusions and the associated Cu-Au mineralization, indicating significant potential for discovering similar mineralization in aged intrusive complexes within this accreted terrane.

presentations.presentation_title: Lateral and Vertical Variations of Mineralization and Alteration in the Hoshino Epithermal Gold-silver System, Northern Kyushu, Japan
presentations.abstract: Northern Kyushu is a large epithermal gold metallogenic province in Japan which produced more than 1.5 million ounces of gold. The Hoshino epithermal gold-silver system is a prospective exploration area within Northern Kyushu as evidenced by occurrences of silica sinter, steam-heated alteration zones, and large quartz veins, although the distribution of these geological manifestations is not uniform across the area. This study investigates the lateral and vertical variations of mineralization and alteration of the system using surface rocks and newly drilled core samples. The western part is characterized by a huge hydrothermal breccia vein with black color matrix consisting of cryptocrystalline quartz. In the central part, crustiform-banded quartz vein is commonly distributed on surface, whereas colloform sulfide bands are partly present. A minor quartz-chlorite ± smectite vein is also observed. The eastern part is characterized by huge, massive quartz veins with a width of several meter. Bladed quartz after calcite are common across the system. The most proximal alteration zone is marked by intense silicification, whereas the dominant clay minerals tend to differ between the western (illite and interstratified illite-smectite) and eastern parts (chlorite and interstratified chlorite-smectite). δ³⁴S values of alunite from the advanced argillic alteration zone in the northern part range from −8.5 to −7.3 ‰, indicating a non-hypogene origin despite their relatively coarse crystal size. The modal homogenization temperature and average salinities of fluid inclusions in vein quartz show a systematic increase from the western (180–190 °C; 0.8 wt% NaCl eq.) to the eastern parts (230–240 °C; 2.1 wt% NaCl eq.). The erosion level is also higher in the eastern part of the system, inferred from boiling point with depth curves. Given the evidence presented here, the lateral variation in mineralization and alteration may reflect differences in the vertical level of exposure.

presentations.presentation_title: In-situ S Isotope Composition of Pyrite from the Shimokawa and Makimine Volcanogenic Massive Sulfide Deposits, Japan
presentations.abstract: Along with development of in-situ analytical techniques using LA-ICP-MS and/or SIMS, highly negative d 34 S value in pyrite has been recently reported from several volcanogenic massive sulfide (VMS) and seafloor massive sulfide (SMS) deposits. Since such a highly negative d 34 S value can be only produced by bacterial sulfate reduction (BSR), importance of microbial activity at the initial sulfide mineralization has been started to be recognized. In order to prove universality of importance of microbial activity related to the initial sulfide mineralization, we performed an in-situ S isotope analysis on pyrite using SIMS from two Besshi-type VMSs of the Shimokawa and Makimine deposits, Japan, which were formed by ridge subduction beneath the Japanese Islands. Pyrite in the Shimokawa and Makimine VMSs shows framboidal, recrystallized framboidal, colloform and euhedral textures along with the mineralogical evolution. d 34 S values in pyrite range from –30.5‰ to +16.5‰ at the Shimokawa deposit and from –25.3‰ to +9.0‰ at the Makimine deposit, respectively. Assuming the seawater d 34 S value of +20‰, the maximum isotopic fractionation is 50.5‰ and 45.3‰. Average d 34 S values in framboidal pyrite of two VMS deposits are both negative values, but the lowest d 34 S value was detected from euhedral pyrite. Based on the previous studies (Sato and Kase, 1996; Nakayama et al., 2022), handpicked sulfide minerals show the d 34 S value from –2 to +14‰ at the Shimokawa deposit and from +4 to +7‰ at the Makimine deposit, much narrower range than our results by SIMS. These mineralogical and geochemical lines of evidence indicate that pyrite with the low d 34 S value was formed by H 2 S produced by BSR and d 34 S values in pyrite were overprinted by later-stage mineralization. However, such an overprinting of later-stage mineralization is heterogenous and the lowest d 34 S values might have been partly preserved in euhedral pyrite.

presentations.presentation_title: Role of Magmatic Evolution in the Formation of Porphyry Cu Deposits
presentations.institution: Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences
presentations.abstract: Porphyry deposits are the world’s most significant source of Cu and an important source of Au. Most of these deposits are associated with arc magmas of intermediate to felsic composition. Hydrous, sulfur-rich, and relatively oxidized arc magmas, generated by partial melting of the metasomatized mantle wedge, pool in the lower crust and form large magma reservoirs. The evolving magmas, driven by buoyancy, ascend to the upper crust and accumulate in batholithic magma chambers with intermediate to felsic compositions. Voluminous hydrothermal fluids released from the upper crustal magmas extract, transport, and precipitate Cu and Au, forming porphyry deposits. During magmatic evolution, many factors influence the formation of porphyry mineralization, including the timing of sulfide saturation relative to volatile exsolution. If an evolving magma reaches sulfide saturation well before volatile saturation and precipitates a large amount of sulfides, the chalcophile elements, which include Cu and Au, will be trapped in sulfide phases in the cumulate pile of a deep magma chamber, where they will be unavailable to enter the hydrothermal fluid. Alternatively, if sulfide saturation occurs earlier than volatile saturation but only precipitates a small amount of sulfide, or sulfide saturation occurs after volatile saturation, the chalcophile elements will be available to enter the ore-forming fluid, resulting in porphyry mineralization. We have used platinum-group element geochemistry to identify sulfide saturation of the Northparkes and Escondida porphyry systems. We show that the late sulfide saturation in the Northparkes suite and a small amount of sulfide precipitation in the Escondida suite play an important role in their ore formation. In addition, we have investigated the sulfide saturation history of giant porphyry Cu systems to show that Au concentration in the magma, modulated by average magma differentiation depth and sulfide saturation history, has the dominant control on the Au grade of giant porphyry deposits.

presentations.presentation_title: Structure–geothermal Coupling and Fault-controlled Reservoirs in the Boye Area, Central North China Craton
presentations.institution: Institute of Geophysical and Geochemical Exploration, Chinese Academy of Geological Science
presentations.abstract: The distribution of geothermal resources is strongly influenced by the surface–subsurface structural architecture of a region; however, the quantitative linkage between fault systems and geothermal reservoirs remains insufficiently constrained in extensional basins. In this study, a multi-disciplinary approach, integrating gas geochemistry, controlled-source electromagnetic surveys, and geothermal well logging, was applied to the Boye area to elucidate its structure–geothermal coupling. Results indicate that NE–SW-trending listric normal faults, dipping NW or SE, dominate the structural framework and control the spatial distribution of heat sources, reservoirs, and migration pathways. Deep carbonate geothermal reservoirs mainly comprise Middle Proterozoic dolomites (Jxw and Chg), characterized by abundant fractures and cavities that provide effective storage and enhance convective heat transfer, consistent with the reduced geothermal gradients recorded in boreholes. Geothermal accumulation in the Boye area is governed by the integrated effects of source, migration, reservoir, and cap structures. Source structures facilitate the upward transfer of crust–mantle heat flow, whereas migration structures, including faults and unconformities, act as conduits linking deep heat sources with reservoirs. Reservoir structures consist of both fault-related and intra-reservoir fractures and cavities, providing favorable storage and flow conditions. Cap structures, modified by Cenozoic faulting, regulate meteoric recharge and thermal preservation. This study establishes a structural–geothermal framework for the Boye area, highlighting the role of extensional fault systems in controlling heat and fluid migration, and providing a methodological reference for geothermal exploration in comparable tectonic settings.

presentations.presentation_title: The Magnetic Signature of Ultramafic-hosted Hydrothermal Vents: Effects of Size, Temperature, and Time
presentations.institution: Université Paris Cité / National Centre for Scientific Research
presentations.abstract: Ultramafic-hosted hydrothermal sites involve the formation of new magnetic minerals which presence, abundance, and magnetization rely on transformations that depend on temperature of emitted fluids, size of sites, and time spent after initiation then cessation of the hydrothermal activity. The magnetic signature of such sites therefore reflects these three parameters. Near-seafloor magnetic surveys of Sites Rainbow, Ashadze, Logachev, Lost City, and Van Damm have shown the requirement of a significant size for any clear magnetic signature (Szitkar et al., Geology, 2014) and the dependence of the magnetic mineralogy to the fluid temperature at the large sites (Szitkar and Murton, Geology, 2018). Site Rainbow shows a weak positive magnetic anomaly at the initiation of a site (East of Site Rainbow) and very strong positive anomalies when the site is fully developed (Eastern mound) or recently abandoned (Western mound). These observations relate to the abundance of magnetite formed in the stockwork during hydrothermal activity and preserved by reducing environment shortly after its cessation. During Cruise Hermine 2, two extinct ultramafic-hosted sites, Pompeii 1 and 2, have been discovered on a large oceanic core complex of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge at 21°19'N. Pompeii 1 is a large hydrothermal mound, 150m wide and 40m high, made of sulfide-bearing rocks suggestive of high temperature fluids. Pompeii 2 is a smaller mound, 70m wide and 20m high, located 200m westward, made of talc and silica-rich rocks suggestive of low temperature fluids. Weak hydrothermal activity in still observed at Pompeii 1, with fluids at 4.25°C. A weak positive magnetic anomaly is observed on Pompeii 1, whereas Pompeii 2 does not display any anomaly. This suggest that, after high temperature activity ceases, seawater pervasively alters the hydrothermal deposits, oxidizing magnetite to maghemite and non-magnetic minerals and erasing the positive magnetic anomaly of ultramafic-hosted sites.

presentations.presentation_title: Delineation of Subsurface Configuration and Associated Thermal Regime of the Mahanadi Geothermal Province, Odisha, Based on Gravity Modelling and Magnetic Spectral Analysis
presentations.abstract: In the present work, gravity-magnetic data are utilised to decipher the crustal setup and the thermal regime of the central part of EGMB, which hosts four non-volcanic hot springs: Atri, Tarabalo, Deulajhari, and Taptapani. Regional-scale investigations based on acquired and global gravity and magnetic data have delineated the deeper structural features and their effects on the region's geothermal activities. 3D gravity inversion for Moho depth estimation as well as spectral analysis of magnetic data, Curie point depth (CPD) estimation, and heat flow values due to radiogenic crustal elements provided a better understanding of the variation of thermal structure (e.g., CPD, heat flow, geothermal gradient) with crustal thickness (e.g., Moho surface) and their correlation with the locations of four hot springs in the study area. The observed Curie depth surface below the study area is shallower than the Moho interface obtained from the 3D inversion, resulting in a higher geothermal gradient and higher heat flow estimates due to CPD. Further, surface heat flow due to radiogenic heat production (RHP) of the high-grade metamorphic rocks of the study area is estimated and compared with that obtained from the CPD estimates. Both these estimates are higher than the global mean heat flow value associated with stable continental regions, implying a collective contribution of RHP from lithology of the thin magnetic crust, along with basal heat flux from the deeper part. The major shear zones in the vicinity of the hot springs occur in the region with shallower CPD and higher heat flow, suggesting a possible role played by them and associated fracture/fault networks in transferring the geothermally heated fluid. Thus, the present study provides a better understanding of the thermal aspects of a portion of the EGMB crust and their consequences for the geothermal setup of the study area.

presentations.presentation_title: The 1762 Damaging Earthquake in Sado Island Revisited: Reanalysis of Historical Materials and Numerical Modeling of Seismic Intensity and Tsunami
presentations.abstract: The 1762 Horeki Sado earthquake (October 31, 1762) caused damage on Sado Island, Japan’s largest island in the Sea of Japan, including collapses of stone walls and houses and tsunami inundation and washout. With the recent development of fault models in the Sea of Japan from the integrated research project on seismic and tsunami hazards around the Sea of Japan, we reassess the most plausible source fault for this event through (i) reexamination historical materials and (ii) numerical forward modeling of seismic intensity and tsunami. A newly compiled intensity map based on highly reliable sources indicates that damage on the terrestrial area of Sado Island was relatively minor, whereas the felt area extended toward the northeast and southeast. Forward calculations of intensity distributions for candidate fault models near Sado Island show that two models—SD09 (Mw 7.1) and MRK08+SD10 (Mw 7.4), a composite rupture model combining the adjacent MRK08 and SD10 faults—reproduce these characteristics, while other models overestimate intensities either on Sado Island or on the mainland. Tsunami simulations further suggest that SD09 best explains both the documented locally high tsunami along the northeastern coast of Sado Island and the low, largely unrecognized tsunami along the mainland coast inferred from no tsunami records. In contrast, MRK08+SD10 produces nearly comparable tsunami heights along the coasts of Sado Island and the mainland. These results indicate that the source fault of the 1762 earthquake was located offshore to the north of Sado Island with a magnitude of approximately Mw 7. The integrated approach combining historical-source reassessment with intensity and tsunami modeling is applicable to other historical earthquake–tsunami events along the Sea of Japan, such as the 1833 Tempo earthquake.

presentations.presentation_title: Multiple Volcanic Sources of Drift Pumice Collected on Modern Beaches in Japan
presentations.abstract: Pumice is a pyroclastic material with low apparent density (often < 1 g/cm³). Because of its high vesicularity, some pumice clasts can float on water. Once pumice enters the ocean, it may be transported over long distances by surface currents and then washed ashore or eventually sink as pores become waterlogged or encrusted with marine organisms. Such material, commonly referred to as drift pumice, is widely observed along coasts and within sediments. In Japan, drift pumice frequently found on modern beaches and is preserved in geological records.In 2021, the submarine volcano Fukutoku-Oka-no-Ba in the Izu–Ogasawara arc erupted, and a large volume of pumice discharged into the ocean formed extensive pumice rafts stranding along the Nansei Islands. If similar drifting events occurred in the past, their evidence may remain along coasts and in coastal sediments. However, the processes linking pumice production, marine transport, and deposition remain poorly understood.This study analyzed the major element compositions of volcanic glass shards in 603 drift pumice samples collected from five beaches along the Pacific coast of Japan between September 2018 and August 2019. The samples originated from multiple sources, including the Aira, Aso, and Kikai or Ata calderas, as well as Fukutoku-Oka-no-Ba volcano, the submarine volcano north-northeast of Iriomotejima, Changbaishan volcano, and Sakurajima volcano. The results indicate that, during periods without direct pumice supply to the ocean, remobilization and fluvial transport from subaerial pyroclastic-flow deposits likely represent a major source of drift pumice. These findings clarify the life cycle of drift pumice and contribute to its application in tephrochronology and to improving the chronological precision of eruption histories of submarine volcanoes.

presentations.presentation_title: Revisiting the 1604 M8.0 Quanzhou Earthquake and Tsunami Event: Insight from a Physics-based Simulation Framework
presentations.abstract: The 1604 M8.0 Quanzhou earthquake is the largest historical seismic event recorded along the Southeastern China coast. Occurring in the seismically active Taiwan Strait, this event poses a significant challenge for modern hazard assessment due to the lack of instrumental data. Specifically, the source mechanism—whether it was a strike-slip or thrust event—and the origin of the accompanying tsunami remain controversial. In this study, we reconstruct this earthquake using a physics-based simulation framework. First, based on the detailed geometry of the Littoral Fault Zone, we constructed a 3D non-planar fault model. Using the Curved Grid Finite-Difference Method (CGFDM), we performed dynamic rupture simulations constrained by the regional tectonic stress field and depth-dependent friction laws. We tested various rupture scenarios to identify the model that best matches historical observations. The resulting seafloor deformation was then used to initiate a hydrodynamic model to simulate the tsunami generation and propagation processes. To validate our approach, we compare the simulated seismic intensities and tsunami run-up heights with records from historical chronicles. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the role of fault geometric complexities in tsunami excitation. We explicitly aim to quantitatively evaluate whether the localized vertical deformation induced by a complex strike-slip rupture is sufficient to trigger the historically documented tsunami. This study seeks to provide a physical explanation for the source mechanism of the 1604 event and offers insights into the compound earthquake-tsunami hazards posed by complex fault systems along the Southeastern China coast.

presentations.presentation_title: Switchover of the Volcanism Phases of Kirishima Volcano Deciphered from Eruption Records of the Historical Period
presentations.abstract: Kirishima Volcano, similar to the Aso and Fuji volcanoes, is one of the most active volcanoes in Japan, with many historical records of eruptions dating back to the 8th century. Kirishima Volcano has erupted primarily andesitic magma and is one of the most widely distributed volcanoes in Japan. Accurate analysis of historical eruption records is important for comparative studies of seismic activity and magma supply systems. However, official eruption records of this volcano in the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) catalogue (JMA ed., 2013) include cases wherein accidental fires were misinterpreted as eruptions. Therefore, these records need to be reviewed. Recent studies on Kirishima Volcano have more accurately compiled records from the 8th to 13th centuries, as well as from the period after the 18 century. However, records from the late 13th to 17th centuries have not been subjected to extensive scientific study and warrant detailed examination. This study reviewed the records of this period principally based on the “Geihan Meishokou” geographical document and “Kagoshimaken Kazanshi” chronological document found that several of the approximately 25 records in the JMA catalogue were not eruption records compared with other historical records but were misinterpreted. Six of the eruption records provided insufficient evidence to be identified as Ohachi eruptions, and two records might be identified as eruptions of Ebinokogen-Ioyama. One record suggests that the Shinmoedake had spent a long quiet time before 1656 CE. The results of this study together with those of Tajima (2026) indicate that the mode of activity of Kirishima Volcano changed significantly from a single volcanism phase up to the around 14th century to a multiple volcanism phase beginning in the mid-16th century.

presentations.presentation_title: Paleoseismic Signatures of Historical Earthquakes (16th and 19th Centuries) from Kumaon-garhwal, Central Himalaya
presentations.abstract: The paleoseismic study from the Kaladungi Fault (KF) in the Kumaon-Garhwal Himalaya was carried out to constrain the rupture history of major historical earthquakes. A paleoseismic trench excavated at the base of a 15 m high fault scarp at Nandpur revealed geological evidence of four surface-rupturing paleoearthquakes. In total 24 Optically Stimulated Luminescence (OSL) and 24 radiocarbon (14C) ages allowed robust bracketing of these events. Based on offsets of sedimentary units and ages we infer that Event-I took place between BCE 2945-1990 and BCE 1480-862, and Event-II was between BCE 1264-643 and BCE 793-287. These events could not be correlated with any paleo-earthquakes due to broad age brackets and non-availability of any pre-historic records. Event-III occurred between CE 1242–1408 and CE 1415–1529, while Event-IV (MRE) was between CE 1692–1761 and CE 1689–1822. To constrain and correlate the rupture lengths of Event III and Event IV, we considered historical records and regional paleoseismic data from Nepal, Kumaon-Garhwal to the western Himalaya. The Event-III corresponds to the CE 1505 earthquake and Event-IV (MRE) represents the CE 1803 earthquake.

presentations.presentation_title: Reassessing Tsunami Hazards Along the Western Indian Margin: Insights from Far-field Makran and Local Seismic Sources
presentations.abstract: The western coast of India is highly susceptible to tsunami hazards due to its proximity to the Makran Subduction Zone (MSZ), one of the most seismically active convergent margins in the northern Indian Ocean. During the Late Holocene, the Great Rann of Kachchh (GRK) functioned as an embayment of the Arabian Sea, acting both as a receiver of far-field tsunami waves and as a potential local tsunami source due to regional seismicity. Such events may have contributed to the relocation or abandonment of past settlements in Kachchh. Geological records, including tsunami deposits along the western Indian coast and within the GRK, indicate multiple Holocene tsunami events and highlight the need for numerical simulations to understand their dynamics and impacts. Here, we numerically simulate tsunami generation, propagation, and inundation under present-day and paleo-bathymetric conditions for two source scenarios: MSZ-sourced far-field events and GRK-sourced local events. Paleo-shorelines are incorporated using bathymetric reconstructions for relative sea-level highstands of +5 m and +9 m. Far-field scenarios generate moderate wave heights (0.6–1.0 m) along the western Indian coast, with limited impact on settlements. In contrast, locally generated scenarios produce higher wave amplitudes, reaching ~3.7 m within inland basins and ~1.5 m along coastal margins. Inundation modelling shows that only GRK-sourced events cause significant flooding at key archaeological sites, with depths of ~0.5–1 m during Holocene highstands. These results demonstrate the role of relative sea-level fluctuations in modulating tsunami hazards and emphasize integrating paleo-sea-level, geological, and archaeological data for long-term coastal risk assessment (Sharma et al., 2026, Geoscience Letters (https://doi.org/10.1186/s40562-025-00453-y)).
